# by_design.md — intentional divergences from matter.js

This is the divergence catalogue the Go code cites. When a comment in this
module says `see notes/parity/by_design.md <ID>`, the entry is here.

**What belongs here.** A deliberate deviation from
[matter.js](https://github.com/matter-js/matter.js) HEAD — the Matter-side
gold standard this module is a semantic port of (see
[`CLAUDE.md`](../../CLAUDE.md) and
[`docs/matter-parity-contract.md`](../../docs/matter-parity-contract.md)).
Each entry names what matter.js does, what this module does instead, why, what
pins it, and — where one exists — the condition that would retire it.

**What does not.** A defect is not a divergence. Open behaviour gaps live in
[`matter_behaviour_findings.md`](./matter_behaviour_findings.md); closing one
removes it from that list rather than adding it here. And schema values —
cluster IDs, revisions, attribute IDs, constraint defaults — are never a valid
divergence: they come verbatim from the embedded matter.js extract.

**Provenance and stale paths.** These entries were written while the Matter
stack lived inside [OpenCCU-Loom](https://github.com/SukramJ/openccu-loom) as
`internal/north/matter/`. Paths into this module have been rewritten to its
root. Paths that still read `cmd/openccu-loom/…`, `internal/model/…`,
`internal/central/…` or `internal/store/…` are the **reference host's** wiring,
not this module's: they are left as written because the decision they record
was made against that code, and a host embedding this module wires the same
seams under its own names. Divergences that are purely a host-side device
projection stayed in OpenCCU-Loom's own
[`notes/parity/by_design.md`](https://github.com/SukramJ/openccu-loom/blob/main/notes/parity/by_design.md).

Some entries are part-German; that is how they were written and the text is
left verbatim rather than re-translated after the fact.

## Ahead of matter.js — register

Behaviour this module implements where matter.js implements none
([`CLAUDE.md`](../../CLAUDE.md), workflow step 5). Each row names the
**marker**: the matter.js line at the pin that shows the gap. At every pin
lift the markers are re-read at the new pin; a marker that no longer holds is
the verdict **caught up** in [`pin-lifts.md`](./pin-lifts.md), and the two
implementations are reconciled onto matter.js before the row closes. A new
ahead-of-matter.js implementation adds its row in the same change.

Markers below were checked at the pin `862ad75f` where a matter.js file is
named. At `db021da0` every marker text is still a substring of its file, or
its class body unchanged, as `script/aheadcheck`'s
`TestAheadcheckRegisterHoldsAtThePin` measured in review II, phase 5b; the
line numbers in the `matter.js marker` column were not re-read with it
unless the row names `db021da0`. At the pin lift to `b25ed960` the rows whose marker
moved or no longer stood for the gap were re-read and name `b25ed960`; the
rows that lift found caught up stay open until their reconcile unit closes them
([`pin-lifts.md`](./pin-lifts.md)). "Not recorded" means the entry states that matter.js has no logic but
cites no matter.js line; the marker is set when the entry is next touched or
at the next pin lift, read from the tree — never assumed.

**The marker columns are machine-read** by `script/aheadcheck`
(`make ahead-check`, and weekly in `.github/workflows/matterjs-pin.yml`
against matter.js `origin/main`). The contract:

- `marker file` holds one or more matter.js paths from the tree root, each in
  backticks, several separated by `<br>`.
- `marker text` holds one marker per path, in backticks and in the same
  order: a Go-quoted string (`\n` is a line break, `\"` a quote; no `|` and
  no backtick inside) that is a substring of that file **while the gap
  exists**, or `class <Name>`, which stands for the whole body of that
  class as it reads at the pin — from its declaration line through the
  lone `}` that closes it — and holds while the file still contains that
  body unchanged.
- A **presence** marker quotes the line that states the gap (a doc sentence
  that leaves the work to the device, the code that accepts everything). An
  **absence** marker quotes the text that would have to change for matter.js
  to add the logic — the whole class body (`class <Name>`, or a quoted
  one-line class); the `matter.js marker` column says which kind the row's
  marker is. An absence marker over a whole class body reports every edit
  of that class, a cosmetic one included; that is intended — a sure
  trigger is worth a re-read that finds nothing.
- Both columns read `not recorded` for a row without a marker; the check
  refuses such a row (the transitional allowance file
  `script/aheadcheck/todo-marker.txt` went with the last of the six
  `BD-chip` rows on 2026-10-25).
- `surface` is `yes` when enabling the row's elements changes what a
  controller sees (FeatureMap, AttributeList, AcceptedCommandList,
  GeneratedCommandList or EventList), measured by building the cluster
  with and without them (`script/aheadcheck`'s surface test); `no`
  otherwise. A `yes` row is served only behind `surface.Policies.Extensions`
  (ADR 0030 decision 3).

The check reads every marker at the pin (absent there: the row is wrong)
and at the ref it is given (absent there: the finding "caught up?", which a
pin lift confirms by re-reading the row, [`pin-lifts.md`](./pin-lifts.md)).
A row a pin lift found caught up, whose reconcile unit has not landed yet,
is listed in `script/aheadcheck/caught-up.txt` (`<entry> <pin sha> <unit>`)
and keeps its marker as it stood before the lift, recording what vanished;
for it the check inverts — the marker must no longer hold at the pin the
line names, and that pin must be the current one, so a caught-up row closes
within its lift's waves and never rides across another lift. The closing
unit removes the line with the row.

### BD-Matter-SmokeCoAlarmRulesInServer — ExpressedState, the self-test gate and the events are derived by the server

matter.js `SmokeCoAlarmServer`
(`packages/node/src/behaviors/smoke-co-alarm/SmokeCoAlarmServer.ts:18-42` at `b25ed960`)
seeds the initial state and nothing else: which condition ExpressedState
shows, refusing SelfTestRequest while alarming, and emitting the eleven
events are left to the application that subclasses it.
[`cluster/alarm`](../../cluster/alarm) does all three, from the
specification text matter.js carries in
`packages/model/src/standard/resources/smoke-co-alarm-cluster.resource.ts`:

- **ExpressedState** is derived from the host's snapshot through a
  priority order (`DefaultExpressedStatePriority`, overridable per host,
  since the resource says the order is the manufacturer's, :27-30);
  `State.Inoperative` takes precedence. The default order is the one
  connectedhomeip's smoke-co-alarm example application passes to
  `SetExpressedStateByPriority`, as `cluster/alarm/smokecoalarm_server.go:296-317`
  cites it (`examples/smoke-co-alarm-app/silabs/src/SmokeCoAlarmManager.cpp:32-36`
  at `6170af84`); the findings register's row for it closed with that
  citation (#137). The example application lies outside the export review
  II read and was not re-read (unverified).
- **SelfTestRequest** answers BUSY while ExpressedState is SmokeAlarm,
  CoAlarm, Testing, InterconnectSmoke or InterconnectCO (:201-204) and
  only then reaches the host's `SelfTester`. A source without one leaves
  the optional command out of AcceptedCommandList, which is what matter.js
  does for an optional command it was given no implementation for.
- **Events** are the difference between two snapshots (`Server.Refresh`),
  one rule per event as the resource words it (:124-195), at the
  element's priorities. The baseline before the first Refresh is
  matter.js's initial state.

**Rationale.** In a bridge the application is the host, whose device model
knows nothing about Matter's event rules; spreading them across every host
would produce a different reading of the same specification per host. The
wire surface is unchanged against matter.js — same attributes, same event
payloads (pinned against matter.js encodings in
`bridge/testdata/application-wire-fixtures.json`).

### BD-Matter-FanControlCouplingInServer — FanMode / PercentSetting / SpeedSetting coupling and a default Step

matter.js `FanControlServer`
(`packages/node/src/behaviors/fan-control/FanControlServer.ts:13-19`) only
defaults FanMode to Off. [`cluster/fan`](../../cluster/fan) resolves every
speed-oriented write into one `fan.Settings` before the host sees it:

- FanMode Off → PercentSetting 0 / SpeedSetting 0; Auto → both null
  (`fan-control.resource.ts:82-84`, :120-122); Low / Medium / High leave
  both to the device's own mode mapping (nil fields), because the
  percentage a mode means is the manufacturer's.
- PercentSetting p → SpeedSetting ceil(SpeedMax × p / 100); SpeedSetting s
  → PercentSetting floor(s × 100 / SpeedMax); either at 0 → FanMode Off.
  The resource refers to "Percent Rules" (§4.4.6.3.1) and "Speed Rules"
  (§4.4.6.6.1) without carrying them; the formulas are connectedhomeip's
  `src/app/clusters/fan-control-server/FanControlCluster.cpp:197` and `:224`
  at `6170af84`.
- A null PercentSetting / SpeedSetting write succeeds and changes nothing
  (:86-87, :126); a FanMode the FanModeSequence does not offer is
  CONSTRAINT_ERROR (:48-51, :62-63), where connectedhomeip answers
  INVALID_IN_STATE under a TODO for the ConstraintError
  (`FanControlCluster.cpp:394-398`); the deprecated On maps to High and
  Smart to Auto or High, as connectedhomeip does (`FanControlCluster.cpp:401-411`).
- Step goes to a host `Stepper` when there is one; otherwise the server
  steps one unit of SpeedSetting (MultiSpeed) or one rung of the
  sequence's speed modes, honouring Wrap and LowestOff. The resource calls
  the interpretation "implementation specific" (:214-215); the mode ladder
  is its own example (:219-224).

**Rationale.** Same as for SmokeCoAlarm: the coupling is identical for every
fan, and a host that had to re-derive it would differ from the next host.
Validation that matter.js's generated behavior does perform — types, enum
membership, "max 100", "max speedMax", bitmap bits — is mirrored as such.

### BD-Matter-OperationalStateRulesInServer — command answers and state-list rules the specification text adds to OperationalStateServer

matter.js `OperationalStateServer` / `RvcOperationalStateServer`
(`packages/node/src/behaviors/operational-state/OperationalStateServer.ts`,
`.../rvc-operational-state/RvcOperationalStateServer.ts`) keep the state
consistent through reactors and implement no command; the device that
subclasses them calls `OperationalStateUtils.assertPause` /
`assertRvcPause` / `assertResume` / `assertRvcResume` / `assertRvcGoHome`
and moves the state. [`cluster/opstate`](../../cluster/opstate) mirrors the
reactors and the Utils checks as code and hands every command that passes
them to the host's `CommandHandler`. On top it applies, from
`operational-state.resource.ts` / `rvc-operational-state.resource.ts`:

- A command that finds the device in its target state — Pause while
  Paused, Stop while Stopped, Start or Resume while Running, GoHome while
  SeekingCharger — answers NoError and does not reach the host ("respond
  with … NoError but take no further action", :176, :213, :241, :266;
  GoHome).
- OperationalStateList must contain the state each supported command
  leads to (Paused, Running, Stopped, SeekingCharger), "at a minimum, …
  the set of states matching the commands that are also supported"
  (:98-99); the initial state must be listed (:106-107); no state is
  listed twice, and a reserved (undefined, non-manufacturer) id is
  refused.
- OperationalStateList is fixed at construction. matter.js lets a device
  replace it at run time; no appliance seen so far changes its state set,
  and a fixed list keeps every OperationalState assertion stable.
- The state the device ends up in after a successful command is the
  host's to set, as in matter.js; the server does not guess it.

CountdownTime's "Q" reporting is matter.js's own (QuietEvent, at most one
report a second, at once to or from null) — the specification's fuller
list of reportable changes is not implemented by either.

**Rationale.** As for SmokeCoAlarm: the rules are the same for every
appliance, and a host should not re-derive them. The wire surface is
matter.js's, pinned in `bridge/testdata/application-wire-fixtures.json`.

### BD-Matter-ModeBaseRulesInServer — ModeBase tag rules from the specification, and ChangeToMode decided by the device

matter.js's mode servers (`RvcRunModeServer.ts`, `RvcCleanModeServer.ts`,
`LaundryWasherModeServer.ts`, `DishwasherModeServer.ts`, with
`mode-base/ModeUtils.ts`) check labels and mode values for duplicates and
each derivation's required tags, and their default `changeToMode` sets
CurrentMode to any supported mode. [`cluster/modebase`](../../cluster/modebase)
mirrors those checks as code and differs in two respects:

- **Spec-text checks at construction** (`mode-base.resource.ts`,
  SupportedModes and ModeOptionStruct.ModeTags): the tags of one mode are
  distinct, no two modes carry the same set of tags (order-independent),
  and every mode has at least one standard tag (one without MfgCode).
- **ChangeToMode is the device's**: a supported mode other than the
  current one goes to the host's `ModeChanger`, which may refuse with
  GenericFailure, InvalidInMode, a derivation status (Stuck, BatteryLow,
  CleaningInProgress, …) or a product-specific status (128 to 191, the
  element's `MfgCodes`, `mode-base.element.ts:79` at `b25ed960`;
  `validHostStatus`, `cluster/modebase/modebase_server.go:793-805` — the
  findings register's row for the range closed with #137); only Success
  moves CurrentMode. matter.js's
  default accepts every supported mode — a bridged device has to be asked.
  A host answering UnsupportedMode (the server's own verdict) or an
  undefined status gets FAILURE; StatusText is cut to its "max 64" bytes.

DIRECTMODECH is advertised as configured. RvcRunMode's half of its rule the
server applies itself: without the feature, a change between two modes that
both lack the Idle tag answers InvalidInMode before the host is asked
(`runModeLocked`, `cluster/modebase/modebase_server.go:704-709`, `:738-743`;
the rule's text is `rvc-run-mode.resource.ts:24-28` at `b25ed960`, and
`BD-chip-RvcRunMode-InvalidInMode` records it). RvcCleanMode's half
(InvalidInMode while the RVC is not in an Idle mode) involves RvcRunMode's
state and is the host's to apply in its `ModeChanger`, as matter.js leaves
it to the device.

**Rationale.** A bridge cannot accept a mode change on the device's behalf;
the tag rules are the specification's and the same for every host.

Review II, close-out C3 (R2-C2-par-1456): the derivations' required-tag and
exclusive-tag rules match a mode tag by value alone and do not read
`mfgCode`, as matter.js: `modeTags.some(({ value }) => value === …ModeTag.Normal)`
(`packages/node/src/behaviors/laundry-washer-mode/LaundryWasherModeServer.ts:26-27`,
`packages/node/src/behaviors/rvc-run-mode/RvcRunModeServer.ts:26-27`,
`:33-34`, `:42-44` at `b25ed960`; only these two derivations were read).

### BD-Matter-ModeSelect-HostOwnsTheMode — ModeSelect serves neither StartUpMode nor OnMode, and reads null without a source

matter.js's `ModeSelectServer` applies StartUpMode at start-up (unless the
boot reason is SoftwareUpdateCompleted) and, with DEPONOFF, OnMode when the
endpoint's OnOff turns on or its StartUpOnOff is On
(`packages/node/src/behaviors/mode-select/ModeSelectServer.ts:31-62`,
`:97-101` at `862ad75f`). `cluster/modeselect.Server` advertises no feature
and serves neither attribute (`modeselect_server.go` `featureMap`): the mode
is the host's `ModeSource`'s, so a start-up or on-mode is the device's
decision, made where the device powers up, and advertising DEPONOFF would
promise an OnMode the server does not hold. A write to either answers
UNSUPPORTED_ATTRIBUTE. Without a `ModeSource` the four projected attributes
read as null (only StandardNamespace carries quality X): `NewServer` returns
no error, so refusing a nil source would change its signature, and a value
invented here could not be told apart from one the device confirmed.
Reasoning: the scope cut keeps the mode in one place (W3-club2-04, -06).
Retire when a host needs a start-up mode the server applies; then mirror
`ModeSelectServer.ts:31-62` through the source.

### BD-Matter-TemperatureControl-RulesInServer — SetTemperature checked as connectedhomeip checks it; matter.js has no server logic

matter.js `TemperatureControlServer.ts` adds nothing to the generated
behaviour; SetTemperature is the host's. `cluster/thermo.TemperatureControlServer`
checks the request before it calls the host, following Matter Application
Cluster Specification 1.6.1 §8.8 as connectedhomeip implements it
(`src/app/clusters/temperature-control-server/TemperatureControlCluster.cpp`,
harness pin 6170af84):

- only the field of the server's own feature is read; the other one is
  ignored (`HandleSetTemperature` :174-217);
- a missing own field is INVALID_COMMAND (:176, :196);
- a TargetTemperature outside MinTemperature..MaxTemperature, or with STEP
  not on a step from MinTemperature, is CONSTRAINT_ERROR
  (`SetTemperatureSetpoint` :119-125);
- a TargetTemperatureLevel not below the length of
  SupportedTemperatureLevels is CONSTRAINT_ERROR (:135);
- a change the device cannot accept now is INVALID_IN_STATE (:191, :215);
  the host signals it with `thermo.ErrTemperatureRefused`, any other host
  error is FAILURE.

On success the setpoint or level becomes the requested value (:127, :138);
MaxTemperature is not required to lie on a Step (:48-51). chip is the
authority here because matter.js models no behaviour for this cluster.
Guards: `TestTemperatureControlSetTemperature`,
`TestParityMatterJS_TemperatureControl` (PR #41).

### BD-Matter-ClosureWithoutTagList — the Closure endpoint omits the TAGLIST feature its device type marks mandatory

A garage drive projects as the Closure device type (0x0230) carrying
ClosureControl (0x0104). matter.js's `closure-device.element.ts:17` (at `b25ed960`)
marks the Descriptor's `TAGLIST` feature conformance `M` for that device
type; our Descriptor advertises `FeatureMap=0` and reports TagList as
unsupported by default (`cluster/core/descriptor.go`, `descriptorAttrTagList`).
`Descriptor.EnableTagList` turns the feature on per endpoint; the endpoint
assembler calls it for an endpoint that carries tags (`enableTags`,
`endpoint/materialize.go:580-588`) and leaves it off for one without, so
the divergence holds as a default.

**Rationale.** The Descriptor is shared by every endpoint, and TagList is
already disabled there for a controller-interop reason that predates this
work: Apple's iOS Matter SDK does not ship a `semtag` struct schema, so an
endpoint that reports TagList makes Apple reject the whole Descriptor
cluster and abort the HAP service build with `HAPErrorDomain Code=14`.
Turning the feature on to satisfy the Closure device type would trade a
conformance gap no controller currently checks for a pairing abort that
was observed in practice.

The gap is narrow: TagList carries semantic tags that describe an
endpoint's role within a composed device, and the garage projects as a
single endpoint with nothing to disambiguate. Revisit together with the
Descriptor-wide TagList decision — the two are the same switch, and this
entry exists so that switch is not flipped for the Closure device type
alone.

Since the schema pin 85cf6647 matter.js generates the Closure, ClosurePanel
and ElectricalEnergyTariff device types with `DescriptorServer.with("TagList")`
(08ef820f, #4576), so the divergence is now one from matter.js's code as
well as its model. A Closure endpoint built without `Options.Tags` is such
an endpoint: the device-type validator (ADR 0016, warn mode) reports it at
every start as `matter.devicetype.violation … requirement=Descriptor.TAGLIST`;
that warning is this entry, not a new defect.

Phase 31 ported matter.js's corpus case "refuses a Closure endpoint without
the tags its Descriptor TagList requires"
(`StandardDeviceTypeCorpusTest.ts:548-559` at 862ad75f): matter.js refuses
the endpoint at construction, because its generated `ClosureDevice` turns
TagList on and the Descriptor fails to initialize without
`descriptor.state.tagList`. The kit builds a Closure without
`Options.Tags` with the feature off, so the same endpoint is refused only
by the device-type judge — a strict validator refuses it, the default warn
mode reports it (`device:TestStandardDeviceTypeCorpusParityMatterJS`);
with `Options.Tags` (phase 30) it conforms. The Duplicate condition's
TagList requirement of Base is judged as matter.js judges it
(`DeviceTypeConformance.ts:1189-1214` at `b25ed960`, the Aggregator waiver), so the
kit's default bridge composition — bridged siblings below the Aggregator
— owes none; composed siblings without Tags are warned of the same way.
The same Apple reason holds for both.

Since phase 38 the reference daemon opts in: its garage door
(`examples/reference-bridge/fleet_closure.go`) carries the Closure
namespace's GarageDoor tag (0x44 / 0x05) and its patio door panel the
ClosurePanel namespace's Rotate tag (0x45 / 0x03), so both meet their
device types and TC-DESC-2.2 runs with TAGLIST on a bridged endpoint
(`main:TestGarageServesTagList`, `main:TestPanelUnlatchesAndMoves`). The
kit default stays off, for the Apple reason above.

### BD-Matter-ClosureControl-StopObserver — a bridged host hears of a Stop the server ignores

`cluster/closure` answers a Stop while the closure is not Moving,
WaitingForMotion or Calibrating with SUCCESS and changes nothing (cluster
§5.4.8.1); matter.js's `ClosureControlServer.ts` has no Stop logic at
`862ad75f`. A bridged drive's MainState follows the device's own motion
report and can lag a motion that has already started, so a declared `Mover`
may implement `closurecontroldef.StopObserver` (#232, v0.10.2): the server
calls `StopIgnored` for such a Stop and keeps its own handling, and an error
answers FAILURE as a `Mover.Stop` error does. Without the interface the
behaviour is unchanged. Pinned by the StopObserver tests in
`cluster/closure`.

### BD-Matter-GarageIsClosureNotWindowCovering — the garage drive left the WindowCovering projection

A garage drive used to project as WindowCovering (0x0102) with its door
state encoded as a lift percentage: open = 0, ventilation = 5000,
closed = 10000. That is a faithful reading of the only axis
WindowCovering has, and it loses the thing that matters — the ventilation
stop is a named physical position, not a point on a continuum. As a
percentage it could not be labelled by a controller, could not be
selected other than by dragging a slider to the right region, and could
not be told apart on a read from a door resting halfway.

ClosureControl carries `OpenedForVentilation` as a first-class
`CurrentPositionEnum` value and `MoveToVentilationPosition` as a
`TargetPositionEnum` value, gated behind the `VT` feature. The garage now
projects as the Closure device type with `FeatureMap = PS | VT`.

**Consequence.** The two projections cannot coexist: the Closure device
type lists WindowCovering with conformance `X` — disallowed
(`closure-device.element.ts:20`). A controller that had the drive paired
as a window covering sees the endpoint change device type, which
ecosystems treat as a new accessory. This is a deliberate one-way
migration, taken because the previous projection could not express the
device.

### BD-Matter-TLVPermissive — responder TLV decode is more permissive than chip

connectedhomeip enforces container/tag strictness on every element via the
always-on `VerifyElement` (`src/lib/core/TLVReader.cpp`) and rejects
unordered Sigma/PASE optional fields, trailing bytes after the top-level
container, and missing-mandatory post-decrypt fields (`VerifyElement` is
`TLVReader.cpp:847` and `:850` at `6170af84`; the three rejections were not
established from `src/protocols/secure_channel/CASESession.cpp` at that
commit: unverified). go-fabric's live
`Decoder.Next()` (`tlv/`) enforces these only via the
opt-in `Validate()`, which the Sigma/PASE decoders do not call.

**Rationale (corrected 2026-07; review II, phase 6a):** go-fabric is a pure Matter
**responder** — but the permissive command-field decode path is NOT dead
defensive code. No capture of a controller that omits TransitionTime is on
record (the claim that Google Home's brightness slider omits it came with
the extraction commit `f2f65e6a`); the lenient decode follows chip,
BD-Matter-LevelControl-LenientDecoders: when the mandatory-but-nullable
TransitionTime field of LevelControl MoveToLevel / MoveToLevelWithOnOff /
Step is absent (an absent context tag, not TLV Null), the bridge's generated LevelControl
decoder fills the omitted field with its fallback, null
(`bridge/fields_definition.go` `requestFallbacks`, BD-Matter-LevelControl-LenientDecoders),
and `cluster/wire/levelcontrol.go` `DecodeMoveToLevel` / `DecodeStep` keep
decoding that shape to `TransitionTime == nil`. matter.js HEAD itself decodes an absent struct
member leniently (`packages/types/src/tlv/TlvObject.ts:205`
`decodeTlvInternalValue` leaves it unset); the strict mandatory-field
rejection (`ValidationMandatoryFieldMissingError`, `TlvObject.ts:261`)
lives only in the separate `validate()` step, invoked at command-invoke
time by `packages/protocol/src/action/server/CommandInvokeResponse.ts:486`
— so stock matter.js HEAD rejects the field-absent shape at its invoke
validate step with INVALID_COMMAND (`CommandInvokeResponse.ts:529-535`), and
go-fabric deliberately diverges from matter.js's strictness here. The earlier
claim that "real controllers emit spec-valid TLV, so the permissive path is
never reached on the wire" is WRONG for command fields and is withdrawn.

The wire shape is pinned by regression tests:
`TestDecodeMoveToLevelOmitsTransitionTime`,
`TestDecodeStepOmitsTransitionTime` (cluster/wire),
`TestDecodeMoveToLevelRequest_AbsentTransitionTime`,
`TestCommandFieldsReader_MoveToLevelVariants_AbsentTransitionTime`,
`TestCommandFieldsReader_LevelControlStepAbsentTransitionTime`
(bridge). A strict-validation refactor keeps tolerating absent
LevelControl TransitionTime tags until the entry is retired (owner
decision 168). Sigma/PASE container/tag strictness remains a fuzz/robustness
backlog item (parity audit CHIP L9-01..04), not an interop gap. The crypto
core (HKDF salts/info/nonces, Sigma TLV tags, status codes, control octets)
IS byte-verbatim with connectedhomeip HEAD.

The leniency is the absent field only. A present field of the wrong type
or above its width is refused — INVALID_ACTION and CONSTRAINT_ERROR, as
matter.js's `TlvNumber.validate` refuses it (`TlvNumber.ts:145-156`,
`ValidationError.ts:35-38`) — rather than masked into a different, valid
value (`cluster/wire/field_bounds.go`, W3-clucore-08).
### BD-Matter-TLVSchemaLayer — the generated codecs are the TLV schema layer; tlv/ has no TlvObject

matter.js's TLV package is a schema layer: `TlvObject` / `TlvTaggedList`
encode a JavaScript record in the order of its field definitions
(`packages/types/src/tlv/TlvObject.ts:147-154`, `:182-184` at `b25ed960`),
inject and remove a field (`injectField` / `removeField`, `:299-339`),
refuse an unknown property of a tagged list (`:161-169`) or a non-context
tag unless `allowProtocolSpecificTags` (`:212-213`), hold the length limits of a
repeated field, and `TlvArray` encodes and assembles chunked lists. In this
module `tlv/` is the raw element codec and the schema layer is the
generated code: `script/clustergen` writes each struct's `EncodeTLV` in tag
order and its `DecodeTLV` through `spec.DecodeFields`, which skips a member
it does not bind; list chunking is the interaction layer's
(`client/interaction/report.go`, `im/write_chunking.go`). The
`TlvObjectTest.ts` and `TlvArrayTest.ts` cases of that API are `left` rows
of the test register (phase 33), which also retired the five FixMe skips
that stood for them in `tlv/object_parity_test.go`. Reasoning: a typed Go
struct cannot carry an unknown property, a field of the wrong type or a
caller's member order, so the checks that guard a JavaScript record have
no value to act on.

### BD-Matter-TLVNullIsTheNullElement — a nullable value is null only as the TLV null element

matter.js's `TlvNullable` decodes a zero-length string or list as null when
the inner schema has a minimum length above zero, and a zero-length octet
string as null always (`packages/types/src/tlv/TlvNullable.ts:84-104` at
`862ad75f`, citing connectedhomeip-spec issue 11387 for the ambiguity).
`cluster/spec.DecodeNullable` and `DecodeValue` read null only from the
TLV null element; a zero-length value decodes as itself and is then
judged by its bound. The seven "zero length" cases of `TlvNullableTest.ts`
are `left` rows of the test register (phase 33). Reasoning: matter.js's
own comment (`:85-96`) calls the empty-as-null reading a specification
versus SDK interpretation issue and applies it only in part, so the module
keeps the value as encoded and leaves the null-or-empty reading to the host
that consumes it.

### BD-Matter-HostEncoderFailureCostsItsPath — a value encoder that fails answers FAILURE for its path

matter.js at `b25ed9604f` has no containment per attribute: an encode that
throws (`packages/protocol/src/interaction/InteractionMessenger.ts:581`, no
catch in `sendDataReport`) fails a Read as a whole with `Failure` or the
error's own code (`:425`, `:431`, `:433-435`, `:459`); a priming report closes
the subscription and answers a status only for a `StatusResponseError`,
otherwise nothing (`packages/node/src/node/server/InteractionServer.ts:824-830`,
`:734-759`); an ongoing update is requeued twice, then dropped, and the
subscription stays (`packages/node/src/node/server/ServerSubscription.ts:563-606`,
`:530-532`). An event payload is encoded at report time with the same outcome
(`InteractionMessenger.ts:621-626`); a command response is encoded before the
command's transaction commits, and a throw rolls the transaction back and
answers that command a status
(`packages/protocol/src/action/server/CommandInvokeResponse.ts:490-493`,
`:516`). go-fabric encodes every attribute value, event payload and command
response once, alone, on an encoder of its own under a recover
(`internal/valueenc`; #625, owner decisions 694–701): a failing attribute value
answers an AttributeStatusIB `Failure` for its path and the rest of the Read,
priming or ongoing report goes out, as connectedhomeip rolls back to the
checkpoint taken before the attribute and writes the status
(`src/app/reporting/Engine.cpp:449-450`, `:487`, `:498` at `6170af84`; the code
is `Failure`, `src/app/data-model-provider/ActionReturnStatus.cpp:125-127`,
`src/protocols/interaction_model/StatusCode.cpp:41-63`); a failing event
payload is refused when it is emitted — not recorded, no event number
consumed — as chip, which encodes the payload when the event
is logged and vends the number only on success
(`src/app/EventManagement.cpp:468-483`). The record keeps the Go value, so
the payload is encoded again for every report; one that fails only then
answers an EventStatusIB `Failure` for its path and the rest goes out.
That floor follows neither reference: chip stores the encoded bytes, and a
stored event that cannot be copied into a report rolls the writer back,
is skipped for the next attempt and fails the report, which closes the
ReadHandler (`EventManagement.cpp:635-647`, `:679-688`;
`src/app/reporting/Engine.cpp:697-703`, `:812-814`, `:861-869`); matter.js
fails the report as above and does not check a payload when it is emitted
(`packages/node/src/behavior/Events.ts:203-208`,
`packages/protocol/src/events/OccurrenceManager.ts:295-309`). A failing
command response answers a CommandStatusIB `Failure` on the request's path
after the handler has run, without a rollback of its effect, as chip
(`src/app/CommandHandlerImpl.cpp:232-240`); matter.js answers `Failure`
too unless the thrown error is a `StatusResponseError`, whose code it
answers (`CommandInvokeResponse.ts:512`, `:518-523`). Reasoning:
`contract/` is a trust boundary matter.js does not have — a host encoder
is code this module does not control — so one bad host value costs its
own path, not a wildcard Read or a subscription.

### BD-Matter-SetupCodecShape — the setup-code codecs always validate, take no flow and encode no TLV data

matter.js's pairing-code codecs can skip validation on decode
(`Schema.decode(encoded, validate = true)`,
`packages/types/src/schema/Schema.ts:18` at `b25ed960`), take a
commissioning flow on a manual-code encode and refuse a non-standard one
without VID/PID (`packages/types/src/schema/PairingCodeSchema.ts:430-437`),
and build a QR code's TLV data from a record (`encodeTlvData`, `:386-404`,
refusing PBKDF iterations without salt and a reserved tag). `secure/setup`
decodes with validation always on (`DecodeQRCode`, `DecodeManualCode`,
`DecodeExtra`), offers `ManualCode` as the standard-flow code and
`ManualCodeLong` as the one carrying VID/PID, and writes a QR code's TLV
data as the bytes a caller gives (`Extra.Raw`). Twelve
`PairingCodeSchemaTest.ts` cases are `left` rows of the test register
(phase 33); the decode halves of the TLV-data cases are ported. Reasoning:
the module reads codes to commission and prints the standard-flow codes of
its own node, so a validation switch, a flow argument and a TLV-data
builder would serve no caller.

### BD-Matter-MdnsRelevancePreFilter — no packet pre-filter in front of the mDNS decode

matter.js's MdnsSocket runs every inbound packet through a relevance
filter before decoding it: interested components register names, the
filter reduces each to a hashed footprint label and scans only a packet's
name structure, keeping any packet it cannot judge
(`packages/general/src/net/dns-sd/MdnsRelevanceFilter.ts:63-75` at
`862ad75f`). The module decodes every packet (`mdns.ParseDNSMessage`) and
admits records by the discovery cache's ingress filter (client/discovery
`Names`, `TestParityDiscovery_IngressFilter`), as `mdns/query_conn.go`
states. The 36 cases of `MdnsRelevanceFilterTest.ts` and the 12 relevance
cases of `MdnsSocketTest.ts` are `left` rows of the test register (phase
33). Reasoning: the filter saves decode work and by its own contract never
drops what the later gates would keep, so it has no wire behaviour to
mirror.


### BD-Matter-MdnsResponderKeepsTheSurvivingFamily — the mDNS responder serves the IP family that bound when the other cannot

matter.js's `UdpMulticastServer.create` tolerates a missing IPv4 (the
socket or its group join fails: logged, the server runs IPv6-only,
`packages/general/src/net/udp/UdpMulticastServer.ts:52-68` at `b25ed960`)
but not a missing IPv6: that failure is logged as "required my Matter"
(sic) and rethrown, and both sockets are closed (`:70-83`, `:95-106`;
`UdpMulticastServerTest.ts:354-360`, "closes the IPv4 socket when the IPv6
socket cannot be created", "closes both sockets when the IPv6 socket cannot
join the multicast group"). `mdns/socket.go` `openSockets` keeps whichever
family bound and fails only when neither did, each failure logged
(`mdns.responder.udp4_join_failed`, `udp6_join_failed`) and the result in
`mdns.responder.started` (`ipv4`, `ipv6`). Owner decision 2026-11-05
(phase 33 question 3). Reasoning: on a host whose IPv6 stack is down the
node stays reachable for the controllers that commission and operate over
IPv4 (chip-tool and the ecosystems do), and the log names the degraded
state; an all-or-nothing start would turn a host misconfiguration into a
silent absence from the network.

### BD-Matter-AESCCMMatterOnly — AES-CCM with Matter's parameters only, and no AES-CMAC

matter.js's crypto offers AES-CCM with a configurable tag length and L (an
8-byte tag, a 12-byte nonce with L=3, the NIST SP 800-38C Example 3 KAT)
and an AES-CMAC (`packages/general/test/crypto/aes/CcmTest.ts:230-301`,
`StandardCryptoTest.ts:102-105` and `:270-303`,
`packages/nodejs/test/crypto/NodeJsCryptoTest.ts:76-113` at `862ad75f`).
`secure/aesccm` fixes Matter's parameters — a 13-byte nonce, a 16-byte tag,
L=2 (`secure/aesccm/aesccm.go:19-25`) — and the module implements no
AES-CMAC. Those cases are `left` rows of the test register (phase 33),
and `CmacTest.ts` is excluded. Reasoning: every Matter protocol the
module speaks uses AES-CCM-128 with these parameters (Core § 3.6) and none
uses CMAC, so a configurable mode would add attack surface without a
caller.

### BD-Matter-MessageCodec-PrivacyWithExtensions — a header with the privacy flag and message extensions is decoded (caught up at the db021da0 lift)

Until the pin lift of 2026-11-06 an *Ahead of matter.js* row: matter.js at
862ad75f refused a packet header that set both the P and the MX flag
(`packages/protocol/src/codec/MessageCodec.ts:243-245` at 862ad75f,
`NotImplementedError("Privacy enhancements with message extensions not
supported.")`), while `transport/message.UnmarshalHeader` reads the MX
length after the destination and skips the block, and the privacy mask
(`bridge/privacy.go` `privacyHeaderEnd`) stops before it, as chip does
(`src/transport/raw/MessageHeader.cpp:224-232` at 6170af84). matter.js
caught up with #4843 (`fix(protocol): group message decode checks
GroupKeyMap for the destination group`): `decodeFixedHeader` keeps the
obfuscated region of a privacy packet and the MX flag
(`MessageCodec.ts:258-272` at db021da0) and the message extension is read
length-checked after the fixed header (`:328-340`); a P flag on a unicast
session is refused "as in the CHIP SDK" (`:251-253`), which the bridge
already did (`bridge/privacy.go` `maybeUnmaskPrivacy`). The two
implementations agree; no code moved here. Pinned by `transport/message`'s
header tests and `bridge/privacy_test.go` (review 2026-11 W1-wire-05).

### BD-Matter-MdnsFollowsAdvertisedAddresses — the responder follows the advertised addresses per interface; the host name stays the Service's

matter.js's MdnsServer follows `Network.interfacesChanged`, which compares
the MAC and every address of each interface every 60 s while observed
(`packages/general/src/net/Network.ts:142-215` at `b25ed960`), and on a
change reads the details again, chooses the host name again and publishes
on the changed interfaces — or on every interface when the host name moved
(`packages/protocol/src/mdns/MdnsServer.ts:321-339` at `b25ed960`). The
module's responder (`mdns/follow.go`) compares, per interface index, the
addresses its advertise policy publishes there — the inputs of its records,
so a change on an excluded container bridge moves nothing — and publishes
on the changed interfaces with the repeat a second later, as matter.js
does; every record rebuild reads the addresses again, so it keeps no
details-retry interval of its own (`InterfaceResponder.ts:43-44`,
`:166-221` at `b25ed960`). It never re-chooses the host name: the SRV target is the
`mdns.Service`'s (the MAC-derived default the `Build*` helpers fill in, or
`Responder.HostName`), a host decision the responder does not override,
so matter.js's every-interface publication after a host-name move has no
counterpart (`MdnsServerAddressChangeTest.ts` "publishes on every interface
when the host name changes" is a `left` row). Reasoning: the host name is
part of the Service the host builds, and the advertised addresses are what
a peer caches.

An interface the policy leaves without advertised addresses carries no
service records at all (`mdns/answer.go` `recordsForLocked`). matter.js's
generator yields PTR, SRV and TXT for details with no addresses
(`packages/protocol/src/advertisement/mdns/MdnsAdvertisement.ts:154-177` at
`db021da0`), but its details are every address of the interface
(`packages/nodejs/src/net/NodeJsNetwork.ts:207-213` at `b25ed960`), so that case is an
interface that has none. Here the advertise policy can leave an interface
with addresses it does not publish — a carrier-less container bridge, say —
and a multicast sent there loops back to the host, so a controller on the
same host receives an SRV with no A or AAAA; connectedhomeip's resolver
keeps the lookup per interface (not read: unverified) and gives up with `CHIP_ERROR_TIMEOUT` once
no address arrived (`src/lib/address_resolve/AddressResolve_DefaultImpl.cpp:115-125`
at `6170af84`). Observed 2026-11-07 against the chip harness on a host with
Docker bridges: the review fix of PR #437 answered the service records on
such an interface and every commissioning failed after AddNOC; the rule
was restored the same day with a regression test
(`TestRecordsForAddresslessInterfaceAreEmpty`). A goodbye for an
interface left without advertised addresses therefore names the service
records too, where matter.js's names the addresses alone.


### BD-Matter-ButtonGroupCurrentPositionReporting — Switch.CurrentPosition answered on read, not proactively reported

**Superseded 2026-10-19 (brief BK, PR #171).** The materialised
`cluster/switch.Server` owns CurrentPosition and reports its changes:
a gesture moves it 0→1→0 and a position source reports through
`contract.SwitchPositionSink`; a host's `MatterSwitchCurrentPosition` is
the start position only. Kept for the history of the wrapper's behaviour.

matter.js's reactive state proactively reports Switch.CurrentPosition
(quality N) changes to subscribers whenever `state.currentPosition` moves.
go-fabric's consolidated button endpoint answers CurrentPosition READs
live (1 while a long-press cycle is held open, 0 idle, via
`wire.GenericSwitchPositionSource`) but does not proactively dirty-mark the
attribute on press flips: press gestures are delivered exclusively through
the §1.13 event pipe.

**Rationale:** the bridge's measurement-notifier wiring scopes a notifier to
its own cluster only when the notifier is itself a cluster server
(`filterPathsByNotifierCluster`); a model-side group notifier would fall back
to dirty-marking EVERY reportable path on the endpoint (Identify, Descriptor,
BridgedDeviceBasicInformation) per press — exactly the bursty multi-cluster
report shape the bridge deliberately avoids for Apple Home. Short presses are
atomic on the CCU wire (press+release in one frame), so there is no
observable position interval to report anyway; only CONT-holds would ever
surface a transient 1.

### BD-Matter-LevelControl-NativeRamp — a host chooses, per endpoint, who ramps the level

matter.js LevelControlServer manages transitions host-side only when
`managedTransitionTimeHandling` is set (`Transitions.ts`); by default it
applies every level at once, and it explicitly sanctions handing the ramp to
hardware that transitions natively (`LevelControlServer.ts` class doc,
`createTransitions` override note). The module offers the same choice per
endpoint ([ADR 0014](../../docs/adr/0014-transitions-optional-per-endpoint.md)):

- **Hand-off (default).** `levelcontrol.Server` forwards the eight commands to
  the host's `LevelSource`, TransitionTime and Rate included, and the device
  ramps natively — a CCU actor, say, that takes `{LEVEL, RAMP_TIME}` in one
  put. The host reports progress, if any, through its own change
  notification; RemainingTime (served with `Config.Lighting`) reads 0,
  because nothing on this side knows how far the device has come. matter.js
  would read the application's `transitionEndTime` or `remainingTime` here;
  that application-stated remaining time is not ported — a host that knows
  its device's ramp end would need it, none does yet.
- **Engine (`Config.Transitions`).** For a device that cannot ramp, the
  server runs matter.js's command logic on `cluster/transition` (the port of
  `Transitions.ts`) and hands the host each stepped level as an immediate
  MoveToLevel; RemainingTime is live and reported by the Q rules. The
  reference daemon's ceiling light takes this path, its speaker the
  hand-off one. `light.ColorControlServer` offers the same switch as
  `ManageTransitions`; without it a colour temperature command applies at
  once, as matter.js does by default.

Null and zero transition times take the instant path either way, matching
`moveToLevelLogic`'s truthy-only rate derivation
(`LevelControlServer.ts:335-338` at `b25ed960`) and the falsy `changePerS`
that takes the immediate path (`packages/node/src/behavior/Transitions.ts:133`).

On the native-ramp path (`levelcontrol.NewNativeSource`, and since v0.10.2
`levelcontroldef.Declare.Ramp`, #228) the source holds Options and OnLevel
in memory and hands each accepted write to the host before it takes effect:
`NativeConfig.Persist`, or the ramp's optional `levelcontroldef.NativePersister`
on the declaration route. matter.js keeps both attributes in its own node
storage; a bridge's attribute state belongs to the host, so the host stores
it, and a refused write keeps the previous values.

### BD-Matter-LevelControl-NoFrequency — the Frequency feature is refused; neither reference implements it

The FQ feature (CurrentFrequency, MinFrequency, MaxFrequency,
MoveToClosestFrequency) is provisional in the model
(`level-control.element.ts:26` at `862ad75f`, conformance `P`), and
matter.js's server excludes it (`LevelControlServer.ts:51`
`LevelControlBehavior.with(LevelControl.Feature.OnOff, LevelControl.Feature.Lighting)`).
connectedhomeip's server has no logic for it either: its frequency handling
is commented out pending the feature leaving provisional status
(`level-control/codegen/level-control.cpp:207-232` at `6170af84`), and no
server under `src/app/clusters` handles MoveToClosestFrequency.
`levelcontrol.New` therefore refuses the feature (`cluster/levelcontrol/held.go`
`ErrFeatures`), and the device kit keeps the generated server for a
LevelControl with FQ (`ErrSelectionNotServed`). Retire this entry when
either reference implements the feature or the conformance leaves `P`
(owner decision 2026-11-06, phase 38).

### BD-Matter-ColorControl-SceneRecall — a recalled colour is applied in every mode the light has

matter.js ColorControlServer `#applySceneValues`
(`packages/node/src/behaviors/color-control/ColorControlServer.ts`) recalls a
scene's colour, and `light.ColorControlServer.MatterApplySceneValues` ports
it — the colour loop restarted through ColorLoopSet when the scene has it
active, otherwise the scene's EnhancedColorMode choosing which values move.
Three departures, each where matter.js would leave a recalled colour
unapplied:

- **The scene's EnhancedColorMode counts on every light.** matter.js reads
  it only with the EHUE feature and otherwise recalls in the hue and
  saturation mode, so a light without EHUE — every ColorTemperatureLight,
  every XY-and-CT ExtendedColorLight — never recalls its colour
  temperature or x/y. The module honours the stored mode wherever the
  server supports it; a CT-only light also recalls a scene stored without
  a mode as a colour temperature, as this module did before.
- **Every mode's transition is in tenths of a second.** ScenesManagement
  hands the apply function milliseconds; matter.js divides by 100 for the
  saturation only and passes milliseconds to the XY, CT and enhanced-hue
  logic, which reads tenths — a one-second scene transition would take a
  hundred. LevelControl divides, and so does the module for every mode.
- **The light switches to the scene's mode.** matter.js calls the `*Logic`
  methods, which move values without touching ColorMode; the module
  switches the mode first (`setEnhancedColorMode`), as the commands do, so
  ColorMode never contradicts the colour shown. A hue-and-saturation scene
  also moves the hue from its EnhancedCurrentHue (the hue attribute with
  the "S" quality), as the module recalled it before; matter.js moves the
  saturation alone.

Pinned by `TestSceneRecall` (`cluster/light`) and
`TestScenesRecallThroughTheServersApplier` (`cluster/core`). Retire each
bullet when matter.js changes the corresponding line.

### BD-Matter-ColorControl-XYToHS — a switch from x/y to hue and saturation converts with xyToHsv

matter.js ColorControlServer `switchColorMode`
(`packages/node/src/behaviors/color-control/ColorControlServer.ts:1493` at
the schema pin, unchanged at matter.js HEAD) converts the XY colour into
hue and saturation with `hsvToXy(this.x, this.y)` — the inverse function,
handed x as a hue in degrees and y as a saturation — although `xyToHsv`
exists next to it (`ColorConversionUtils.ts:30`). Every switch from the XY
mode to hue and saturation therefore starts from a hue near 0 and a
saturation of about y × 254, and a controller sees those values reported.
It is a transcription error, not a behaviour an ecosystem was found to
need, so `light.ColorControlServer` converts with `XYToHSV` (the port of
`xyToHsv`); every other conversion follows matter.js. Pinned by
`TestXYToHueSaturationConvertsTheColour` (`cluster/light`), which fails on
matter.js's call. Upstream matter.js issue candidate: call `xyToHsv`
there. Retire this entry when matter.js does.

### BD-chip-ColorControl-NumberOfPrimaries — NumberOfPrimaries counts the primaries a light supplies

matter.js keeps the primaries as plain state and leaves NumberOfPrimaries to
the application: its test "accepts a primary a light supplies without
stating the number of primaries"
(`packages/node/test/behaviors/color-control/ColorControlServerTest.ts:74-86`
at `b25ed960`) serves `primary1X` beside `numberOfPrimaries: null`. Here
`light.ColorControlServerConfig.Primaries` (and the kit's
`colorcontroldef.Patch` Primary1X … Primary6Intensity) supplies them, and
NumberOfPrimaries reads their count, null without any. connectedhomeip
derives the count from the supplied table (`ColorControlCluster.cpp:178-191`
at `6170af84`; it reads null only without a static configuration and 0
with one that lists no primaries — a distinction the kit has no
counterpart for, so none supplied reads null here) and lists only the
supplied descriptors (`:1780-1806`). The white point and the colour points
are served the same way. Reasoning: TC-CC-2.1 step 24 checks that
NumberOfPrimaries matches the PrimaryN attributes listed, which a null
beside a served primary fails; the kit numbers the primaries without a gap
for the same reason. Pinned by `cluster/light:TestParityMatterJS_ColorControlPrimaries`
and `TestColorControlPrimaries`.

### BD-Matter-BridgedVendorNameFallback — a bridged endpoint without a vendor serves the node's

matter.js treats BridgedDeviceBasicInformation `vendorName` as optional on a
bridged device (`basic-information-validators.ts`) and its bridge example
(`examples/device-bridge-onoff/src/BridgedDevicesNode.ts`) sets none, so an
unset vendor is simply absent. The module serves the host's
`endpoint.Spec.VendorName`, and when the host leaves it empty it falls back
to the node's own BasicInformation VendorName (`endpoint.Config.VendorName`)
instead of leaving the attribute out: Apple Home projects a bridged
accessory only when VendorName, ProductName, VendorID and ProductID are all
non-empty (`endpoint/materialize.go`). With neither value set the attribute
is not served, as in matter.js. Pinned by
`TestParityMatterJS_BridgedVendorNameComesFromTheHost`.

Review II, phase 4 (2026-11-14): matter.js's
`examples/device-bridge-onoff/src/BridgedDevicesNode.ts` is outside the
exports the review read and was not re-read; what this entry says of it is
unverified.

### BD-Matter-ControllerProgressAndUpdateEvents — two Go-named commissioning steps and two Go-only update events

`controller.PairOptions.Progress` reports matter.js's commissioning steps by
their names and numbers (`ControllerCommissioningFlow.ts:536-656` at
`862ad75f`: `GetInitialData` 0.1 … `Reconnect` 18.1, which includes the
CASE connection, `GeneralCommissioning.Complete` 20.1). matter.js names no
step before its flow runs, so the module names the two phases Go runs there
itself: `Discovery` 2.1 and `PASE` 2.2 (`controller/commissioner/progress.go`).
Nor does it name the node's start after the flow (the initial read and the
default subscription, `CommissioningClient.ts:343-361`), which the module
reports as `Subscribe` 21.1 from `client.Registry.Commission`. It is never
skipped, and as in matter.js a failed step is the last report.
`softwareupdate.Manager.Observe` mirrors the four events of
`SoftwareUpdateManager.ts:1420-1438` (`updateAvailable` :886, `updateApplying`
:1317, `updateDone` :829/:1279, `updateFailed` :878/:1123) and adds two the
host needs to drive a UI and matter.js does not emit: `consent_changed`
(AddUpdateConsent / RemoveConsent) and `check_finished` (the end of
QueryUpdates, with the per-product errors it logged and passed over). Both
are marked Go-only in the doc comments. Two more are Go-only too:
`queued`, where `#queueUpdate` (`:892-920`) adds an entry or gives a queued
one a new target, and `transfer_started`, at the entry's first `Downloading`
in `onOtaStatusChange` (`:1253-1321`), which the provider reports when the
node's BDX session starts (`OtaSoftwareUpdateProviderServer.ts:308-327`).
Pinned by
`controller/pair_progress_test.go` and `controller/softwareupdate/observe_test.go`.

> **Rule of thumb (CLAUDE.md):** matter.js HEAD is the gold standard for everything under ``. Cluster IDs / revisions / attribute IDs / constraints / defaults / wire shape are taken verbatim. Any item below is a **deliberate** divergence with a documented reason. Bug-class drift (hand-coded revisions etc.) does **not** belong here — it belongs in a fix.

### BD-Matter-SurfaceChange-ConfigurationVersion — a changed surface raises ConfigurationVersion by itself

matter.js provides the mechanism and leaves the trigger to the
application: `BasicInformationServer.ts:35-37` at `862ad75f` documents
`ConfigurationVersion` as "seeded to 1 and constrained to only ever
increase" and tells the application to "bump it with
`increaseConfigurationVersion`" (the method, `:132`) when "the node's
configuration changes in a way clients should detect";
`BridgedDeviceBasicInformationServer.ts:49-59` does the same for a bridged
node and `:86` raises the bridge's own version in the same change. No
matter.js code raises either version when a behavior's features or
elements change — the only production caller at the pin is that coupling
line (`git grep increaseConfigurationVersion 862ad75f -- packages`, tests
aside).

go-fabric raises it by itself (concept v11 §C.9, ADR 0030 decision 6,
wave S4, `node/surface_stability.go`): after every assembly the node
compares each endpoint's effective surface (`surface.Endpoint.Digest`:
device types, FeatureMap and the four global lists of every cluster) with
the one it persisted in its settings next to the ConfigurationVersion
(`bridged_surface_digest.<key>`, `basic_information.surface_digest`); when
the same `StableKey` comes back with a different surface, one
`bridge.Bridge.IncreaseNodeConfigurationVersionWith` change raises the
changed endpoints' versions and the root's once (matter.js's coupling),
bumps the Descriptor's and the changed clusters' data versions, records the
diff in `Report.Changed` and logs one `surface changed` record per
endpoint. A first assembly persists without raising; a withheld endpoint's
stored surface is dropped, so its return is a first assembly. The host's
own `IncreaseConfigurationVersion(s)` is unchanged and adds to it.

Reason: a surface change under a paired controller is exactly the case
the attribute exists for, and a host cannot see it — the surface is
composed here, from the host's declaration, the kit's defaults and the
node's policies. Leaving the trigger to the host would repeat the loom
0.94.0 incident (an element enabled late, Apple Home loading no data) with
no signal on the wire. Mirroring matter.js here would mean mirroring an
absence. Behaviour source: this module; connectedhomeip's bridge example
was not consulted (not recorded).

### BD-Matter-ProvenOperationalHost — the SRV target that owned the session's address ranks first on reconnect

matter.js orders a peer's discovered addresses by class, health and DNS priority (`ServerAddressSet.ts:165-184` at b25ed960) and persists the last operational address, not its host (`PeerDescriptor.ts:48`); chip ranks alike (`IPAddressSorter.cpp:44-50` at 6170af84). This module records, with the operational address, the discovered SRV target that owned it (`peer.Descriptor.OperationalHost`) and, while discovery still advertises that host, tries its addresses first. The service delivers addresses one at a time in desirability order, so the proven host's may arrive after an attempt at another target has started; it then starts at once, outside the stagger, and the attempt already running continues — a preemption, not a wait. Reason: issue 478 — a border router (tvOS) answered a Thread node's instance with an SRV to its own host, so the node's candidate set alternated between two hosts and every reconnect spent 45 s on the router's link-local address; the session already proves which host is the node's. The host is also learned after the handshake, when discovery first names the target that owns a live session's operational address — a session made from the stored address at start precedes discovery. While the proven host is known but no discovered address carries it, a reconnect tries the last operational address first, as matter.js tries it when nothing is discovered (`PeerConnection.ts:362-382` at b25ed960): another responder's cache-flush SRV removes the node's own SRV from the cache for as long as the node takes to answer again (RFC 6762 §10.2), and the session, not the momentary cache, says which target is the node (issue 488). Register row above; the row closes when matter.js ranks by a proven host. What happens to the proven host's addresses when discovery withdraws them is `BD-Matter-ProvenAddressRetention` (issue 507).

### BD-Matter-OnboardingCodeKept — the controller keeps a node's onboarding code and lists an inventory

matter.js keeps no pairing code: `CommissioningClient.State` persists the discriminator, vendor and product of a peer (`CommissioningClient.ts:959` ff., `:1046` at db021da0) and hands the passcode to the commissioner only (`:290-291`). This module can keep the code the passcode came from — at pairing with `controller.Config.KeepOnboardingCodes`, or attached afterwards with `client.Node.SetOnboardingCode` — under its own store cluster id `0xFFFFFFFC` beside the record (not in `Record`, which diagnostics render), and lists it with `Controller.Inventory()`. A kept QR code yields both forms to show (`OnboardingCode.Codes`, `controller/client/onboarding.go:173-200`): the manual code is the short one, or the 21-digit one with the vendor and product ids when the code's commissioning flow is not Standard, as connectedhomeip generates it (`src/setup_payload/ManualSetupPayloadGenerator.cpp:116` at `6170af84`). An attached code is compared with the node's vendor, product and advertised discriminator and refused on a difference; its passcode stays unproven. A code is kept at pairing, and the advertised discriminator compared, only for a node seen in Basic commissioning mode (`CommissioningMode.ts:7-11`): in an Enhanced Commissioning Window both are the window's, and a node paired by address advertised nothing. Reason: the code is needed after a factory reset and cannot be read from a commissioned device; the controller's input is the only place it exists in software. matterjs-server at 0bd06f2 renders a QR code only for a window it opens (`WebSocketControllerHandler.ts:2324-2325`, `dashboard/src/pages/components/node-details.ts:435-436`); a grep for a stored device code found none there (grep only, not a full read).

### BD-Matter-PeerAttemptFailAdvance — a failed connection attempt starts the next discovered address at once

matter.js starts the next address of a peer `delayBeforeNextAddress` (45 s, `PeerTimingParameters.ts:195`) after the previous attempt *started*, whatever became of it (`PeerConnection.ts:236-256`; `lastAttemptAt` is reset only when the fallback is retired, `:300-303`). This module keeps the 45 s as the stagger between attempts still in flight but, when an attempt ends in a timeout or network error and addresses are pending, starts the next one at once — connectedhomeip's `OperationalSessionSetup::OnSessionEstablishmentError` (`src/app/OperationalSessionSetup.cpp:457-480` at 6170af84) moves to the next resolved address on `CHIP_ERROR_TIMEOUT`/`CHIP_ERROR_BUSY` without a fixed delay. An unacknowledged Sigma1 counts: the contact schedule's switch to a fresh one (`PeerConnection.ts:639-653` at b25ed960) is, in connectedhomeip, the `CHIP_ERROR_TIMEOUT` the exchange's response timer reports once the retransmissions are exhausted (`src/messaging/ReliableMessageMgr.cpp:186-205`, `src/protocols/secure_channel/CASESession.cpp:575-584` at 6170af84), and the next address starts then. Reason: a dead first candidate (issue 478: a border router's address published for a Thread node) otherwise costs every reconnect 45 s. Retires when matter.js advances on failure.

### BD-Matter-SuspectProbeWalksAlternates — a session-suspect probe tries the other discovered addresses before the session is given up

matter.js's `PeerAddressMonitor` walks the discovered alternates only on an mDNS address change; a session-suspect run probes the current address and, failing, closes the session (`packages/protocol/src/peer/PeerAddressMonitor.ts:105-106`, `:219-221` at b25ed960, stated as a decision). This module probes the alternates on a suspect session too and migrates the session to one that answers, because the full reconnect that follows `handlePeerLoss` costs a Thread node a minute or more (issue 478) while a probe costs one small exchange per address. Retires when matter.js walks alternates on suspect.

Review II, run 3 (R3-bound-3551): the address monitor applies the connection's unicast filter to the discovered set before an ICD adoption or a probe (`client/peer/monitor.go` `unicastDestinations`), so a multicast or unspecified address from a discovery record is neither adopted nor probed. matter.js adopts `candidates.find(same family) ?? candidates[0]` unfiltered (`packages/protocol/src/peer/PeerAddressMonitor.ts:149-172`, the pick `:160`, adopted without a probe `:170`, at `b25ed960`). Pinned by `client/peer:TestMonitorTakesOnlyUnicastDestinations`.

### BD-Matter-ProvenAddressRetention — the proven host's last addresses outlive a foreign SRV

matter.js deletes an address when discovery drops it and aborts the attempt in flight on it; it keeps the operational address only as the last attempt left (`deleteAddress`, `PeerConnection.ts:419-441` at b25ed960, the guard at `:428`), and retires a fallback that discovery has superseded after `addressChangeStabilizationDelay` (`retireStaleFallback`, `:277-322`). This module retains, while a connection runs, the addresses of the peer's proven host (`BD-Matter-ProvenOperationalHost`) that discovery withdraws while no discovered address carries that host: they stay candidates ranked ahead of every other target, and the attempts in flight on them continue. For a peer whose host was never learned the stored operational address is the anchor instead — queued, ranked first and retained whenever discovery advertises addresses and not it; the first discovered address then starts beside it without the inter-address stagger, as matter.js lets the address that replaces a retired fallback start (`lastAttemptAt = undefined`, `:300-303`), so a genuinely new address does not wait behind a stale one. A retention ends when the host or the address is advertised again (an address the returned host no longer carries is deleted), when a session is established, or after `Timing.ProvenAddressRetention` (10 min by default, measured from each withdrawal; a negative value retains nothing), and is not retired as a superseded fallback before that. Reason: issue 507 — a border router answers a Thread node's operational instance with an SRV to its own host, and the node's SRV set flipped between the two hosts thousands of times a day; every flip aborted the attempts at the node's addresses, among them one waiting out the node's Busy answer, and the node was tried again only when its own host returned. A foreign SRV is no evidence that the node's addresses are stale; the session proved them, and the stagger still starts the other targets beside them, so a dead retained address strands nothing. Cost: after a node re-registers under a new host, its old addresses are tried first until a session proves the new one. Retires when matter.js keeps a withdrawn address of a known peer.

### BD-Matter-PeerBusyDeadline — a Busy answer's delay is held for the peer, not for the attempt

matter.js waits the delay of a Busy status report — `busyDelay` plus a random part of `delayAfterNetworkError` (`PeerConnection.ts:700-701` at b25ed960) — inside the attempt that received it, so an abort of that attempt, or an attempt at another address, sends the next Sigma1 at once. This module records the deadline on the peer when the answer arrives at the peer's operational address — the address a session proved, zone aside — after the host's error handler had its say on the delay: no Sigma1 goes to any address of that peer before it, and a session clears it. A Busy from any other address is unauthenticated and need not be the node's — a foreign SRV target's (issue 507), or another address of the node's own host, whose AAAA record any host on the link can announce: it holds only the attempt that received it, as matter.js waits it (review II, R2-P1-net-05, and R2-P3-ctl-lan-07, which took the other addresses of the operational host out of the proven ones on 2026-11-14; pinned by `client/peer:TestBusyAtAnUnprovenAddressHoldsOnlyItsAttempt` and `TestBusyAtAnotherAddressOfTheProvenHostHoldsOnlyItsAttempt`). A node that answers Busy from another of its own addresses is therefore held per attempt, as in matter.js. Reason: issue 507 — the node answered Busy with the 16-bit maximum (65.5 s), the waiting attempt was aborted by the next change of its SRV set, and the node's return sent a fresh Sigma1 into the window the node had asked to be left alone in. The node, not the path, is busy. Retires when matter.js holds the delay per peer.

### BD-Matter-Commissioner-ReconnectProbe — during Reconnect the commissioner asks the device for its network state and connects to the addresses it reports

matter.js's reconnect step re-arms the fail-safe and calls `transitionToCase` (`ControllerCommissioningFlow.ts:2029-2046` at db021da0); the peer then connects on what DNS-SD delivers (`ControllerCommissioner.ts:692-709`). connectedhomeip does the same (`CHIPDeviceController.cpp:4487-4497` at 6170af84) and knows one address beside DNS-SD, the commissioning session's own, for UDP and TCP only (`:4469-4482`). In a concurrent flow — the commissioning session still open — this module reads over that session, 2 s into the step and every 10 s, one read of at most nine concrete paths on endpoint 0: NetworkCommissioning `LastNetworkingStatus`, `LastConnectErrorValue` and `Networks`, GeneralDiagnostics `NetworkInterfaces`, ThreadNetworkDiagnostics `RoutingRole`, `NetworkName`, `Channel`, `PartitionId` and `MeshLocalPrefix`, each cluster only when the root's ServerList names it. A changed report is logged; the routable addresses of operational interfaces — not link-local, not inside the mesh-local prefix (an `ipv6pre`, the length in bits then the prefix, as connectedhomeip encodes it, `DirectThreadNetworkDiagnosticsProvider.cpp:167-174`), not an RLOC or ALOC — are handed once per connection process to the peer's running process at port 5540 (`Peer.HintAddresses`), ranked after discovered addresses, which are not staggered behind a hinted attempt; a failed step names the last report in its `OperativeConnectionFailed` text. What is taken is bounded by what the attribute may hold: the probe takes at most 8 operational interfaces from one report — those with an address the connection can use (routable and not mesh-local) first, in the device's order, and before any other the one that names the commissioning session's own address, which is then the first address hinted (only when it is usable by that test: a link-local one is not, the report carrying no zone); usable interfaces past the bound are counted and logged, not refused, and the slots they leave go to the other operational interfaces, of which nothing is attempted (review II, R2-P0-rv-C08), and a connection process takes at most `peer.MaxHintedAddresses` = 96 hinted addresses — 8 interfaces of 8 IPv6 and 4 IPv4 addresses each, the constraints "max 8", "max 8" and "max 4" of `packages/model/src/standard/elements/general-diagnostics.element.ts:27`, `:195` and `:191` at `db021da0`; connectedhomeip sizes the two address arrays the same (`src/include/platform/DiagnosticDataProvider.h:42-43` at `6170af84`) and encodes its platform's whole interface list (`src/app/clusters/general-diagnostics-server/GeneralDiagnosticsCluster.cpp:437-446`), which is why a longer list is cut and not refused. A hinted or probed address must also name a single host: `peer.unicastDestination` and the probe's `routableAddr` pass over the unspecified address, multicast and the IPv4 blocks 0.0.0.0/8 and 240.0.0.0/4 (RFC 1122 §3.2.1.3 and RFC 1112 §4, as the comment in `client/peer/hint.go` quotes them), and judge a zoned or IPv4-mapped address as the address it is. matter.js has no hinted address to filter, and takes a discovered A or AAAA record's value as it stands (`packages/general/src/net/dns-sd/IpService.ts:392-407`: only a zone is added to a link-local address); this module's discovered addresses do not pass the filter either — its one caller is `HintAddresses` — and what `client/discovery` filters was not read (unverified). Review II, R2-P0-bound-E01; pinned by `client/peer:TestHintAddressesBounded`, `TestHintAddressesUnicastOnly`, `TestUnicastDestination`, `controller/commissioner:TestReconnectProbeBoundsReportedAddresses`, `TestReconnectProbeJudgesBeforeItBounds` and `TestRoutableAddr`. A probe that fails ends the probing and never the step. Reason: on a live Thread network the border router's advertising proxy published a commissioned plug 2 min 47 s after it joined, and never published a bulb, three times — the device was commissioned up to its last step and nothing said whether it had attached. The address needs no trust: CASE authenticates the node. The port is Matter's default because the node's own is only in its SRV record; when discovery delivers it, discovery's addresses take over. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js reads the device at this step.

### BD-Matter-ControllerDiagnostics — the controller serves a diagnostics snapshot, a trace and mDNS findings

matter.js exposes the controller's state as live observable sets — `PeerSet.peers` (`packages/protocol/src/peer/PeerSet.ts:218` at db021da0), `Peer.sessions` (`Peer.ts:259-265`), `SessionManager.sessions` (`SessionManager.ts:376`) — rendered by its `Diagnostic` presentation; no snapshot, trace or finding type is served to a host. matterjs-server (`0bd06f2`) offers the controller's client only Thread diagnostics (`get_thread_diagnostics`, `get_thread_border_routers`; `packages/ws-controller/src/server/WebSocketControllerHandler.ts:144`) and session loss only as a node state event. This module serves the controller the facade the node has: `Controller.SessionDiagnostics()` (`diag.SessionDiagnostics`: the sessions flat, the peers with their state), `Controller.DiagnosticEvents()` and `OnDiagnosticEvent` on a `diagevent.Ring` (pairing, session, discovery, reachability, icd, ota, camera), `Controller.DiagnoseMDNS()` and `contract.Metrics`. Reason: a host running the controller half alone shows its operator the paired nodes but nothing about why one is reconnecting (issue 483); the shapes are shared with the node so one page model serves both roles. The row closes when matter.js serves a diagnostics snapshot or trace.

Review II, phase 4 (2026-11-14): matterjs-server at `0bd06f2` is outside the
exports the review read and was not re-read; what this entry says of it is
unverified.

### BD-Matter-LinkLocalZoneVariants — a link-local address leaves the service on every interface it was heard on

matter.js keys a cached AAAA record by its address (`DnssdName.ts:348` at b25ed960), keeps the interface of its last arrival, and zones a link-local address to it when the service reads the record (`IpService.ts:392-408`); an arrival on a second interface adds a second zoned address (`:315-328`), and the record's deletion removes only the variant of the last interface (`:330-340`). The other stays in the service's address set until the service closes. This module removes every zoned variant of the address with the record. Reason: issue 488 — a border router's link-local address, reflected onto a second host interface, stayed a connection candidate after its SRV target was gone. Retires when matter.js removes them.

### Idiomatic translations TypeScript → Go (not real divergence)

| matter.js pattern | Go idiom in go-fabric | Files |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Behavior.with(BasicInformationServer, ...)` Mixin | Concrete struct `core.BasicInformation` with the same fields + `MatterRead`/`MatterWrite`/`MatterAttributes` methods | `cluster/core/basic_information.go` |
| `Promise<T>` async chain | Goroutine + `context.Context` + return value | every I/O method |
| `@matter/types` `TlvSchema<T>` derived from class fields | `tlv.Encoder` / `tlv.Decoder` with explicit `PutUint16` / `PutUint32` per spec-typed slot | `tlv/encode.go` |
| Decorators (`@validate`, `@quality(...)`) | Comment + manual constraint check at write boundary | `cluster/core/*_information.go::MatterWrite` |
| Behavior-state proxies via Reflect | Direct struct fields under `sync.RWMutex` | every cluster server |

These rewrite TypeScript constructs into Go. Wire output is identical; the surface API differs because Go does not have decorators or Reflect-based mixins.

### L00 Schema Audit — cluster-stub design choices (2026-05-12)

- **L00-BD-Groups** ScenesManagement as a stub — the ScenesManagement cluster server returns an empty scene table and rejects all writes. Presence is mandated by Matter device-type requirements (OnOff Light, Dimmable Light, etc.), not feature preference. matter.js `packages/node/src/behaviors/scenes-management/`. Reason: no scene store; the stub satisfies the device-type conformance requirement without exposing broken functionality. Groups is no longer part of this entry: it is a real server since [ADR 0009](../../docs/adr/0009-groups-and-group-messaging.md).
- **L00-BD-OnOffDefault** OnOff default-false on unobserved state — matter.js `OnOffServer.ts` defaults `onOff` to `false` when the underlying DP has not yet reported; go-fabric mirrors this rather than returning null (which matter.js also documents as not spec-nullable for the OnOff attribute). Reason: spec-aligned default; null would be a schema violation.
- **L00-BD-BoolStateEvent** BooleanState no StateChangeEvent — StateChangeEvent (event id 0x0) has conformance `"O"` in matter.js `packages/model/src/standard/elements/boolean-state.element.ts`; go-fabric omits it because HM push events are handled via DP value changes, not a dedicated state-change event mechanism. Reason: optional event, no HM-side equivalent event source.

#### L10-D05 detail — SuppressResponse not set on ongoing subscription ReportData (parity, no divergence)

This entry recorded a deliberate divergence from matter.js until review II
(phase 4, R2-P4-imread-13): it said matter.js sends an ongoing report with
`suppressResponse: true`. At the pin it does not.

**matter.js ref:** `packages/node/src/node/server/ServerSubscription.ts:921-936`
at `db021da0` — a report with data is sent with `suppressResponse: false`
(:928, "Non-empty data reports always need to send response"), and so is the
keep-alive (:909-920, :914).

report builder sets SuppressResponse only for a Read, never for a
subscription's report.

**go-fabric:** the same: a report with data and a keep-alive both go out
with SuppressResponse false, and the peer's StatusResponse is read (the
keep-alive since review II, phase 4; the closed findings row "Keep-alive
reports suppress the response"). Since review II, phase 5b an update counts

95; the closed findings row F-db021da0-36).

| ID | Severity | Status | Notes |

| L6-D04 | MED | **Fixed** (2026-05-12), **withdrawn 2026-11-14** (review II, owner decision 61) | The reap went: matter.js ends no subscription when an endpoint goes (`packages/node/src/node/integration/ProtocolService.ts:216-220` at `db021da0`), and since 2026-11-14 a `Reassemble` ends none either (`bridge/bridge.go:1404-1409`; `Manager.CloseEndpoint` is deprecated, `im/subscription/manager.go:813-820`). Pinned by `bridge:TestReassembleRemovingAnEndpointEndsNoSubscription`; `TestCloseEndpoint_ClosesMatchingSubscriptions` still holds the deprecated method. |

#### L5-D5 detail — Resumption store: SQLite upsert vs. in-memory LRU cap

**matter.js ref:** `packages/protocol/src/session/SessionManager.ts` —
in-memory `ResumptionRecord` map; no hard cap; bounded by fabric/node count.

**chip ref:** `src/protocols/secure_channel/DefaultSessionResumptionStorage.h:kSessionResumptionStorageMaxEntries = 8` per node.

**go-fabric:** `store/resumption.go:UpsertResumption` uses
`ON CONFLICT(fabric_index, peer_node_id) DO UPDATE` — exactly **one row per (fabric, peer) pair**.
The unique constraint on `(fabric_index, peer_node_id)` already enforces a natural cap: each peer
has at most one active resumption record at any time. Adding a per-fabric LRU cap (chip's 8 / matter.js
soft 32) would require a DELETE-after-upsert pass over the SQLite table. For a bridge with a typical
fleet of 3–10 controllers per fabric this would be pure overhead; the SQLite unique index is a more
durable and auditable enforcement mechanism than an in-memory counter.

**Rationale:** The by-design cap is one-per-peer (implicit via the DB unique constraint), which is
stricter than chip's 8-per-node in the single-peer case and weaker in the many-peer case. For a
homematic bridge with a single controller hub this is never observable. If a future production scenario
requires 8+ distinct peers per fabric, a `LIMIT 8 ORDER BY last_used_at` eviction pass can be added
to `UpsertResumption` without a schema change (migration `last_used_at` column is already present).

**L02-D01** Siren: BooleanState removed from `Siren.MatterClusterServers()`. BooleanState
(0x0045) is not in the OnOffPlugInUnit (0x010A) mandatory/optional cluster set per

**L02-D02** OccupancySensing on a measurement-projected endpoint
(`cluster/measurement.OccupancySensingServer`, rewritten in phase 36): the
FeatureMap is the source's `contract.OccupancySelection` — its detector
types, PassiveInfrared when it names none, and OccupancyEvent unless it
leaves the event out — and OccupancySensorType and its bitmap follow the
detectors as matter.js's initialize sets them
(`OccupancySensingServer.ts:27-65` at `862ad75f`). HoldTime and the

are not served there: the projected server is rebuilt on every dispatch
