This module departs from that order (amended 2026-11-14: owner decision 52 of review II, which changes decision 30): `im/write.go` takes the hold once the ACL gate and the accessing-fabric gate have granted the write, before the DataVersion check and the write, so a write its subject may not make holds nothing; and the key carries the accessing fabric for an attribute whose write is fabric-scoped (`schema.IsFabricScopedWrite`: AccessControl's Acl and Extension, Binding and the others it names), so one fabric's chunked write of such an attribute leaves the other fabrics' writes of it free. Check and take are one step under the hold table's lock: a path another interaction took since the Busy check is answered Busy. The rest is as before: the marker of the last accepted path moves as in matter.js; a session has at most `maxChunkedWritesPerSession` = 4 chunked writes open, and the chunk that would open a fifth is answered Busy before anything is held (`bridge/exchange_routing.go`, `Bridge.dispatchWriteRequest`); a closed session's open writes end with it and release their holds (`dropSessionWriteTxs`), as a write without a chunk for `writeTxTTL` does. The number and the answer are connectedhomeip's: `CHIP_IM_MAX_NUM_WRITE_HANDLER` 4 (`src/lib/core/CHIPConfig.h:991-992` at `6170af84`) and `Status::Busy` when no write handler is free (`src/app/InteractionModelEngine.cpp:951-960`). Its pool is the engine's one pool; the bound here is per session, so one session cannot use up another's, as in `BD-chip-TimedRequestsBounded`. Where connectedhomeip checks access relative to its write handler was not read (unverified). What a controller sees of the departure: a writer the ACL refuses is answered UNSUPPORTED_ACCESS and makes no other writer's write Busy, and two fabrics can each run a chunked write of their own ACL at once; a granted chunked write still makes another write of the same attribute — of the same fabric, for a fabric-scoped one — Busy until its final chunk. Reason: a hold is a claim on an attribute, and a subject without the right to write it has none; a fabric-scoped attribute is one list per fabric, so one fabric's write does not touch another's. Review II, R2-P1-req-03 and R2-P1-dr-req-02; R2-P3-admin-01. Pinned by `bridge:TestChunkedWritesOfOneSessionAreBounded`, `TestClosedSessionReleasesItsChunkedWrites`, `im:TestChunkedWriteHoldsOnlyWhatTheSubjectMayWrite` and `fabrictest:TestRefusedChunkedWriteHoldsNothing`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js bounds the chunked writes a session may hold open.

### BD-Matter-BTP-HandshakeTimerFromAccept — the BTP handshake timer runs from the accept, and a handshake that opens no session drops the connection

matter.js's peripheral starts no timer when a central connects: its
`accept` handler records the client address and updates the RSSI
(`packages/nodejs-ble/src/BlenoBleServer.ts:189-193` at `b25ed960`). It
starts `btpHandshakeTimeout` at the handshake request (`:258`;
`BTP_CONN_RSP_TIMEOUT`, 15 s, "timer starts when receives handshake request
& waits for a subscription request on c2",
`packages/protocol/src/ble/BleConsts.ts:56`), so a central that connects
and never writes holds the connection. It stops the timer at the C2
subscription, before the session is created (`BlenoBleServer.ts:297`,
`:299`): a request that names no supported version is disconnected
(`packages/protocol/src/ble/BtpSessionHandler.ts:106-108`); one whose
version nibbles are all zero fails in the decode before that
(`packages/protocol/src/codec/BtpCodec.ts:219-222`, called at
`BtpSessionHandler.ts:95`), the rejection is logged
(`BlenoBleServer.ts:76-78`) and the connection stays with no timer left.
In this module the accept starts the timer of `ConnRspTimeout`
(`transport/btp/accept.go`): a central that has not completed the
handshake when it ends is disconnected, a silent one included; the timer
stops only once a session exists; and a kept handshake request that opens
no session drops the connection at once. Both are this module's own rule
(owner decision 31 of review II): a central that holds the connection
keeps a commissioner out. connectedhomeip's peripheral was not read for
either (unverified). Review II, R2-P1-req-07 and R2-P1-dr-req-03. Pinned
by `transport/btp:TestAcceptSilentCentralIsDisconnected`,
`TestAcceptHandshakeInTimeIsUntouched` and
`TestAcceptRefusedHandshakeIsDisconnected`. Register row above; the row
closes when matter.js starts its handshake timer at the accept.

Review II, phase 6a (R2-P6-fsm-0204, -0205, -0206): the bound counts from the accept and nothing renews it — a repeated handshake request does not extend it, where matter.js starts its timer per request (`BlenoBleServer.ts:258` at `b25ed960`); a request on a connection that already holds a session arms none; and it holds while the handshake response waits for its confirmation, where matter.js stops its timer before the response is awaited (`:292-297`).

### BD-Matter-ChunkWaitsBounded — a session may leave at most four interactions waiting for a chunk's StatusResponse

matter.js sends a report chunk and waits for the peer's StatusResponse
inside the interaction
(`packages/protocol/src/interaction/InteractionMessenger.ts:839-844` at
`db021da0`; `waitForSuccess`, `:221-227`); nothing at these lines counts
the interactions of a session that wait. matter.js bounds the open
exchanges of a secure session at 30 and closes the least recently active
one beyond it (`packages/protocol/src/protocol/ExchangeManager.ts:63`,
`:551-566`, `:578-596` at `db021da0`); what ends such a wait when its
exchange or its
session closes was not read (unverified). In this module the wait is bounded
twice (`bridge/chunk_waits.go`): it ends with its session, with the
bridge's `Stop` and with its priming subscription, and one session holds
at most `maxChunkWaitsPerSession` = 4 of them — the request beyond is
answered Busy, an InvokeRequest before any command runs, a ReadRequest
after it was read and chunked. The number is this module's own choice;
connectedhomeip's node-wide pools of command and write handlers are 4 each
(`src/lib/core/CHIPConfig.h:922`, `:992` at `6170af84`) and are the
comparison, not the source. With it, a `KeepSubscriptions=false` teardown
leaves a subscription that is still priming, as matter.js adds a
subscription to its session only when it activates
(`packages/node/src/node/server/ServerSubscription.ts:411-421`) and the
teardown walks the sessions' subscriptions
(`packages/node/src/node/server/InteractionServer.ts:647-665`). Review II,
R2-P1-req2-01. Pinned by `bridge:TestChunkWaitsOfOneSessionAreBounded`,
`TestStopEndsPendingChunkWaits`, `TestSessionCloseEndsItsChunkWaits` and
`TestSubscriptionCloseEndsItsPrimingWait`; the limit is in
`docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js
bounds the interactions of a session that wait for a chunk's
StatusResponse.

### BD-Matter-ChunkWaitsSharedByFabric — past half the dispatch budget, a fabric holding more than its share of the chunk waits is answered Busy

matter.js has no such resource — a wait is a promise on its event loop — and bounds a session at 30 exchanges (`packages/protocol/src/protocol/ExchangeManager.ts:63` at `db021da0`), nothing per fabric (inferred). connectedhomeip reserves per fabric: at least 3 subscriptions and 1 read (`src/app/InteractionModelEngine.h:113-116`, `:674-687` at `6170af84`), kept by `EnsureResourceForSubscription` and `EnsureResourceForRead` (`InteractionModelEngine.cpp:1249`, `:1432`; bodies not read). `Bridge.SetFabricCounter` gives the bridge the node's fabric count; once the chunk waits held bridge-wide reach `chunkWaitFabricThreshold` = 512, half the dispatch budget, a fabric holding its share (512 / fabrics) is answered Busy for a further claim as the per-session bound answers (`BD-Matter-ChunkWaitsBounded`): it holds at most its share. A session without a fabric (PASE, unresolved, no `SessionFabricResolver`) is held to no share and has no cap of its own: it asks no count, its claims count towards the threshold, and it is bounded by `maxChunkWaitsPerSession` (`bridge/chunk_waits.go:73`) and the listener's dispatch slots (`transport/udp/listener.go:50`, `maxConcurrentDispatch` = 1024). The reason: with a resolver, fabric 0 is the PASE sessions (and a session already gone); without one every session is fabric 0, and a share of that one bucket could not work (owner decision 281). The node's counter keeps the count and lists the store again only after a fabric is installed or removed, and keeps nothing while a fail-safe is armed — an AddNOC's pending row can be rolled back without a hook (`node/fabric_count.go`) — so it lists on every call then (owner decision 280); a host that wires its own counter decides its own caching. No counter, an error or one fabric: no share. The node wires the counter. The share and its numbers are this module's own. Review II, TM R3.7, owner decision 245; strict share and fabric 0 excluded, R2-P7-req-05, owner decisions 275, 280, 281. Pinned by `bridge:TestTMR37`, `TestTMR37Claims`, `TestChunkWaitShareIsStrict`, `TestChunkWaitShareExcludesFabricZero`, `TestClaimChunkWaitAsksNoCountForFabricZero`, `node:TestFabricCountIsCachedUntilAFabricChanges`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js bounds what one fabric's sessions hold.

### BD-Matter-MdnsTruncatedQueryBounds — a truncated mDNS query and its continuations are bounded

matter.js merges a truncated query with its continuations without a
bound: `#prepareMessage` spreads the held queries, answers and additional
records with the new ones
(`packages/protocol/src/mdns/MdnsServer.ts:519-527` at `b25ed960`), starts
a new 400–500 ms timer for every continuation that still carries TC
(`:538-545`), and keeps the held queries in `#truncatedQueryCache`, a map
without a size limit (`:61`). This module's responder (`mdns/answer.go`)
counts the wait from the first packet — a continuation does not move it —
completes a query at `maxTruncatedPackets` = 32 packets or at more than
`maxTruncatedQuestions` = 64 questions, keeps of the known answers only
those that suppress one of the interface's own records and none of the
additional records, and holds at most `maxTruncatedQueries` = 64 truncated
queries, answering the one beyond at once. At every bound the query is
answered with what has arrived; nothing that arrived is dropped. The
numbers are this module's own; connectedhomeip was not read for truncated
queries (unverified). Reason: every dimension of the merge is the
sender's, and the sender is unauthenticated — before `8c19b9d4` one that
kept the TC bit set held one ever-growing query alive (review II,
R2-P1-net-01). Pinned by `mdns:TestTruncatedQueryBounds`; the limits are
in `docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when
matter.js bounds a truncated query.

### BD-Matter-StoreEraseScrub — the factory reset's erase leaves none of the erased bytes in the database file

matter.js's SQLite driver erases with plain `DELETE` — one key
(`packages/nodejs/src/storage/sqlite/SqliteStorageDriver.ts:200-204` at
`db021da0`), a context and its children (`:206-209`), everything at
`clearOnInit` (`:305`) — and a search for `VACUUM` and `secure_delete`
under `packages/nodejs/src/storage` finds no line. `store.Store.Erase`
deletes and then scrubs (`store/erase.go`, `Scrub`): the database is
rebuilt without its free pages and the `-wal` is truncated, so none of the
erased bytes remain in the database file, its `-wal` or its `-shm`. A
scrub that does not finish after the deletes committed answers
`ErrScrubIncomplete` — the store is erased, a later `Scrub` removes the
bytes — and the node's factory reset still pins its fresh UniqueID then.
`node.FactoryReset` erases the endpoint records before the scrub and
scrubs the file when its credential store is an override. The mechanism
is this module's own (review II, R2-P1-misc-01, R2-P1-dr-rest-02);
connectedhomeip's stores were not read (unverified). Pinned by
`store:TestStoreEraseLeavesNoResidue`,
`TestStoreEraseWhoseCheckpointAReaderBlocks` and
`node:TestFactoryResetWhoseScrubAReaderBlocksStillPins`. Register row
above; the row closes when matter.js's erase removes the deleted bytes.

### BD-Matter-ReservedLocalIDs — a caller-chosen local node id is reserved, and an allocation skips an id a node holds

matter.js creates a client node under the id the caller gives or under an
allocated one (`packages/node/src/node/client/Peers.ts:960` at `db021da0`:
`options.id ?? …clientStores.allocateId()`), and `allocateId` returns the
counter's next value
(`packages/node/src/storage/client/ClientNodeStores.ts:77-81`). The
counter is kept "ahead of any persisted "peerN" id" when the stores are
constructed (`:47-54`); nothing at these lines moves it past an id a
caller chose at run time. What matter.js does when an allocation then
reaches such an id was not traced (unverified). `client.Registry` reserves
a caller-chosen id as it reserves a stored one, and `allocateIDLocked`
skips any id a node holds (`controller/client/registry.go`,
`addresses.go`), so no two nodes share an id and with it their store rows.
This module's own rule. Review II, R2-P1-ctl-01. Pinned by
`controller/client:TestCallerChosenIDIsReserved`. Register row above; the
row closes when matter.js reserves a preassigned id.

### BD-chip-SessionRouteByNewCounter — a secure session's route moves with every message that carries a new counter

connectedhomeip sets a session's peer address only for a message that is
not a duplicate, on any exchange — "Only a message with a new message
counter may change the peer address" (`src/transport/SessionManager.cpp:1054-1068`
at `6170af84`, the comment at `:1058`). matter.js adopts the address only
when a non-duplicate initiator message opens a new exchange — "the new
message wins" (`packages/protocol/src/protocol/ExchangeManager.ts:462-486`
at `db021da0`, the comment at `:480`) and "We ignore "inter exchange"
address changes for now" (`:482`). This module follows connectedhomeip
(`bridge/receive.go`, `bindSessionRoute` in `bridge/conn.go`): every
authenticated datagram with a new message counter moves the route its
session's reports, BDX and OTA exchanges and the CloseSession farewell
take, on any exchange; a duplicate moves nothing and is still
acknowledged. Reason: a peer whose address changed is reached again by
its next message of any kind, where matter.js's rule waits for it to open
an exchange. Neither rule lets a replayed datagram move the route; before
`8c0fa135` this module's did — it bound the route on every datagram that
decrypted, duplicates included, under a comment that cited
`ExchangeManager.ts:425-431` for "the new message wins", lines that are
the acknowledge-and-close of a closing exchange at the pin (review II,
R2-P1-req-01). Pinned by
`bridge:TestReceive_ReplayDoesNotMoveSessionRoute` and
`TestReceive_NewMessageFromNewAddressMovesSessionRoute`. Retire when
matter.js moves a session's address on every new message.

### BD-Matter-MdnsLegacyQuerierNoSpecialCase — an mDNS query from a source port other than 5353 gets no special case

Parity with matter.js, recorded because connectedhomeip differs (owner
decision 32 of review II, R2-P1-net-03). matter.js does not tell a legacy
(one-shot) querier apart: "A legacy resolver, which we cannot distinguish
because the source port does not reach us"
(`packages/protocol/src/mdns/InterfaceResponder.ts:938-939` at
`b25ed960`); its multicast server hands a listener the message, the peer
address and the interface and drops the port
(`packages/general/src/net/udp/UdpMulticastServer.ts:142-156`). This
module's responder reads the source port nowhere on its answer path
(`mdns/answer.go`, `mdns/hold.go`): where an answer goes is decided by the
QU bit, whatever port the query came from, and no answer repeats the
question. connectedhomeip answers a query from another port by unicast
and with the question section
(`src/lib/dnssd/minimal_mdns/ResponseSender.cpp:45-53` at `6170af84`:
`SendUnicast()` is the query's unicast request or
`SrcPort != kMdnsStandardPort`, `IncludeQuery()` is
`SrcPort != kMdnsStandardPort`), and its own resolver may query from an
ephemeral port, such queries "being considered LEGACY by mdns"
(`src/lib/dnssd/minimal_mdns/Server.cpp:233-237`,
`CHIP_MINMDNS_USE_EPHEMERAL_UNICAST_PORT`). Cost: a one-shot querier that
sends from an ephemeral port without the QU bit (RFC 6762 §6.7) is
answered by multicast to port 5353 and does not receive it. Not pinned by
a test. Retire when matter.js answers a legacy querier by unicast, or the
owner reopens the decision.

### BD-Matter-MdnsOnLinkSource — an mDNS query is answered only from a source on the link of the interface it arrived on

matter.js gets this filter from how it finds a packet's interface when
its socket has none configured
(`packages/nodejs/src/net/NodeJsUdpSocket.ts:227` at `b25ed960`): the
source's zone, else the interface one of whose addresses contains the
source under its netmask (`packages/nodejs/src/net/NodeJsNetwork.ts:144-166`;
`onSameNetwork`, `packages/general/src/util/Ip.ts:108-130`), else `""` for
an IPv6 source that starts with `fd` and `undefined` otherwise. A packet
without an interface is dropped
(`packages/general/src/net/udp/UdpMulticastServer.ts:142-156`), and the
`""` interface has no details (`NodeJsNetwork.ts:207-209`;
`packages/protocol/src/mdns/InterfaceResponder.ts:206-213`), so its query
is not answered (`InterfaceResponder.ts:254-259`, `:796-800`). This
module's responder applies the same filter (`mdns/answer.go`, `onLink`):
a source is on the link when it is IPv6 link-local or inside one of the
prefixes of the interface the query arrived on; any other is answered
neither by multicast nor by unicast and is not held as a truncated query.
An IPv4 link-local source (169.254/16) is on the link only when the
interface holds a 169.254 address, as matter.js's netmask test has it
(R2-P1-dr-rest-07; `docs/guides/operations.md` names the sources a real
network has that the check refuses). One difference: matter.js matches
the source against every interface of the host and answers on the one
that contains it; this responder answers on the interface the query
arrived on (the control message's, `mdns/socket.go`) and checks that
interface's prefixes. Reason: the sockets bind the wildcard address, so a
datagram sent by unicast to the host's port 5353 reaches the responder
from anywhere (RFC 6762 §11; review II, R2-P1-net-02). Pinned by
`mdns:TestResponder_AnswersOnlyOnLinkSources`. Retire when the responder
matches a source as matter.js does, or matter.js checks the arrival
interface.

The hop limit of a received packet is not read, as in both references: matter.js's receive callback takes only the remote address and port (`packages/nodejs/src/net/NodeJsUdpSocket.ts:225-232` at `b25ed960`) and no hop-limit or TTL option is set or read anywhere in its sources; connectedhomeip requests only `IP_PKTINFO`/`IPV6_RECVPKTINFO` (`src/inet/UDPEndPointImplSockets.cpp:538-553` at `6170af84`) and sends multicast with hop limit 64 (`src/inet/InetConfig.h:250-252`, applied at `UDPEndPointImplSockets.cpp:120-125`, `:159-164`), so a hop-limit-255 rule would refuse or demote chip's own queriers. The on-link source check and the per-source unicast budget (`BD-Matter-MdnsUnicastAnswersBounded`) are the bound. Review II, phase 6a (N-net-1 b).

### BD-Matter-PendingNOCMarker — the fabric row carries what an AddNOC or UpdateNOC wrote as pending until CommissioningComplete commits it

matter.js keeps the fabric an AddNOC built in the manager's table, in memory,
and persists the table when the commissioning completes: `buildFabric` adds it
(`packages/protocol/src/common/FailsafeContext.ts:256` at `db021da0`;
`addFabric`, `packages/protocol/src/fabric/FabricManager.ts:202-218`, stores
nothing) and `completeCommission` calls `persistFabrics`
(`FailsafeContext.ts:141-143`). That is not its only write, and this entry's
earlier sentence — matter.js persists a new fabric only in
`completeCommission` — was false. `persistFabrics` writes every fabric of the
table (`FabricManager.ts:187-200`, the list at `:197`), and it also runs from
each fabric's persist callback (`:236-249`), which a label change and a change
of the VID verification data of any fabric reach
(`packages/protocol/src/fabric/Fabric.ts:193-202`, `:243`), after a fabric's
deletion (`FabricManager.ts:262-273`) and in `replaceFabric` (`:381-402`),
which UpdateNOC calls before it answers
(`packages/node/src/behaviors/operational-credentials/OperationalCredentialsServer.ts:366-369`,
`FailsafeContext.ts:167-170`). So an UpdateNOC's credentials are stored with
the command, and an AddNOC's fabric with the next persist of any fabric inside
the window; the stored list carries no mark of a fabric the fail-safe has not
committed (a search of `FabricManager.ts` and `Fabric.ts` for `pending` finds
no line), and the manager's construction adds every stored fabric
(`FabricManager.ts:68-71`). What a restart inside the window then serves was
not run (unverified). connectedhomeip flags an added fabric as pending
(`src/credentials/FabricTable.cpp:1762` at `6170af84`; where the pending
certificates and key are held was not read, unverified) and stores it in
`CommitPendingFabricData` (`:1857`), whose several writes a commit marker
guards: stored first (`:1952`), cleared last (`:2079`), and a start that finds
it deletes that fabric index (`:1129-1140`) and schedules the fail-safe's
cleanup for it once the server is up, as an addition whichever it was
(`src/app/server/Server.cpp:662-679`). This module writes as the commands run
— the fabric, its identity, its key set and its ACL entry — and the fabric row
itself says that the write is not committed (owner decision 36 of review II;
`cluster/core/operational_credentials.go`, the store's `FabricPending`):
AddNOC inserts the row as a pending add; UpdateNOC is one write that marks the
row a pending update and keeps the replaced credentials in it;
CommissioningComplete commits the row with one write, its last
(`OperationalCredentials.CommitFailSafe`); and a fail-safe's end, a fresh arm,
the head of the next AddNOC or UpdateNOC and every start roll back each row
still pending. A start hands the adds it rolled back to the node, which runs
their removal consequences before it serves (`RolledBackFabrics`), as
connectedhomeip does, and the updates it rolled back (`RolledBackUpdates`),
for which the node removes the fabric's resumption records, ends the client
stack's sessions to its peers and tells the host (`OnFabricUpdated`), as the
rollback of an update at run time does (R2-P2-dr-noc-05); no reference was
read for that half (unverified). A fresh arm rolls back before it is recorded,
so an arm from the fabric that rollback removes answers FAILURE and arms
nothing (R2-P2-dr-noc-04). The two settings keys this entry described before
(`operational_credentials.pending_noc`,
`operational_credentials.pending_noc_update`) are only read: a start rolls
back and clears what an earlier build left under them
(`cluster/core/operational_credentials_pending.go`). Reason: the state a
restart must undo sits in the row it describes and moves in the same write —
the markers were a second record beside it, and review II found nine states
that the two keys and the server's memory could not represent or handled
wrongly — and no stored fabric reads as committed before
CommissioningComplete. Review II, owner decision 36, R2-P2-comm-01,
R2-P2-comm-04 to -07, -10 and -12. Pinned by the `TestRow_` cases of
`cluster/core` (`operational_credentials_row_test.go`),
`TestGencomm_CommissioningCompleteCommitsTheRowOrNothing`,
`TestGencomm_CommissioningCompleteCrashPoints`,
`TestOpcreds_RestartBeforeCommissioningComplete_RevertsAddNOC`,
`TestOpcreds_RestartBeforeCommissioningComplete_RevertsUpdateNOC`,
`TestOpcreds_LegacyMarkerRolledBackAtStart` and
`node:TestRestartRollsBackAnUncommittedFabricWithItsRemoval`; the columns and
the two keys are in `docs/guides/persistence.md`.

### BD-Matter-ArmOverDueWindowEndedSession — an arm that rolls back a due fail-safe itself arms nothing when that rollback ended its own session

This module's own rule: neither reference answers as it does (the
entry named at the end). A fail-safe window past its deadline whose
expiry has not run yet is expired by the ArmFailSafe that finds it: the
arm runs that rollback, or waits for one in flight, before it judges the
fail-safe fresh (`cluster/core/general_commissioning_rollback.go`; review
II, the residuals of R2-P1-core-01). When the rollback ended the session
the arm came on — a PASE session the PASE close ends, or a CASE session
of the fabric the window's AddNOC added — the arm arms nothing and the
command answers FAILURE; an arm from a session the rollback left standing
arms a fresh fail-safe (R2-P1-dr-sec-03). Reason: a fail-safe armed for a
session that no longer exists could only run out. Pinned by
`cluster/core:TestGencomm_ArmOverADueWindowArmsNothingForAnEndedSession`,
`TestGencomm_ArmOverADueWindowFromASurvivingSessionArms`,
`TestGencomm_ArmOverADueWindowRollsItBack` and
`TestGencomm_ArmInTheExpiryGapWaitsForTheRollback`. Phase 4 of review II
read both references and found three answers, matter.js's, connectedhomeip's
and this one; the owner kept this one (decision 77), and what the other two
answer is in `BD-Matter-ArmDuringRollbackWaits`.

### BD-Matter-Controller-UnsecuredSessionsBounded — the controller holds at most 256 sessions that unauthenticated peers opened

matter.js keeps its unsecured sessions in a map with no count over it
(`packages/protocol/src/session/SessionManager.ts:257` at `db021da0`;
`createUnsecuredSession`, `:469-508`), one for every unsecured request
that names a new initiator node id
(`packages/protocol/src/protocol/ExchangeManager.ts:312-328`); a session
an inbound message created is closed once that message is handled unless
an exchange holds it — "otherwise any peer can grow the session table
without authenticating" (`:245-257`). The controller's exchange manager
holds at most `maxInboundUnsecuredSessions` = 256 sessions that a peer's
Sigma1 or PBKDFParamRequest opened (`client/exchange/manager.go`); the
next one closes the oldest, with the warning
`matter.controller.unsecured_session_evicted`, and neither a secure
session nor the unsecured session of a handshake the controller opened is
ever taken. The number is the device side's `maxUnsecuredWindows`
(`bridge/securechannel.go`) — owner decision 45 of review II puts the
device side's policy on the controller — and no reference's.
connectedhomeip is the comparison: its pool of unauthenticated sessions
holds `CHIP_CONFIG_UNAUTHENTICATED_CONNECTION_POOL_SIZE` = 4 and rotates
by least recent use (`src/lib/core/CHIPConfig.h:768-777`,
`src/transport/UnauthenticatedSessionTable.h:341-355` at `6170af84`); a
build whose pools are on the heap has no rotation and fails only when the
heap does (`:337-339`). Reason: a session per datagram, each with its
exchange, is state a sender that has not authenticated must not be able
to grow without end. Review II, R2-P2-alloc-02. Pinned by
`client/exchange:TestInboundUnsecuredSessionsAreBounded`; the limit is in
`docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js
bounds its unsecured sessions.

### BD-Matter-Controller-UnsecuredAckWaitsBounded — at most 16 messages to unauthenticated peers wait for an acknowledgement on the controller

The marker is `BD-Matter-UnsecuredRetransmitEviction`'s: matter.js keeps
the message awaiting its acknowledgement and its retransmission timer on
the exchange (`packages/protocol/src/protocol/MessageExchange.ts:285`,
`:293` at `db021da0`), with no table and no count over them. That entry's
rule, set for the device side by owner decision 23 of review II, is the
controller's too by owner decision 45: of the messages sent on sessions
that unauthenticated peers opened, at most `inboundUnsecuredAckWaitLimit`
= 16 wait for their acknowledgement (`client/exchange/manager.go`; the
number of `unsecuredEntryLimit` in `bridge/outbound_reliable.go`), and the
next one ends the oldest wait — that message went out, it loses its
retransmissions and nothing else, and its send returns as if acknowledged
(warning `matter.controller.unsecured_ack_wait_evicted`). connectedhomeip's
table is described in that entry and was not re-read for this one. Reason:
a reply is never refused for a full table, and handshakes that are opened
and not ended free the table themselves. Review II, R2-P2-alloc-02. Pinned
by `client/exchange:TestInboundUnsecuredAckWaitsAreBounded`; the limit is
in `docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes with
`BD-Matter-UnsecuredRetransmitEviction`'s.

### BD-Matter-Controller-UnsecuredSessionLifetime — a session an unauthenticated peer opened on the controller lives at most 60 s

matter.js closes an unsecured session that an inbound message created
after that message only when no exchange holds it
(`packages/protocol/src/protocol/ExchangeManager.ts:252` at `db021da0`),
and sets no timer on the session at these lines. Its PASE responder ends a
pairing after `PASE_PAIRING_TIMEOUT`, 60 s
(`packages/protocol/src/session/pase/PaseServer.ts:33`, `:127`); a search
of `packages/protocol/src/session/case/CaseServer.ts` for `Timer` and
`timeout` finds no line. What else ends the exchange that holds such a
session was not traced (unverified). On the controller a session that an
unauthenticated peer opened is closed, its exchanges with it,
`inboundUnsecuredLifetime` = 60 s after it opened, whatever its handshake
waits for (`client/exchange/manager.go`): the value of the device side's
`unsecuredEntryLifetime` (`bridge/outbound_reliable.go`), which is that
PASE timeout — owner decision 45 of review II. Reason: beside the count,
the lifetime is what gives a place in the table back without a newer
session having to take it, and a handshake takes seconds. Review II,
R2-P2-alloc-02. Pinned by
`client/exchange:TestInboundUnsecuredSessionLifetime`; the limit is in
`docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js
bounds how long an unsecured session a peer opened lives.

### BD-Matter-Controller-UnsecuredSessionOneHandshake — a session an unauthenticated peer opened on the controller holds one CASE handshake

matter.js opens an exchange for every initiator message, not a duplicate,
whose exchange id its session does not hold, and calls the protocol handler
for it (`packages/protocol/src/protocol/ExchangeManager.ts:478-492` at
`db021da0`); the unsecured session is the one of the initiator node id the
message names (`:308-312`). The secure-channel handler hands every such Sigma1
to the CASE server
(`packages/protocol/src/securechannel/SecureChannelProtocol.ts:146-148`),
which starts a handshake for it without a look at what its session already
carries (`packages/protocol/src/session/case/CaseServer.ts:61-64`) and closes
the unsecured session when that handshake ends, however it ends (`:95-99`).
For PASE it has the rule this entry takes: a new exchange is ignored while a
pairing is in progress
(`packages/protocol/src/session/pase/PaseServer.ts:80-86`). On the controller
a session that an unauthenticated peer opened holds at most
`maxInboundUnsecuredHandshakes` = 1 exchange that a Sigma1 opened
(`client/exchange/manager.go`): a further Sigma1 that opens another exchange
on that session while the first runs is acknowledged and dropped, with the
warning `matter.controller.unsecured_handshake_refused`. An ICD Check-In's
exchange, which ends with its message, and a refused PBKDFParamRequest's are
not counted. The number is this module's choice and has two sources in the
module: a session carries one handshake, because the CASE responder closes the
session when its handshake ends (`client/handshake/server.go`, which mirrors
`CaseServer.ts:95-99`), and the device side ignores a second PASE handshake
while one is in progress (`bridge/securechannel.go`, which mirrors
`PaseServer.ts:80-86`). Who reaches the bound: a peer whose Sigma1 opens
another exchange under a source node id whose handshake still runs. A
legitimate device does so only when it starts over on a new exchange under the
same source node id before its earlier handshake ended: it sees the
acknowledgement and no Sigma2, and its retry after that handshake ended — the
session lives 60 s at most (`BD-Matter-Controller-UnsecuredSessionLifetime`) —
is served. Whether real devices keep the source node id across a retry was not
measured, and no run against the production CASE responder with a valid Sigma1
was made (unverified). connectedhomeip's CASE server holds one handshake (`src/protocols/secure_channel/CASEServer.h:99` at `6170af84`, one `CASESession` member). It counts only a handshake in progress as busy (`src/protocols/secure_channel/CASEServer.cpp:85` at `6170af84`). A Sigma1 that meets one is answered with a StatusReport Busy: the minimum wait is the Sigma2 response timeout once Sigma2 is out, else 5000 ms, clamped to 16 bits (`:99-121`). Since review II, phase 6b (R2-P6-par-2902, owner decision 205) this module answers the same way per inbound unsecured session, instead of the acknowledgement and drop above, and a held handshake whose exchange has already ended does not count. connectedhomeip's watchdog (`:92-93`) has no counterpart here: the module runs no background work helper a handshake could be stuck on. A Busy answer waits for its acknowledgement in one of the `inboundUnsecuredAckWaitLimit` = 16 places, so sixteen refused Sigma1 end an earlier message's wait (that message loses only its retransmissions). Reason: the
bound on the sessions (`BD-Matter-Controller-UnsecuredSessionsBounded`) is a
bound on the CASE handlers only when a session carries one. Review II,
R2-P2-dr-ctl-04, owner decision 45. Pinned by
`client/exchange:TestInboundUnsecuredSessionHoldsOneHandshake`; the limit is
in `docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js
bounds the handshakes one unsecured session carries.

### BD-Matter-UnsecuredWindowExchangesBounded — the duplicate-detection window of an unsecured source on the device is bound to at most four exchanges

matter.js keeps the reception state of unsecured traffic in the unsecured
session of the initiator node id a message names
(`packages/protocol/src/session/UnsecuredSession.ts:37`,
`packages/protocol/src/protocol/ExchangeManager.ts:308-312` at `db021da0`),
and a session created for an inbound message lives on only while it has an
open exchange (`ExchangeManager.ts:245-256`;
`packages/protocol/src/session/Session.ts:381-383`). It opens an exchange for
every initiator message, not a duplicate, whose exchange id the session does
not hold (`ExchangeManager.ts:478-492`), and for any other new message that
asks for an acknowledgement, until that is sent (`:496-503`). The session's
open exchanges are one map (`:551-566`), and the bound matter.js puts on that
map — 30 exchanges, the least recently active one closed beyond it (`:63`,
`:583-595`) — leaves out a session that is not secure (`:579-582`, "PASE/CASE
exchanges are not relevant for this limit"). Nothing at these lines bounds the
exchanges one unsecured session holds; the search went no further than
`ExchangeManager.ts` and `UnsecuredSession.ts` (unverified beyond them).

Here the reception state of an unsecured source is its window in
`unsecuredWindowTable` (`bridge/receive.go`), with matter.js's lifetime in
this module's terms: the window is bound to the exchanges of the source's new
messages and stays while one of them holds handshake state — a reply that
awaits its acknowledgement, the PASE exchange, a Sigma1 record
(`unsecuredExchangeLive`). The end of a message drops the exchanges that hold
none, but not while another message of the source is in dispatch. The set
holds at most `maxUnsecuredWindowExchanges` = 4 exchanges: the message that
names a further one is handled as any other, and its exchange is not bound.

The number is this module's choice and has no source in a reference. matter.js
has none at the lines above, and connectedhomeip's
`CHIP_CONFIG_MAX_EXCHANGE_CONTEXTS`, 16, sizes the one pool of its exchange
manager (`src/lib/core/CHIPConfig.h:303-305`,
`src/messaging/ExchangeMgr.h:253` at `6170af84`) — the whole node's exchanges,
not one peer's; a bound per unauthenticated peer was not looked for there
(unverified). The reasoning the fix chose it with: a handshake, PASE or CASE,
runs on one exchange of its source, and 4 leaves room for a handshake retried
on a new exchange while the earlier reply still awaits its acknowledgement. 4
is also the value of this package's caps per session
(`maxChunkWaitsPerSession` in `bridge/chunk_waits.go`,
`maxChunkedWritesPerSession` in `bridge/exchange_routing.go`), which is the
number's shape, not its source.

Who reaches the bound: a source node id — the sender's unauthenticated choice,
as the exchange id is — whose new message names a fifth exchange while four
are bound: four that hold handshake state, or exchanges named while another
message of the source is still in dispatch. What a legitimate commissioner
sees at it: nothing while the exchange of its handshake is one of the four,
and one handshake needs one exchange. A handshake on a fifth exchange is
served too, but the window does not stay for it: once none of the four holds
handshake state and no message of the source is in dispatch the window goes, a
retransmission of that handshake arriving afterwards is no duplicate at the
window and reaches the handshake handler, and the handler's own state-replay
guard is then what stands against it (`bridge/securechannel.go`, the rule past
`maxUnsecuredWindows` as well); the exchange's next new message binds it once
the set has room. That path was read in the code, not run: no test drives a
handshake on an exchange left unbound, and how the guard answers each
handshake message there was not traced (unverified). Whether a commissioner in
the field holds more than four handshake exchanges under one source node id at
a time was not measured (unverified). Reason: the set is state a peer makes
the device hold, and read with every message of that source, before it has
authenticated; the bound on the windows (`maxUnsecuredWindows`) bounds that
state only when a window's own set is bounded too. Review II, R2-P2-rr-dev-02.
Pinned by `bridge:TestUnsecuredWindowExchangesAreBounded`; the limit is in
`docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js
bounds the exchanges an unsecured session holds.

### BD-Matter-UnauthenticatedIntervalsClamped — the MRP intervals an unauthenticated peer states time a handshake with at most one hour each, on the controller and on the device

matter.js bounds the intervals it advertises at one hour and says of the
ones it receives: "This bound is a property of the advertisement encoding
only; SII/SAI in the CASE/PASE session-parameter struct are uint32 and
accepted unbounded"
(`packages/protocol/src/session/SessionIntervals.ts:52-53`, `:57` at
`b25ed960`). Whether it bounds the intervals it reads from a peer's DNS-SD
record was not read (unverified). connectedhomeip takes the struct's
intervals as stated
(`src/protocols/secure_channel/PairingSession.cpp:175-189` at `6170af84`)
and reads a DNS-SD interval over one hour as not stated
(`src/lib/dnssd/TxtFields.cpp:210-218`, `kMaxRetryInterval` in
`src/lib/dnssd/TxtFields.h:38`). `sessionparams.ClampUnauthenticated`
(`secure/sessionparams/sessionparams.go`) reduces the idle and the active
interval to `MaxUnauthenticatedInterval`, 3 600 000 ms — the bound on the
intervals this module advertises (`mdns/service.go`) — and the controller
applies it where it adopts a peer's parameters for a handshake's unsecured
session, from the DNS-SD record, PBKDFParamResponse, Sigma1 or Sigma2
(`client/exchange/session.go`, `client/exchange/manager.go`). The device
applies it since `e261d8c7` where it adopts an initiator's parameters to pace
its handshake replies, from the PBKDFParamRequest or Sigma1
(`handshakePeerTimingOf`, `bridge/securechannel.go`). On both sides the secure
session the handshake establishes takes the parameters as stated. Owner
decision 45 of review II; for the struct's intervals it is ahead of both
references.
Reason: nothing has authenticated the value that paces the handshake's
retransmissions and the wait for their acknowledgement. Review II,
R2-P2-alloc-02. Pinned by `client/exchange:TestUnauthenticatedTimingIsClamped`
and `bridge:TestHandshakeRetransmitClampsUnauthenticatedIntervals`; the limit
is in `docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when
matter.js bounds the session-parameter intervals it accepts.

### BD-Matter-Controller-DnssdCacheBounded — the controller's DNS-SD cache holds at most 8192 records

matter.js keeps the names it collected in a map with no size limit
(`packages/general/src/net/dns-sd/DnssdNames.ts:43` at `b25ed960`); what
it bounds is the address records staged for hosts that have no name yet,
at 250 hosts (`:21`, `:141-143`). The controller's cache holds at most
`maxCachedRecords` = 8192 records (`client/discovery/names.go`); past
that, the record installed or refreshed longest ago is deleted as an
expiry deletes it, with the warning
`matter.discovery.cache_records_evicted`, and the browser asks again for a
name it still needs. The number is chosen, with no source: the fix's
estimate of some ten records per operational device and about 1 KiB per
cached name gives room for several hundred devices on a link at some
8 MiB — an estimate, not measured in this entry. connectedhomeip's
resolver cache was not read (unverified). Reason: any host on the link can
send records the cache admits. Review II, R2-P2-alloc-03, owner decision
45. Pinned by `client/discovery:TestNames_CachedRecordsAreBounded`; the
limit is in `docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes
when matter.js bounds the names it collects.

Review II, U3-ctl-lan-1 (owner decision 240): past the record bound the cache evicts the records of names no operational resolution observes first; a per-name bound is a later decision. A flood of records that names the observed service or its target is among the observed names and can still evict them. Pinned by `client/discovery:TestNames_FloodEvictsUnresolvedNamesFirst`.

### BD-Matter-Controller-HostDiscoveriesBounded — a service resolution runs at most four host discoveries at once

matter.js starts a host discovery for every SRV target without address records: its `hosts.added` handler (`packages/general/src/net/dns-sd/IpServiceResolution.ts:39` at `b25ed960`) skips a host with A/AAAA records (`:40-47`), and every other host gets `hostResolvers.set` (`:54`) and `solicitor.discover` in `workers.add` (`:55-63`) — no count, no bound. Here a resolution runs at most `maxHostDiscoveries` = 4 host discoveries at once (`client/discovery/operational.go`); the rest wait in SRV order until a target is dropped, a host with cached addresses takes none, and an address that arrives ends the resolution as before. The rule and its number are this module's own. The cache's eviction order of the same row is in `BD-Matter-Controller-DnssdCacheBounded`. Review II, U3-ctl-lan-1. Pinned by `client/discovery:TestOperational_ResolveBoundsItsHostDiscoveries`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js bounds a resolution's host discoveries.

Review II, close-out C3 (R2-C2-bound-2152, decision 519): a Service tracks
at most `maxServiceTargets` = 8 SRV targets (2 × `maxHostDiscoveries`,
`client/discovery/names.go`), the one discovered or refreshed longest ago
going first (`client/discovery/service.go`), so a LAN sender cannot set the
number of a peer's connection attempts through extra SRV targets while the
peer has no session. 8 rather than 5 keeps the waiting-target case
`TestOperational_ResolveBoundsItsHostDiscoveries` holds. Whether matter.js
bounds SRV targets per service or connection attempts per peer was not read
(unverified); no register row of its own. Pinned by
`client/discovery:TestService_SRVTargetsAreBounded`.

### BD-Matter-Controller-DnssdTTLCeiling — the controller caches a DNS-SD record for at most 75 minutes

matter.js lets a record expire at its TTL times a grace factor
(`packages/general/src/net/dns-sd/DnssdName.ts:152` at `b25ed960`) and
raises a TTL below its minimum of 15 s
(`packages/general/src/net/dns-sd/DnssdNames.ts:196-197`, `:551`); nothing
at these lines lowers one. The controller caches a record for at most
`maxRecordTTL` = 4500 s, whatever TTL it states
(`client/discovery/names.go`). The number is RFC 6762 §10's recommended
TTL for records other than a host's; the RFC was not re-read for this
entry (unverified), and connectedhomeip was not read (unverified). Reason:
a TTL is the sender's word for how long its record keeps a place in the
cache, and a responder announces again well inside 75 minutes. Review II,
R2-P2-alloc-03, owner decision 45. Pinned by
`client/discovery:TestNames_TTLHasACeiling`; the limit is in
`docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js
puts a ceiling on a record's TTL.

### BD-Matter-Controller-ReportAssemblyBounded — the report chunks a session's interactions hold are bounded, at 2 MiB unless the host sets another bound

matter.js collects the chunks of an invoke response in one array until the
chunk without MoreChunkedMessages, with no count or size over it
(`packages/protocol/src/interaction/InteractionMessenger.ts:1224`,
`:1233`, `:1246` at `db021da0`). A read's reports it does not collect
there: `readDataReports` hands each chunk on as it arrives (`:1012-1053`);
what its consumers keep of them was not read (unverified). This module's
client merges the chunks of a read, a subscription report and an invoke
response before it hands them over, and bounds what the interactions of
one session hold meanwhile — by default at
`DefaultMaxReportBytesPerSession` = 2 MiB of message payload — the three
kinds together
(`client/interaction/report.go`): the chunk that would pass it is answered
ResourceExhausted, the partial report is dropped and the call returns
`interaction.ErrReportTooLarge`. The number is chosen, with no source: the
fix's estimate of about 1.2 KB of a wildcard read per bridged endpoint, so
some 1700 endpoints, is not measured, and the bound counts payload bytes,
not the larger decoded form. Owner decision 48 therefore made it a field of
the configuration: `controller.Config.MaxReportBytesPerSession` (0 is the
default, a negative value `controller.ErrConfiguration`) reaches every
interaction with a paired node, and the commissioning steps keep the default
(`30ffe7ba`).
connectedhomeip's read client was not read (unverified). Reason: a peer
that keeps MoreChunkedMessages set would otherwise grow the merge without
end. Review II, R2-P2-alloc-05, owner decision 45. Pinned by
`client/interaction:TestReportAssemblyIsBounded`,
`TestInvokeResponseAssemblyIsBounded`, `TestReportBoundFromConfig` and
`controller:TestMaxReportBytesPerSessionReachesTheNodes`; the limit is in
`docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js
bounds the chunks of a response it collects.

### BD-Matter-Controller-DclListingBounded — one paginated DCL listing is bounded at 64 MiB of wire bytes and at 65 536 items

matter.js appends every page's items to one array for as long as the answer
names a next key, with no count of pages, no size over the items and no count
of them (`packages/protocol/src/dcl/DclClient.ts:70-86` at `b25ed960`,
`#fetchPaginatedJson`); each answer is read whole (`response.json()`, `:108`).
`dcl` reads at most `maxPages` = 1000 pages of at most
`maxResponseBody` = 16 MiB each and holds, for one listing, at most
`maxListingBytes` = 64 MiB of its items' wire bytes and at most
`maxListingItems` = 65 536 items, decoded one at a time, the listing refused
before the item past the bound is decoded (`dcl/client.go`); a
listing that passes a bound fails with an error. Both numbers are chosen, with
no source. The 64 MiB are four answers' worth of the bound on one answer. The
65 536 are there because the bytes bound the wire and not the memory: an item
of three wire bytes decodes to a whole struct, so 64 MiB of items could be
some 22 million of them. The fix's reasoning for the number is that the
production ledger's listings are far smaller, which it did not measure and
this entry does not either (unverified). The memory ceiling of one decoded
listing is therefore 65 536 structs — about 9 MiB at the 144 bytes the fix
gives for the larger item type, not re-measured here — and the strings of at
most 64 MiB of wire bytes. connectedhomeip was not read (unverified). Reason:
the bound on the pages alone left one listing a thousand times the bound on an
answer, and the bound on the bytes alone left its decoded size open. Review
II, R2-P2-alloc-08, R2-P2-dr-ctl-03. Pinned by
`dcl:TestListingBound` and `TestListingItemBound`; the limits are
in `docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js
bounds a paginated listing.

### BD-Matter-BDX-BlockPastLengthRefusedBeforeWrite — a BDX block that would pass the transfer's definite length is refused before it is written

matter.js's receiver enqueues a block into the write stream
(`packages/protocol/src/bdx/flow/InboundFlow.ts:78` at `b25ed960`), then
counts it against the bytes left (`:80-82`), and compares the two only at
BlockEof, where bytes left over or an overrun end the transfer with
LengthTooShort or LengthTooLarge (`:87-93`). `bdx/session.go` refuses a
block longer than the bytes left of a definite length with LengthTooLarge
before the sink sees it. connectedhomeip's receiver was not read
(unverified). Reason: the length a sender announced is what the receiver
sized its sink for, and a sender that sends no BlockEof would otherwise
write past it. Review II, R2-P2-alloc-06. Pinned by
`bdx:TestReceive_OverrunNotWritten`. Register row above; the row closes
when matter.js checks a block against the bytes left before it enqueues
it.

### BD-Matter-CASE-RemovedFabricRefusedAtCompletion — a CASE handshake that completes after its fabric was removed opens no session

matter.js's CASE responder resolves the fabric while it answers Sigma1
(`packages/protocol/src/session/case/CaseServer.ts:237` at `b25ed960`) —
`findFabricFromDestinationId` refuses there a fabric that is being deleted
(`packages/protocol/src/fabric/FabricManager.ts:360-362`) — and, after
Sigma3's checks, creates the session with that fabric
(`CaseServer.ts:307-327`) without a look at its state in between. A
deletion that runs while the session already exists closes it: the session
is in its fabric's set from its creation (`NodeSession.ts:166`),
`Fabric.delete` force-closes that set (`Fabric.ts:493-496`) and the
responder refuses the closed session at completion (`CaseServer.ts:206`,
`:344`, `:367-376`). A deletion before the session exists is not looked at
on a full handshake (the window above); whether anything closes the session
then created was not traced, nor was resumption (where the fabric comes from
the record, `:155`, and the session is created at `:177`), and a deletion after
the Success's first transmission is not refused (`:337-357`; findings
F-b25ed960-34). The initiator
(`packages/protocol/src/session/case/CaseClient.ts`) was not read for it
(unverified); connectedhomeip was not read (unverified). In this module
`caseIdentities.admitSession` (`node/security.go`) checks that the
fabric's identity is still there before the session of a completed
handshake opens and again after it, as responder and as initiator: a
removal that ran while the handshake did leaves no session, and one that
lands between the two checks either finds the session and closes it or
leaves that to the second check. The controller's responder
(`client/handshake.CASEServer`) refuses likewise a session its fabric's
teardown closed while it established
(`client/handshake:TestCASEServerResponderSessionEstablishing`, pin-lift
unit P1-A); the teardown's `Manager.CloseSession` marks the session closing
before its CloseSession goes out, as `Session.ts:311` precedes `:319`
(fix-up X1 of wave P1). Reason: the removal closes the fabric's
sessions before this one exists, so it would live on the removed index
with nothing to end it, and could keep the node's own window from
reopening after the last fabric's removal. Review II, R2-P2-sess-05,
R2-P2-fabric-09. Pinned by
`node:TestCASEResponderRefusesASessionOfARemovedFabric`,
`TestCASEInitiatorRefusesASessionOfARemovedFabric` and
`TestAdmitSessionClosesASessionWhoseFabricWentWhileItOpened`. Register row
above; the row closes when matter.js checks the fabric before it creates
the session.

A parity statement (review II, run 5, R5-sec-5101 to R5-sec-5103, owner
decisions 638, 643): the session the node installs is the value the
handshake step that established it returns — keys, session ids, peer node
id, CATs, fabric and the resumption record's secret and id
(`sigma.Established`, built under the responder's lock in that step;
`bridge.CaseAdapter.SetOnEstablished`) — and nothing is read back off the
responder after the step. matter.js creates the secure session from the
handshake's own values in one call: `createSecureSession({…})` at
`CaseServer.ts:177-190` (resumption) and `:314-327` (Sigma3) at `b25ed960`,
every value a local of the handshake (`cx.resumptionRecord` `:155`,
`responderSessionId` `:175`, `cx.peerSessionId` `:182` / `:319`, the NOC
subject `:298-301`; fable-diff-h1 §2). The deprecated
`CaseAdapter.SnapshotResponder` read-back keeps the hazard for a host that
still uses it (decision 643: no step lock). Pinned by
`bridge:TestCaseEstablishedIsTheStepsOwnSession`,
`TestResumeAwaitsItsOwnInstalledSession`,
`TestSigma3WithoutStepValueIsNoEstablishment` and
`secure/sigma:TestProcessSigma3EstablishedReturnsTheStepsSession`.

### BD-Matter-NonVolatileWrite-StoredBeforeApplied — a controller's write of a nonvolatile attribute is stored before the server takes it; every other change is stored after the server committed it

matter.js commits state and storage together, whoever made the change: commit
phase one notes each changed value, collects the persistent ones and hands
them to the store
(`packages/node/src/behavior/state/managed/Datasource.ts:1225-1262` at
`db021da0`: `commit1`, the store's `set` at `:1261`; the changed names at
`:1442-1454`), a failure there rolls every participant back
(`packages/general/src/transaction/Tx.ts:933-974`), only phase two makes the
working values canonical (`Datasource.ts:1267-1281`), the change events are
emitted after it (`postCommit`, `:1286-1326`), and a rollback puts the
canonical values back (`:1331-1332`). So at these lines no value is canonical
or announced before it was handed to the store. Where in that sequence a value
the behaviour refuses is stopped was not traced (unverified). What it stores
is every nonvolatile member and every writable or fabric-scoped attribute
(`packages/node/src/behavior/supervision/RootSupervisor.ts:160-173`). This
module has no transaction over a server's state: a server checks and commits
inside one `MatterWrite`, one command or one `Set` of the host. The node's
persister (`node/nonvolatile.go`) therefore has two orders. A controller's
write is stored before the server sees it (through `endpoint.WritePersister`,
after the dispatcher's gates): a store that refuses answers FAILURE and the
server never sees the write; when the server refuses the write, the previous
stored value is put back; and once the server applied it, the value the server
then holds replaces the written one where the two differ (`storeHeld`:
WindowCovering's Mode, a companion the write moved), so the stored form is the
served one, not the written one. Every other change — a command, a companion
attribute the server moves, the host's `Set` — is stored after the server
committed it, from the server's own change notification (`spec.ChangesOf`), as
the value the server then holds. That is the divergence from matter.js's
order, in which the store comes before the value is canonical and before the
notification: on these paths the store cannot refuse the change. A store that
refuses is logged (`nonvolatile.persist`), the value stays in effect, and the
key is owed: it is written again at the attribute's next change, when the node
stops and when the host forgets the device. The persister keeps the attributes
whose generated definition carries the N quality and write access, not
fabric-scoped, of a server the module holds (owner decision 38 of review II) —
the root's own servers, not one the host mounts there (`Config.RootServers`),
and on a bridged endpoint a server its device built — not every writable
attribute, and none a host port carries. It leaves out every fabric-scoped
attribute, which matter.js's `persistentKeys` takes whatever its quality
(`RootSupervisor.ts:168-169`): the state of a fabric is stored by the server
that holds it — the store's fabric, ACL and group rows, the AccessControl
Extension entry, Binding, DefaultOTAProviders — and leaves with its fabric
(`contract.FabricScopedState`), which a value under a `nonvolatile.` key would
not; whether every fabric-scoped attribute the module serves is stored by its
server was not checked here (unverified). What a crash leaves follows from the
two orders. Between a server's commit of such a change and its store write:
the value stored before the change, which the restart serves, so a controller
may have read a value that does not survive. Between a write's store and the
undo of a value the server refused: the refused value — the restore hands it
to the server's checks, which refuse it again, logged as
`nonvolatile.restore`. Between a write's store and the store of the form the
server committed: the written form; what the restore's write of it leaves in
the server was not traced (unverified). Reason: a controller's write is never
in effect without being stored, through one seam at the dispatcher instead of
a pre-commit step in every server; a command and a host's `Set` change the
server with no seam ahead of its commit, so there the store follows the commit
and what it refused is owed. Review II, R2-P2-store-04, R2-P2-store-07,
R2-P2-dr-node-01, R2-P2-dr-node-05. Pinned by
`node:TestNonVolatileWriteSurvivesARestart`,
`TestNonVolatileWriteRefusedByTheStore`,
`TestNonVolatileWriteRefusedByTheServer`,
`TestNonVolatileStoresTheCommittedValue`,
`TestNonVolatileChangeSurvivesARestart`,
`TestNonVolatileChangeOwedWhileTheStoreRefuses` and
`TestNonVolatileHostRootServerIsTheHosts`. Retire when a server's change can
be checked without being committed on every path, so that the store sees a
value the server took before it is in effect.

Review II, phase 6b (R2-P6-par-2903, owner decision 206): a store that refuses answers FAILURE for that attribute path only: the server never sees the value, and the request's other paths are written and answered. matter.js turns only a `StatusResponseError` into the path's status and rethrows the rest (`packages/protocol/src/action/server/AttributeWriteResponse.ts:452-458`, `:459` at `db021da0`), and its messenger answers the interaction with StatusResponse FAILURE (`InteractionMessenger.ts:431-459`); this module keeps the per-path status, so the controller learns which path failed and the statuses of the written ones. Pinned by `endpoint:TestRefusedStoreWriteFailsOnlyItsPath`. The host's rename of a bridged device (`device.Device.Rename` through `node`) follows the rule: the label is stored before it is served, and a refused store is returned to the host and serves nothing (R2-P5-apidev-16, owner decision 200).

### BD-Matter-RevokeCommissioning-PASEArmedFailSafeOnly — RevokeCommissioning expires only the fail-safe that was armed over a PASE session

Both references expire more. matter.js's `revokeCommissioning` closes the PASE
session
(`packages/node/src/behaviors/administrator-commissioning/AdministratorCommissioningServer.ts:138-141`
at `db021da0`) and then closes whatever fail-safe context the environment
holds (`:143-148`), without a look at who armed it — under a comment that
names the "PASE-held fail-safe" (`:137`). connectedhomeip's handler calls
`ExpireFailSafeIfHeldByOpenPASESession` first
(`src/app/clusters/administrator-commissioning-server/AdministratorCommissioningLogic.cpp:113`
at `6170af84`), whose condition is that a PASE session exists: it then expires
the fail-safe if one is armed, whoever armed it
(`src/app/server/CommissioningWindowManager.cpp:641-657`). This module's
condition is that the fail-safe was armed over PASE:
`GeneralCommissioning.ExpireFailSafeArmedOverPASE`
(`cluster/core/general_commissioning.go`), which
`CommissioningWindow.RevokeWindow` calls through `bridge.FailSafeExpirer`,
expires a fail-safe that a PASE session armed from the disarmed state — the
mark stays through its re-arms and through the AddNOC that re-stamps it onto
the new fabric, and goes when the fail-safe ends — and leaves one that an
administrator armed over CASE. Of the other ends of a window, one expires the
same way and one expires nothing: a host's block that finds a window open
(`CommissioningWindow.SetBlocked`) revokes it through `RevokeWindow`, so it
closes the PASE sessions and expires a PASE-armed fail-safe as
RevokeCommissioning does; the PASE lockout does not revoke — it closes the
window as the end of commissioning closes it
(`CommissioningWindow.EndCommissioning`, called from
`bridge/securechannel.go`), expires no fail-safe and closes no PASE session,
as matter.js closes the window once its failed-attempt count reaches
`MAX_FAILED_COMMISSIONING_ATTEMPTS` = 20
(`packages/protocol/src/protocol/DeviceCommissioner.ts:44`, `:181-198`, at
`b25ed960`; the handler of too many PASE errors, `tooManyPaseErrors` →
`endCommissioning`, is gone at that pin), and its `#closeWindow` stops the
window's timer, removes the PASE commissioner and leaves commissioning mode
(`:318-334`); matter.js keeps PASE refused by no timer afterwards — the
timed lockout is ahead of matter.js (`BD-Matter-PASE-TimedLockout`). Until
the rework of review II's phase 2 the lockout revoked (R2-P2-dr-noc-01). The conditions part in two
cases: with a PASE session open and another administrator's fail-safe armed
over CASE both references expire that fail-safe and this module does not; with
a PASE-armed fail-safe running and its PASE session already gone
connectedhomeip expires nothing and this module expires it. Reason (owner
decision 42 of review II): a fail-safe an administrator armed over CASE — an
UpdateNOC, a step of another fabric's commissioning — is not the commissioning
the revoke aborts, and expiring it rolls back another fabric's work. Review
II, R2-P2-comm-08. Pinned by
`bridge:TestCommissioningWindow_RevokeExpiresOnlyThePASEFailSafe`, and
`TestBridge_PaseLockoutClosesOnlyTheWindow` for the lockout. Retire when both
references narrow the expiry to the fail-safe a PASE session armed.

### BD-Matter-PASE-TimedLockout — PASE stays refused for a timed cooldown after the failure cap, beyond the window

matter.js at `b25ed960` counts failed commissioning attempts per window — a
PASE pairing that fails before it establishes a session (`PaseServer.ts`
`pairingFailed`, wired at
`packages/protocol/src/protocol/DeviceCommissioner.ts:251`) and a fail-safe
that ends without commissioning (`:160-174`) — and at
`MAX_FAILED_COMMISSIONING_ATTEMPTS` = 20 (`:44`) closes the window
(`this.#close(() => window)`, `:198`; `#closeWindow` `:318-334` stops the
timer, removes the PASE commissioner and leaves commissioning mode). No timer
keeps PASE refused afterwards. The mechanism this module mirrored at
`db021da0` (`PASE_COMMISSIONING_MAX_ERRORS`,
`MaximumPasePairingErrorsReachedError`, `tooManyPaseErrors`) is gone at that
pin.
This module closes the window at the same cap (`paseMaxErrors` = 20) and in
addition refuses PASE for a timed cooldown, 15 minutes doubling up to 4 hours
(`paseLockoutCooldown`, `paseLockoutMaxCooldown`, `bridge/securechannel.go`);
opening a commissioning window clears it.

Ahead of matter.js (register row `BD-Matter-PASE-TimedLockout`). Reason: an
uncommissioned daemon answers PASE from its configured passcode with no window
open, so a refusal that ends with the window would not end at all, and one
that is dropped at once would leave the passcode open to unbounded guessing;
20 guesses per 15 minutes keeps the passcode space out of reach while an
operator who mistyped the code waits minutes. The fail-safe half of
matter.js's count is mirrored since pin-lift unit P3-C (`recordFailedAttempt`,
`bridge/securechannel.go`; `failSafeSessionsClosed`, `bridge/pase_close.go`).
The cap is reached by either kind of failed attempt — a PASE failure, or a
fail-safe that ends without commissioning in the window it was armed in — and
engages the lockout either way (owner decision O-4, 374); a
RevokeCommissioning whose fail-safe end is the twentieth engages it too and
still answers success, as matter.js's does
(`packages/node/src/behaviors/administrator-commissioning/AdministratorCommissioningServer.ts:137-158`
at `b25ed960`). The count restarts with every window open
(`DeviceCommissioner.ts:289-299`); the lockout ends with its cooldown or a
freshly attached acceptor. PASE failures with no window open are counted as
well — matter.js has no PASE commissioner then (`:323-327`). A fail-safe
armed with no window open is not counted (owner decision O-5, 375; `:162`,
`:170-172`), nor one that outlives its window (`:181-184`). The fail-safe
half is counted where the bridge wires `core.GeneralCommissioning`; a host
with a GeneralCommissioning server of its own has the PASE half only. Pinned by `TestBridge_PaseLockoutExpiresOnItsOwn`,
`TestBridge_PaseLockoutBacksOffOnRepeatedCaps` and
`TestBridge_PaseLockoutClosesOnlyTheWindow`. Retire when matter.js keeps
PASE refused beyond the window.

### BD-Matter-Shutdown-CloseSessionKept — the node's shutdown tells each peer with a CloseSession, where matter.js ends its sessions without one

matter.js's shutdown ends each secure session in two steps
(`closeAllSessions`,
`packages/protocol/src/session/SessionManager.ts:1097-1130` at `db021da0`,
called from `packages/node/src/node/ServerNode.ts:152-155`):
`closeSubscriptionsForShutdown` flushes what the session's subscriptions owe
and closes them without terminating them (`:1108`;
`packages/protocol/src/session/NodeSession.ts:326-329`, `:312-324`), and
`initiateForceClose` (`SessionManager.ts:1113`) marks the peer lost
(`NodeSession.ts:379-382`), so the session's `close` skips the `gracefulClose`
emit (`:419-425`) that sends the CloseSession
(`packages/protocol/src/protocol/ExchangeManager.ts:758`). Its own TODO
questions the silent close: some CHIP tests "expect us to exit without closing
the session", and it "leads to a timeout when the node attempts contact even
if we've already restarted" (`SessionManager.ts:1110-1112`). This module
mirrors the first step — `Bridge.Stop` reports what every subscription owes
before the sessions close (`flushSubscriptionsForShutdown`,
`bridge/bridge.go`), and the close keeps the stored subscriptions for
re-establishment — and keeps a CloseSession for the second
(`operational.Manager.CloseAllGraceful`, `secure/operational/manager.go`):
owner decision 49 of review II. Reason: the cost that TODO names. With the
silent close this module's own controller kept sending on its session of
before the restart, and its request failed only once MRP gave up — after about
49 s in six restart tests, by the fix's measurement, not repeated here; with
the farewell a controller drops the session at once and establishes CASE
again. The decision also has the controller hardened to recover from a peer
that went away without a farewell, as after a power loss: the interaction that
finds the peer gone gives up the session it ran on, and the next one
establishes CASE again.
Review II, R2-P2-sess-03. Pinned by `bridge:TestStop_DrainsSessionsGracefully`
for the farewell and `TestStopFlushesTheSubscriptionsBeforeTheSessionsEnd` and
`node:TestStopFlushesTheShutDownEventToItsSubscribers` for the flush. Retire
when the owner reopens the decision — the controller's recovery from a silent
peer, its precondition, is in the tree — or when matter.js resolves its TODO
for the farewell.

### BD-Matter-Camera-FabricRemovalEndsStreams — a removed fabric's camera sessions and push transports end through the host's ports

matter.js strips a removed fabric's entries from the three lists and tells no
stream. CurrentSessions of the WebRTC provider and of the requestor and
CurrentConnections of the push transport are fabric-sensitive (`access: "R S
M"`,
`packages/model/src/standard/elements/web-rtc-transport-provider.element.ts:25`;
`"R S A"`, `web-rtc-transport-requestor.element.ts:21`; `"R S V"`,
`push-av-stream-transport.element.ts:38` at `db021da0`), so the node's strip
filters them when the fabric is deleted
(`packages/node/src/behavior/cluster/FabricScopedDataHandler.ts:41-73`,
`packages/node/src/node/server/ServerEnvironment.ts:188-195`); the provider's
and the push transport's servers are empty subclasses
(`WebRtcTransportProviderServer.ts:14`, `PushAvStreamTransportServer.ts:14`)
and the requestor's server reacts to no fabric's deletion
(`WebRtcTransportRequestorServer.ts:42-183`). connectedhomeip's three servers
hold no fabric-removal handler at `6170af84`: a search of
`src/app/clusters/webrtc-transport-provider-server`,
`webrtc-transport-requestor-server` and `push-av-stream-transport-server` for
`OnFabricRemoved`, a fabric-table delegate or a removal by fabric finds none;
whether an application's delegate does it was not read (unverified). This
module strips the entries as matter.js does and also tells the host's port,
which holds the stream (`cluster/camera/fabric_state.go`, through
`contract.FabricScopedState`): a provider session ends through
`ProviderPort.EndSession`, a requestor session leaves CurrentSessions and
`RequestorPort.End` is told, each with the end reason UnknownReason, and a
push transport is deallocated through
`PushTransportPort.DeallocatePushTransport`; an entry leaves its list whatever
the port answers. The reason value is chosen: WebRTCEndReasonEnum has no
member for a removed fabric, UnknownReason (12 in `parity/schema.json`) is the
one that claims no cause, and no reference names a value. Reason: without the
port's call the camera goes on streaming or uploading to a peer whose fabric
is gone. Review II, R2-P2-fabric-04. Pinned by
`cluster/camera:TestProviderDropFabricEndsItsSessions`,
`TestRequestorDropFabricStripsItsSessions` and
`TestPushDropFabricDeallocatesItsConnections`; the guide is
`docs/guides/camera.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js's
servers end a removed fabric's streams.

### BD-Matter-FabricState-ReconciledWithoutFabrics — a server's fabric state is reconciled against the fabric table also when the table is empty

matter.js limits fabric-scoped data to the fabrics that remain at two moments
and skips both when none remains: when a fabric is deleted
(`packages/node/src/node/server/ServerEnvironment.ts:188-195` at `b25ed960`,
the skip at `:190`) and when an endpoint's behaviours initialise on a node
that has fabrics
(`packages/node/src/node/server/ServerEndpointInitializer.ts:129-136`, the
skip at `:133`). The strip filters the entries of every attribute the schema
marks fabric-scoped or fabric-sensitive
(`packages/node/src/behavior/cluster/FabricScopedDataHandler.ts:41-73`,
`:178-189`; `packages/model/src/models/AttributeModel.ts:29-32`) and, on a
deletion, removes the fabric's occurrences of fabric-scoped events
(`FabricScopedDataHandler.ts:151-167`). This module mirrors the two moments
through one contract (`contract.FabricScopedState`; `node/fabric_state.go`:
`dropFabricState` when a fabric is removed, `reconcileFabricState` before a
topology is served, at start and whenever an endpoint joins), with two
differences. It does not skip an empty table: the node keeps its endpoints and
what they stored when its last fabric goes
(`BD-Matter-LastFabricReopenWithoutErase`, which records at an earlier pin
that matter.js erases the node then; not re-read here), so what a server still
holds for a fabric that is gone is dropped then as well. And a server says
what it holds (`MatterHeldFabrics`) and drops it itself, from its own
persistence too, where matter.js filters the attribute values by the schema: a
Go server keeps its state in its own fields. The fabric's event occurrences
leave the event log at the removal (`node/node.go`), not at the reconcile.
Review II, owner decision 37, R2-P2-fabric-03, R2-P2-fabric-06. Pinned by
`node:TestStartReconcilesFabricStateAgainstTheTable`,
`TestStartDropsAnExtensionWhoseFabricIsGone` (a node without a fabric),
`TestRemoveFabricDropsTheFabricStateOfEveryEndpoint` and
`TestRemoveFabricReachesTheAggregatorsServers`; the guard
`script/fabricscopecheck` holds every server of a cluster with a fabric-scoped
attribute to a removal path.

### BD-Matter-DoorLock-CreatorFabricIndexCleared — a removed fabric's index leaves a lock user's and credential's creator and last-modified fields, as in connectedhomeip

matter.js stamps the accessing fabric's index into a user's `creatorFabricIndex` and `lastModifiedFabricIndex` (`packages/node/src/behaviors/door-lock/DoorLockServer.ts:286-287` at `db021da0`), lets only the creator's fabric change a user's name and unique id (`:298-303`) or modify a credential (`:531`), and reacts to no fabric's deletion — a search of the file for `deleting`, `FabricManager` and `fabrics.events` finds no line — so a removed fabric's index stays in those fields; the users are a state field of the server (`:1542-1543`), and whether the node's strip of the attributes its schema marks fabric-scoped (`packages/node/src/behavior/cluster/FabricScopedDataHandler.ts:47-56`) could reach such a field was not traced (unverified). This module follows connectedhomeip instead (owner decision 81; review II, phase 4): `DoorLockServer::OnFabricRemoved` (`src/app/clusters/door-lock-server/CodegenIntegration.cpp:1487-1516` at `6170af84`) sets a removed fabric's `createdBy` and `lastModifiedBy` to `kUndefinedFabricIndex`, 0 (`src/lib/core/DataModelTypes.h:69`), on every occupied user (`:2198-2212`) and credential (`:3333-3347`) and removes nothing. The lock server implements `contract.FabricScopedState`: `MatterDropFabric` clears the two fields of every occupied user and of every stored credential and saves the records — no user, credential or schedule is removed and no LockUserChange is emitted — and `MatterHeldFabrics` lists the indices the records name (`cluster/lock/fabric_state.go:23-88`). Two things go beyond connectedhomeip, which clears from its fabric table's removal callback only (`:52-66`): the node calls the same drop at start and when the lock's endpoint joins, for an index its fabric table does not hold (`reconcileFabricState`, `node/fabric_state.go:96-130`), so a record a host seeded in `DoorLockConfig.Initial` with the index of a fabric not commissioned yet loses it; and every stored credential is cleared whatever its type, where connectedhomeip walks the credential types of its supported features — the fix's reading of `:3363-3389`, not repeated (unverified). By design: a later fabric given a removed fabric's index is no creator of that fabric's users and credentials, and the reconcile also covers a removal whose fan-out did not run to its end. Who sees it: a fabric commissioned into a removed fabric's index cannot rename those users or change those credentials as their creator, where on a matter.js node it can. Pinned by `cluster/lock:TestDropFabricClearsTheRemovedFabricFromUsersAndCredentials` and `TestDropFabricHoldingNothingChangesNothing`.

### BD-Matter-SessionRolloverClose — a secure session is closed 100 000 messages before its counter runs out, on the device after a flush of its subscriptions, and on the controller once its exchanges in flight have ended

matter.js winds a secure session down before its message counter rolls over:
the counter calls the session's handler when it reaches its maximum less
`ROLLOVER_INFO_DIFFERENCE`, 100 000
(`packages/protocol/src/protocol/MessageCounter.ts:13`, `:71-76` at
`db021da0`; wired at `packages/protocol/src/session/NodeSession.ts:123`), and
`#scheduleRolloverClose` then runs `initiateClose` with
`closeSubscriptions(true)` on a timer, off the stack of the send that consumed
the counter (`NodeSession.ts:398-412`; the flush through the session,
`:312-323`): the subscriptions are flushed first
(`packages/protocol/src/session/Session.ts:304-320`) and the session then
closes with a CloseSession (`NodeSession.ts:419-425`,
`packages/protocol/src/protocol/ExchangeManager.ts:758`). The number here is
that constant (`rolloverInfoDifference`, `secure/channel/session.go`):
`Session.RolloverDue` reports, once, that the outbound counter has passed
0xFFFFFFFF less 100 000 or is used up. The bridge then reports what the
session's subscriptions owe (`subscription.Manager.FlushSession`), tells the
peer with a CloseSession and closes the session through the registry, on a
goroutine of its own (`endSessionAtRollover`, `bridge/reply.go`). The client
stack asks `RolloverDue` when it seals a message and winds its session down as
matter.js does: the session turns closing (`Session.IsClosing` in
`client/exchange/session.go`; matter.js `Session.ts:190-191`), so an exchange
the peer opens on it is declined (`ExchangeManager.ts:441-444`) and the peer
set gives it no new interaction — the next one establishes a new session — and
the close waits for the exchanges in flight, the one whose send consumed the
counter included. When the last of them has ended the CloseSession goes out,
on a goroutine of the manager, and the session closes (`endSessionAtRollover`
in `client/exchange/manager.go`, `deferClose` and `closeIfDeferred` in
`client/exchange/session.go`). That is matter.js's deferral: `initiateClose`
sets `deferredClose` while the session has active exchanges
(`NodeSession.ts:367-376`) and returns without closing (`Session.ts:315-317`),
and the close runs when the last exchange has closed
(`NodeSession.ts:384-391`); no timer bounds the wait at these lines, and none
does here — an exchange ends by its MRP retransmission limit, its receive
timeout or its caller's context. The two roles differ in this. matter.js has
one class for a secure session in either role (`NodeSession.create` takes
`isInitiator`, `NodeSession.ts:73-74`, `:88-89`), so its deferral holds on a
device as well; this module's device closes at once after its flush and its
CloseSession and does not wait for the session's exchanges in flight
(`endSessionAtRollover`, `bridge/reply.go:90-120`). By design (owner decision
75, 2026-11-14; review II, R2-P4-cert-05): the close comes once a session's
outbound counter has passed 0xFFFFFFFF less 100 000
(`secure/channel/session.go:168-184`), which from a start between 1 and 2^28
(`transport/mrp/counter.go:33-46`) is more than four thousand million messages
on one session, and the device keeps no account of a session's exchanges in
flight and gets none for this case. What the close costs such an exchange was
not traced: whether a reliable reply that still waits for its acknowledgement
is lost with the session, and whether another exchange in flight on it ends
unanswered (unverified). The two differences
this entry recorded at `114dee6d` — no flush before the close, and the device
side only — are closed (review II, R2-P2-dr-req-07, R2-P2-ctr-08), and the
controller's close no longer ends its exchanges in flight (R2-P2-rr-ctl-02).
