What is left besides the device's close is form: a goroutine
where matter.js starts a timer, and no flush in the client stack's close —
whether a peer can hold a subscription on a session of the client stack was
not traced (unverified). connectedhomeip was not read (unverified). Review II,
R2-P2-ctr-08. Pinned by
`bridge:TestSecureSessionClosedWhenItsCounterNearsExhaustion`,
`TestRolloverCloseFlushesTheSessionsSubscriptions`,
`client/exchange:TestSessionClosedWhenItsCounterNearsExhaustion`,
`TestRolloverCloseWaitsForTheExchangesInFlight` and
`secure/channel:TestRolloverDueOnceNearExhaustion`.

### BD-Matter-OTARequestor-BDXSizeCap — an OTA image downloaded over BDX is capped at 256 MiB, and a transfer past the cap is not tried again

matter.js's requestor builds its BDX receiver without a size limit
(`packages/node/src/behaviors/ota-software-update-requestor/OtaSoftwareUpdateRequestorServer.ts:971-977`
at `b25ed960`: the two designators, the driver mode and the block size) and
takes what the transfer delivers (`:986`); a transfer that fails is tried
again, whatever the failure, until the third attempt (`:965`, `:991-1004`).
`cluster/core`'s requestor caps the bytes a BDX download takes at
`otaBdxMaxImageSize` (`cluster/core/ota_software_update_requestor.go`): the
default of the HTTPS path's `HTTPSMaxImageSize`, 256 MiB
(`BD-Matter-OTARequestor-HTTPS`), as a constant that `HTTPSMaxImageSize` does
not move, so that the image either path fetches by default has one size. The
block that would pass the cap is refused: the provider is answered
LengthTooLarge, the download fails with a DownloadError whose platform code is
LengthTooLarge, and the attempts that remain are not made
(`cluster/core/ota_requestor_query.go`) — a second divergence, taken because
the same image would pass the cap again. A length the provider announces above
the cap is not refused before the first block, where the HTTPS path refuses on
Content-Length. No source was read for the number beyond the HTTPS default it
copies (unverified), and connectedhomeip's requestor was not read for a size
bound (unverified). Reason: a transfer without a bound takes as much storage
as its provider sends. Review II, the rework of R2-P2-ctl. Pinned by
`cluster/core:TestOTARequestor_BDXDownloadIsCapped`; the limit is in
`docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js
bounds a BDX download.

### BD-Matter-SubscriptionEndsWithoutReadablePath — a subscription whose subject may read none of its paths any more ends once two consecutive reports find it so

matter.js's subscription sends on its interval whatever its subject may read: the send-interval timer marks a keep-alive as owed and prepares the update (`packages/node/src/node/server/ServerSubscription.ts:481-484` at `db021da0`), and an update without attribute or event data is sent as a keep-alive (`:909-920`); a search of the file for `acl` and `access`, case ignored, finds only `accessed` at `:232`. How the reports of a subject that lost its access come out there was not traced beyond that file (unverified). Here a subscription ends, terminated, and gives its place in the fabric's quota back when two consecutive reports find its subject refused every attribute and every event cluster its paths resolve to — at least one of them refused — under one unchanged ACL of its fabric and one set of the subscription's paths the node serves (`bridge/subscribe.go`, `endIfSubjectReadsNothing`, `subjectReadsNothing`; log `matter.subscribe.subject_reads_nothing`). One observation is not enough (amended 2026-11-14; review II, R2-P3-dr-dev-01, R2-P3-rr-dev-03): a list write of the ACL stores its REPLACE before its appends, and a report between them finds the entries missing. What the two observations compare is the fabric's listed entries and a SHA-256 over the paths the walk judged, not a count of reassemblies, which moves without a change. Nothing is decided while a chunked write of the fabric's ACL holds the attribute (`im.WriteHolds.Held`, the hold of owner decision 52), and the walk is judged against the entries one listing returned, never against a second read. Only a plain refusal by an ACL that could be read counts: a PASE subscription, a dispatcher without an ACL, a session without an accessing fabric, an ACL source that is missing or fails, an answer of the access check other than UNSUPPORTED_ACCESS, a path that resolves to nothing the node serves, and a subscription whose paths resolve to nothing all leave the subscription alone. The walk over the paths runs only when the fabric's entries or the served topology differ from those the subject last passed under; the entries are listed at each report. Who reaches it: a subject whose ACL entry was removed, or narrowed below every one of its paths, whose subscription ends at the second report after the change; a subject that keeps one readable path keeps its subscription. What the subscriber is sent at the end was not read in the code (unverified). The rule mirrors no reference line; connectedhomeip was not read for a counterpart (unverified). Reason: the quota of `BD-Matter-TimedAndQuotaDeferred` is counted per fabric, and a subscription that can report nothing would hold a place of it on keep-alives for as long as its subscriber answers them. Review II, R2-P3-admin-03, owner decision 53. Pinned by `fabrictest:TestSubscriptionEndsWhenItsSubjectReadsNothing` and `TestChunkedACLRewriteKeepsTheFabricsSubscriptions`, and by `bridge:TestSubjectReadsNothingTakesTwoObservationsOfOneACL`, `TestSubjectReadsNothingCountsNoPathThatIsGone`, `TestSubjectReadsNothingIsNotDecidedOnAFailedACLRead`, `TestSubjectReadsNothingWalksOnlyAfterAChange` and `TestSubjectReadsNothingIsDecidedAcrossAnUnchangedReassembly`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js ends such a subscription.

### BD-Matter-FailSafeEndsWithItsFabric — a fail-safe expires when the fabric that armed it is removed

Neither reference ends a fail-safe at the removal of the fabric it was armed for. connectedhomeip's `GeneralCommissioningCluster::OnFabricRemoved` resets the terms and conditions only (`src/app/clusters/general-commissioning-server/GeneralCommissioningCluster.cpp:357-375` at `6170af84`); the two other `OnFabricRemoved` handlers that were read do not name the fail-safe (`src/app/clusters/operational-credentials-server/OperationalCredentialsCluster.cpp:1377-1389`, `src/app/server/CommissioningWindowManager.cpp:468-475`), and `ForceFailSafeTimerExpiry` has two call sites under `src`: ArmFailSafe with expiry 0 (`GeneralCommissioningCluster.cpp:429-432`) and `ExpireFailSafeIfArmed` (`CommissioningWindowManager.cpp:641-648`), which the release of the PASE session calls (`:636`) and, through `ExpireFailSafeIfHeldByOpenPASESession` while a PASE session exists (`:650-657`), RevokeCommissioning (`src/app/clusters/administrator-commissioning-server/AdministratorCommissioningLogic.cpp:113`) and `src/lib/shell/commands/Device.cpp:60`. In matter.js the reaction to a fabric's deletion updates the fabric list and the commissioned state (`packages/node/src/behaviors/operational-credentials/OperationalCredentialsServer.ts:584-587` at `db021da0`), and `CommissioningServer.handleFabricChange` says of it "A deletion is final, whoever holds the fail-safe" (`packages/node/src/behavior/system/commissioning/CommissioningServer.ts:119-127`); of the other listeners of the fabric deletion events under `packages/node/src` and `packages/protocol/src`, `AdministratorCommissioningServer.ts:262-267` clears the window's admin fabric, `SessionManager.ts:308-310` deletes the resumption records, and the eight remaining files hold no `failsafe`, case ignored. Here `GeneralCommissioning.FabricRemoved` (`cluster/core/general_commissioning.go`), which `node` calls after every removal of a fabric, expires the fail-safe armed for that fabric, with the rollback its timeout runs; a fail-safe armed for another fabric, or over PASE before an AddNOC, is left alone. Who sees it: the other fabrics' administrators, whose ArmFailSafe is no longer answered BusyWithOtherAdmin and whose OpenCommissioningWindow no longer Busy for the rest of a removed fabric's fail-safe; and a node whose last fabric had armed the fail-safe, whose own window reopens at once. A fail-safe armed over PASE still makes that reopening wait, as matter.js's `#resetWhenIdle` waits for an active fail-safe (`CommissioningServer.ts:179-189`). Reason, the owner's: a fail-safe exists to roll back what its fabric's commissioner changed; once the fabric is gone it protects nothing and only holds the node's one fail-safe context against every other fabric. Review II, R2-P3-admin-06. Pinned by `node:TestFailSafeOfARemovedFabricEndsWithIt`, `node:TestFailSafeOfTheLastFabricEndsWithIt` and `cluster/core:TestGencomm_FailSafeOfARemovedFabricExpires`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js ends the fail-safe with its fabric.

### BD-chip-BindingListBounded — the Binding list of an endpoint holds at most 64 entries

matter.js's model gives the Binding list no maximum — its constraint is `desc` (`packages/model/src/standard/elements/binding.element.ts:23` at `b25ed960`) — and `BindingServer` registers every entry of a written list without a count (`packages/node/src/behaviors/binding/BindingServer.ts:127-157`); `BindingManager.ts` was searched for `ResourceExhausted` and `MAX_` only and has neither (unverified beyond that). connectedhomeip bounds its table: `Binding::Table::kMaxBindingEntries` is `CHIP_CONFIG_MAX_BINDING_ENTRIES_PER_FABRIC` (4) times `CHIP_CONFIG_MAX_FABRICS` (16) (`src/app/clusters/bindings/binding-table.h:134-135`, `src/lib/core/CHIPConfig.h:1149`, `:799` at `6170af84`), and a write whose list — the table, less the accessing fabric's entries on the endpoint, plus the written ones — would pass it is answered ResourceExhausted (`src/app/clusters/bindings/BindingCluster.cpp:70-80`). Here `bindingMaxEntries` = 4 × 16 (`cluster/core/binding.go`) bounds the list of one Binding server, every fabric's entries together, with connectedhomeip's formula and status; the refused write changes nothing. Two things are this module's choice. The scope: connectedhomeip's table is the node's, the bound here is each endpoint's, since the Binding servers of a node share no counter — a node with n Binding endpoints holds up to 64 n entries. And a write that does not grow the list is taken even past the bound, so that a list a host set larger can still shrink; connectedhomeip's check has no such case. As there, the bound keeps no share per fabric: one fabric's entries can fill an endpoint's list. Who reaches it: a controller that writes a 65th entry on one endpoint. Reason: the list is stored and read back whole, and the model lets a subject with Manage make it any size. Review II, R2-P3-admin-04. Pinned by `cluster/core:TestBinding_ListIsBounded`; the limit is in `docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js bounds the list.

Review II, phase 6a (R2-P6-bound-1008, owner decision 134): a fabric's share is bounded too. connectedhomeip sizes its binding table as `CHIP_CONFIG_MAX_BINDING_ENTRIES_PER_FABRIC` (4) × `CHIP_CONFIG_MAX_FABRICS` (16) = 64 entries, one table for the node (`src/app/clusters/bindings/binding-table.h:134-135`, `src/lib/core/CHIPConfig.h:1149`, `:799` at `6170af84`), and enforces only that total — one fabric can take all 64 (`BindingCluster.cpp:70-80`, `binding-table.cpp:46-50`). The module keeps the total per endpoint and refuses, with ResourceExhausted, a request's write that grows its fabric's list past 16 entries — four times chip's nominal 4 per fabric, so it refuses nothing chip's sizing promises a fabric (`cluster/core/binding.go` `bindingMaxEntriesPerFabric`); a host write and a write that does not grow the list pass. The share bounds one fabric; it reserves nothing: four fabrics at 16 fill an endpoint's 64 (SupportedFabrics defaults to 254). Whether a certification case writes more than 16 entries from one fabric was not measured (the BIND family run is owed).

### BD-Matter-Controller-ResponderSessionsPerPeer — a peer holds at most five sessions it established with the controller's CASE responder, as in matter.js

A parity statement: not a divergence, and not an Ahead row. matter.js caps the sessions a peer established with a node at `MAX_SESSIONS_PER_PEER` = 5 (`packages/protocol/src/session/SessionManager.ts:205` at `db021da0`). Every added session that the node did not initiate is checked (`:312-318`), a PASE or closing one aside (`:698-700`); the peer's sessions that claim a slot are counted, closing ones included, and beyond the cap the least recently used one that is not closing is closed (`:702-714`; `#leastRecentlyUsedSession` on `session.timestamp`, `:554-562`), by force, without the CloseSession of the graceful path (`:721-723`). The device side has mirrored it (`secure/operational.MaxSessionsPerPeer`); the controller's side now does too: `maxSessionsPerPeer` = 5 (`client/exchange/manager.go`), applied to the sessions registered with `SecureSessionConfig.Responder` — those the CASE responder of `client/handshake` establishes — and closing the peer's least recently used such session without a CloseSession on the wire (`matter.controller.session_evicted`). Sessions the controller opened do not count, as matter.js leaves an initiator's sessions to "the peer loss its own traffic reports" (`:313-314`). No idle reaper was added for these sessions: matter.js has none at these lines, and the device side's is this module's own (`BD-Matter-IdleSessionReaper`). Review II, R2-P3-ctl-dev-01. Pinned by `client/handshake:TestCASEServerHoldsAtMostFiveSessionsPerPeer`; the limit is in `docs/guides/limits.md`.

### BD-Matter-Controller-ResumedSessionCountedAtRegistration — a resumed responder session takes its place in the per-peer cap before the initiator's success report, as in matter.js

A parity statement: not a divergence, and nothing changes. matter.js's CASE server, resuming, sends Sigma2_Resume (`packages/protocol/src/session/case/CaseServer.ts:196-201` at `db021da0`), then adds the session to the manager — "Now we are sure, add the session to the manager", `this.#sessions.sessions.add(secureSession)` (`:208-211`) — and only then waits for the initiator's success report (`waitForSuccess`, `:215-216`). The add is what the per-peer cap hears: `sessions.added` runs `#evictExcessSessionsFor` for a session the node did not initiate (`packages/protocol/src/session/SessionManager.ts:312-318`), which counts the peer's sessions against `MAX_SESSIONS_PER_PEER` (`:697-725`). A resumed session so counts against the cap from its registration, before the initiator's success report. The controller's CASE responder has the same order (`client/handshake/server.go`, `resume`): `sendAnswer` with the Sigma2_Resume, then `NewSecureSession` with `Responder: true` — where `client/exchange` applies `maxSessionsPerPeer` (`BD-Matter-Controller-ResponderSessionsPerPeer`) — then the wait for the StatusReport; that the send returns only once the Sigma2_Resume is acknowledged is the review's measurement and was not repeated here. connectedhomeip differs: its resumed responder session is activated when the success StatusReport arrives (`OnSuccessStatusReport`, `src/protocols/secure_channel/CASESession.cpp:2315-2339` at `6170af84`, whose `Finish` at `:2339` activates the session, `src/protocols/secure_channel/PairingSession.cpp:62-66`, `Activate` at `:54`); whether connectedhomeip caps a peer's sessions at all was not searched (unverified). The module stays with matter.js: sessions the controller opened are neither counted nor chosen, and a peer whose session the cap closed connects again. Review II, R2-P3-dr-ctl-03, recorded without a change. `client/handshake:TestCASEServerHoldsAtMostFiveSessionsPerPeer` pins the cap; the order has no test of its own. The device's CASE responder: `BD-Matter-CASEServer-ResumptionRecordSingleUse`.

### BD-Matter-Controller-NodeImageBounded — the controller's image of a node keeps what the node's structure names or the interaction asked for, within a quota per node

matter.js stores every path a report names: `#mutateAttribute` opens an update set for whatever endpoint and cluster a reported path names (`packages/node/src/node/client/ClientStructure.ts:582-624` at `b25ed960`, the set at `:606-617`), and `#endpointFor` and `#clusterFor` create the endpoint and the cluster's store for any number (`:1118-1164`); nothing at these lines counts what one peer's reports store, and the search went no further than this file (unverified beyond it). Here a report's attribute data passes `structure.admit` first (`controller/client/image_bounds.go`). A path is kept when the peer's own structure names its endpoint — endpoint 0 and every endpoint reached from it through Descriptor PartsLists, judged on the report's own PartsLists where it carries them, else on the image's — or when its endpoint describes itself: the report carries the endpoint's Descriptor DeviceTypeList or PartsList, or the image already holds one — the evidence matter.js takes to treat an endpoint a PartsList names as existing (`ClientStructure.ts:1503`, `:1513-1515` at `b25ed960`; owner decision 342, which narrows decision 54 as decision 57 did, so that an aggregator and its devices reported before the root's PartsList names the aggregator are kept and placed once it does, 097e5a8da) — or when the request named its endpoint or its cluster, or its attribute alone — a path that names an attribute and neither an endpoint nor a cluster asks for it on every endpoint and cluster (R2-P3-dr-ctl-04); any other path is dropped before it reaches the image, with one warning per node (`matter.controller.client.report_path_dropped`). Behind that stands a quota: a report whose kept values would raise what the image is charged above `MaxImageBytesPerNode`, and above the image's present charge, is refused whole (`matter.controller.client.image_quota_reached`), and an image stored above the quota is cut back to what the structure names when it loads (`matter.controller.client.image_cut_at_load`) — only the endpoints and clusters it does not name are erased from the store; the node's record, its settings, its ICD entry and every kept endpoint stay (R2-P3-dr-ctl-01). The image is charged each value's stored bytes and what each entry holds in memory (amended 2026-11-14; review II, R2-P3-dr-ctl-02): `imageElementBytes` = 112 per TLV element of a value and `imageAttributeBytes` = 136 per attribute, the sizes of their Go types on a 64-bit platform, `imageClusterBytes` = 2048 per cluster and `imageEndpointBytes` = 512 per endpoint. None of the four is sourced: the last two are the fix agent's measurements rounded up — 1605 and 303 heap bytes on darwin/arm64 with go1.27.4, as the constants' comments record them — and the factor of two within which the charge bounds the image's heap is the test's, chosen above a measured 1.38. The quota so bounds the heap and the store's rows, one per attribute and one per cluster, and not only the values' bytes. The default, `DefaultMaxImageBytesPerNode` = 32 MiB, is chosen without a source — sixteen times `interaction.DefaultMaxReportBytesPerSession`, the reviewer's proposal — and under these charges admits about two thousand bridged plugs of three clusters, some 15.5 KiB each, by the fix agent's measurement; a host sets `controller.Config.MaxImageBytesPerNode`. Beside the Ahead part this is a divergence: under a wildcard matter.js stores an endpoint no PartsList reaches, and this module does so only for an endpoint that describes itself. The cluster level stays as matter.js has it: a cluster a peer reports without naming it in its ServerList is kept — "Schrödinger's cluster", `ClientStructure.ts:668-673`; owner decision 57, which narrows decision 54 — so the quota alone bounds the clusters of a named endpoint. Who reaches the rule: a device that reports endpoints its PartsLists do not name and that never reported a DeviceTypeList or PartsList of their own, whose values the controller no longer holds unless a request names them. Who reaches the quota: a device whose image would be charged more than 32 MiB, whose reports that would grow it further are not applied — its events still flow — until the host raises the quota. Reason: the image and its store are filled by what a commissioned device reports, and neither had a bound. Review II, R2-P3-ctl-dev-02, owner decisions 54, 57 and 342. Pinned by `controller/client:TestImageKeepsWhatTheStructureNamesOrTheReadAskedFor`, `TestImageKeepsAnAttributeTheReadAskedForOnEveryEndpoint`, `TestImageKeepsAnEndpointThatDescribesItself`, `TestImageQuotaRefusesAReportBeyondIt`, `TestImageQuotaBoundsMemoryAndRows`, `TestStoredImageIsChargedAsTheImage`, `TestStoredImageBeyondQuotaIsCutBackAtLoad`, `TestImageCutAtLoadErasesOnlyWhatItDrops` and, for the tolerance that stays, `TestClientNodeSchrodingersClusterParity`; the limit is in `docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js bounds what a peer's reports store.

### BD-Matter-Controller-OneHandshakePerSigma1 — the controller's CASE responder runs one handshake per Sigma1

matter.js's CASE server starts a handshake for every Sigma1 handed to it (`packages/protocol/src/session/case/CaseServer.ts:61-64` at `db021da0`) and keeps the Sigma1's initiator random as the handshake's `peerRandom` (`:383`), for the session salts and the destination id (`:157`, `:174`, `:191`, `:239`); it compares it with no earlier Sigma1's. connectedhomeip's `CASESession.cpp` uses the random for a salt and the destination id as well (`src/protocols/secure_channel/CASESession.cpp:620-624`, `:1058-1060`, `:1075` at `6170af84`); a memory of randoms elsewhere in connectedhomeip was not looked for (unverified). Both initiators draw a fresh random for every Sigma1 (`packages/protocol/src/session/case/CaseClient.ts:120`; `CASESession.cpp:750-752`). Here the controller's CASE responder (`client/handshake/server.go`) remembers the initiator randoms of the Sigma1s that started a handshake — at most `seenSigma1Limit` = 256, each for `seenSigma1Lifetime` = 60 s, and only those of Sigma1s that addressed one of the controller's fabrics — and answers a Sigma1 whose random it remembers, or is still checking, with nothing, under any source node id. The two numbers are constants of this module carried over, not read from a reference: the count is `maxInboundUnsecuredSessions` and the lifetime `inboundUnsecuredLifetime` (`client/exchange/manager.go`) — one entry for every handshake that can hold a session, for as long as it can. Who reaches it: a second Sigma1 that carries a random already seen. A device's retransmission is answered by the duplicate detection of the session it came on and does not get here; a device that starts over draws a new random and is served. One Sigma1 is forgotten at once (added 2026-11-14; review II, R2-P3-dr-ctl-06): the one whose first answer, Sigma2 or Sigma2_Resume, the controller's socket refused to send (`sendAnswer`, `forget`; `exchange.ErrNetwork`, which the exchange returns for a refused first transmission only) — nothing reached the initiator, so its retransmission of that Sigma1 is the only way the handshake can go on. An answer that left and was not acknowledged keeps the Sigma1 remembered, as a copy of it would. A bound per source address was not built: the source address of a datagram is not authenticated, and nodes that share an address would meet it. Reason: the bound on the sessions that unauthenticated peers open (`BD-Matter-Controller-UnsecuredSessionsBounded`) bounds the handshakes only when one Sigma1 starts one. Review II, R2-P3-ctl-lan-02. Pinned by `client/handshake:TestCASEServerAnswersASigma1Once`, `TestCASEServerCompletesAHandshakeWhileASigma1IsRepeated` and `TestCASEServerAnswersASigma1WhoseAnswerNeverLeft`; the limit is in `docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js recognises a Sigma1 it has already answered.

### BD-Matter-Controller-StagedAddressesBounded — the addresses staged for hosts no SRV has named yet stand inside the DNS-SD cache's bound, five per host

matter.js stages the A and AAAA records of a host it has no name for, to replay them when a later SRV creates the name (`packages/general/src/net/dns-sd/DnssdNames.ts:273-311` at `b25ed960`): an address not yet staged for its host is appended to the host's list, with no count over the list (`:299-306`); the staged hosts are bounded at 250 and cut back to 200 (`:21-22`, `:141-148`); and a stale address goes when the prune runs (`:125-139`). The staged addresses in all have no bound at these lines. Here (`client/discovery/names.go`) the staged addresses count against `maxCachedRecords` = 8192 together with the cached records (`BD-Matter-Controller-DnssdCacheBounded`), and at the bound a staged address goes before any cached record — the one received longest ago of the host touched longest ago, with the warning `matter.discovery.staged_addresses_evicted` — so that staging cannot displace a record a name holds; a host stages at most `maxStagedAddressesPerHost` = 5 addresses, the one received longest ago replaced; and a staged address goes at its TTL with the grace factor, as a cached record does, not at the next prune. Five is connectedhomeip's number of addresses per resolved node (`kMaxIPAddresses` = `CHIP_DEVICE_CONFIG_MAX_DISCOVERED_IP_ADDRESSES`, `src/lib/dnssd/Types.h:94`; `chip_max_discovered_ip_addresses = 5`, `src/platform/BUILD.gn:90` at `6170af84`); applying it to staging is this module's transposition, and that staged addresses go first is this module's choice. Who reaches it: a host that announces more than five addresses before its SRV arrives, of which the five received last are replayed; a device with up to five loses nothing. Reason: staging is filled by any host on the link before any record names it, and the cache's bound bounds the browser's memory only when the staged addresses stand inside it. Review II, R2-P3-ctl-lan-01. Pinned by `client/discovery:TestNames_StagedAddressesAreWithinTheCacheBound`, `TestNames_StagedHostReplaysAtMostItsBound` and `TestNames_StagedAddressGoesWhenACachedRecordWould`; the limits are in `docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js bounds the staged addresses.

### BD-Matter-Controller-BleScannerBounded — the controller's BLE scanner holds at most 8192 records

matter.js keeps the devices its BLE scanner discovered in a map with no size limit (`packages/protocol/src/common/BleScanner.ts:130` at `b25ed960`); a record leaves it when it is older than the maximum age (`:288-296`) and at `:308`, `:317`, `:413` and `:556`, lines found by a search for the map's `delete` and not read further (unverified). Here the scanner holds at most `maxScannerRecords` = 8192 records and forgets the one seen longest ago beyond that (`controller/ble/scanner.go`; `matter.ble.scan.records_evicted`). The number is chosen: no reference has one, and it carries over the DNS-SD cache's bound (`maxCachedRecords`, `BD-Matter-Controller-DnssdCacheBounded`), this module's other bound on what unauthenticated senders make the controller hold. Who reaches it: more than 8192 distinct advertising addresses within the life of the records; a device forgotten at the bound is found again at its next advertisement. Reason: any party in radio range advertises from as many addresses as it likes, and while a discovery runs no record ages out. Review II, R2-P3-ble-02. Pinned by `controller/ble:TestScanner_RecordsAreBoundedDuringADiscovery`; the limit is in `docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js bounds the scanner's records.

### BD-chip-BTP-RepeatedAckRefused — a BTP ack number already received closes the session, as in connectedhomeip

matter.js accepts an ack number it has already received: it refuses an ack only when its distance from the previous one is greater than the outstanding interval (`packages/protocol/src/ble/BtpSessionHandler.ts:287-295` at `b25ed960`), so a distance of 0 passes, stops the ack-received timer and starts it again while a fragment is still unacknowledged (`:297-304`). connectedhomeip refuses it: `BtpEngine::IsValidAck` is false when no ack is awaited, and otherwise true only from the oldest to the newest unacknowledged sequence number (`src/ble/BtpEngine.cpp:142-162` at `6170af84`); `HandleAckReceived` returns `BLE_ERROR_INVALID_ACK` (`:169`), and the endpoint closes on the error (`src/ble/BLEEndPoint.cpp:1293-1297`). This module follows connectedhomeip (`transport/btp/session.go`): an ack at distance 0 from the previous one, like one beyond the outstanding interval, is a protocol error that closes the BTP session and drops the connection. Who reaches it: a peer that sends the same ack number twice. Whether a matter.js or connectedhomeip sender ever does was not read (unverified); connectedhomeip's receiver refuses it as this one does. Reason: a repeated ack number acknowledges nothing, and accepting it restarted the timer that ends a session whose peer has stopped acknowledging. Review II, R2-P3-ble-03. Pinned by `transport/btp:TestSession_RepeatedAckIsRefused`. Retires when matter.js refuses an ack that acknowledges nothing.

### BD-chip-BLE-WindowEndDisconnectsCentral — the end of a commissioning window disconnects a BLE central that has not completed PASE

matter.js removes its BLE transport when the node is commissioned (`endUncommissionedMode`, `packages/node/src/behavior/system/network/ServerNetworkRuntime.ts:294-308` at `b25ed960`, wired to the `commissioned` event at `:386`); `#bleTransport` is named nowhere else under `packages/node/src` than where it is created (`:71`, `:147-150`), so at these lines the end of a window that commissioned nothing leaves a connected central as it is. Whether the peripheral itself drops a central when its advertisement stops was not read (unverified). connectedhomeip closes every BLE connection when a window closes while it still listens for PASE — "We never established PASE, so never armed a fail-safe and hence can't rely on it expiring to close our BLE connection" (`src/app/server/CommissioningWindowManager.cpp:431-438` at `6170af84`). This module follows connectedhomeip, in its own terms: `Bridge.WithdrawBLE` (`bridge/ble.go`), the BLE end of a window, disconnects a connected central that has no secure session bound to its connection, and leaves one that completed PASE to its commissioning and its fail-safe. Who sees it: a central that connected and did not finish PASE before the window ended; it connects again in the next window. Reason: the peripheral serves one central at a time, and nothing else ends the connection of one that never armed a fail-safe. A central whose PASE attempt failed inside an open window is not disconnected by this; the handshake bound of `BD-Matter-BLE-CentralWithoutPASEGivenUp` reaches it. Review II, R2-P3-ble-05. Pinned by `bridge:TestWithdrawBLEDisconnectsCentralWithoutSecureSession`. Retires when matter.js ends such a connection with the window.

### BD-chip-WiFiRejoinBackoff — a Wi-Fi node off its committed network rejoins it with a backoff, and a fail-safe expiry brings the radio back

Under the Ahead row of `BD-chip-WiFiNetworkCommissioningServer`: matter.js's `NetworkCommissioningServer` is the generated empty class (`packages/node/src/behaviors/network-commissioning/NetworkCommissioningServer.ts:18` at `b25ed960`). connectedhomeip on Linux leaves the return to the committed network to wpa_supplicant: `CommitConfiguration` has the configuration saved (`src/platform/Linux/NetworkCommissioningWiFiDriver.cpp:164`; `CommitConfig`, `src/platform/Linux/ConnectivityManagerImpl_NetworkManagementWpaSupplicant.cpp:1118-1135` at `6170af84`), and `RevertConfiguration` restores the staged record and does not touch the radio (`NetworkCommissioningWiFiDriver.cpp:169-173`). This module's driver saves no configuration (`BD-chip-WpaSupplicantDriver` (2)), so the return is the cluster's (`cluster/core/network_commissioning_wifi.go`): a join of the first committed network that fails at `Start` is retried on the node's clock after `wifiRejoinFirstDelay` = 5 s, doubling up to `wifiRejoinMaxDelay` = 5 min, until it succeeds or the node stops; a fail-safe expiry or a CommissioningComplete that leaves the link on no committed network starts the same rejoin at once, where connectedhomeip restores the record only; an attempt is put off while a fail-safe is armed or a command runs. An attempt that runs, the first at `Start` included, holds the driver until it ends, a fail-safe expiry notwithstanding (amended 2026-11-14; review II, R2-P3-dr-net-05, R2-P3-rr-dev-05), and a NetworkCommissioning command that arrives meanwhile is not answered Busy: it cancels the attempt, waits for it to end and runs, and the next attempt follows after the backoff's current wait, at least 5 s (R2-P3-dr-net-06). The reason lies with the commissioners, as far as they were read: connectedhomeip completes its AddOrUpdateWiFiNetwork stage with the failure the command returned (`OnBasicFailure`, `src/controller/CHIPDeviceController.cpp:2157-2162`, wired at `:4287`) and its `AutoCommissioner` goes to `kCleanup` after any error (`src/controller/AutoCommissioner.cpp:465-468`), and matter.js's flow ends the commissioning on a CommissioningError or a StatusResponseError (`packages/protocol/src/peer/ControllerCommissioningFlow.ts:437-462` at `db021da0`); a Busy answer to its AddOrUpdateWiFiNetwork reaches that branch as a StatusResponseError — `#invokeCommand` throws one for a command status that is not success (`:519-522`), and the fallback around the step's invoke (`:1686-1705`) rethrows an error that is no channel drop (`:1005-1012`, `:1047`) — and a retry of the network step was not looked for beyond these lines. A command whose context ends while it waits is still answered Busy. No rejoin runs while InterfaceEnabled is false, which it is only while a driver that can switch its interface has it off (`BD-chip-WiFiInterfaceEnabled-DriverSwitch`, owner decision 80): the switch off disarms the retry and cancels a running attempt, the switch on starts the rejoin at once (R2-P3-dr-net-07); connectedhomeip was not read for what a disabled interface does to its reconnect (unverified). A network reads Connected while the link is on it. After a join that did not succeed the link is where the driver reports the radio, through the optional `contract.WiFiLinkReporter` (R2-P3-dr-net-04): `wifi/wpasupplicant` reports the interface's CurrentNetwork, read as connectedhomeip's `GetConfiguredNetwork` reads it (`src/platform/Linux/WpaSupplicantClient.cpp:396-422` at `6170af84`) — connectedhomeip's iterator asks `IsWiFiStationConnected` too before it calls a network connected (`src/platform/Linux/NetworkCommissioningWiFiDriver.cpp:300-309`), this driver does not — and with a driver that reports nothing no network reads connected. 5 s is connectedhomeip's `CHIP_DEVICE_CONFIG_WIFI_STATION_RECONNECT_INTERVAL`, "the interval at which the chip platform will attempt to reconnect to the configured WiFi network", 5000 ms (`src/include/platform/CHIPDeviceConfig.h:406-414`); which of its platforms use it, and how, was not read (unverified). The doubling and the 5 min are chosen, with no reference: an attempt holds the radio for up to ConnectMaxTimeSeconds, and 5 min keeps a node whose access point is gone for hours trying twelve times an hour. Three things stay open: the cluster gets no signal of a lost link (`contract.WiFiDriver` reports the results of a scan and of a join, and the reporter answers only when it is asked), so the return after a lost link is wpa_supplicant's, which keeps the joined network; a fail-safe that expires with no network committed leaves the radio on the uncommitted one, the port having no call to leave it; and after a rejoin that fails at a fail-safe expiry the driver puts the radio back on the reverted, uncommitted network, where the cluster, which now knows it, keeps retrying with the backoff (R2-P3-dr-net-01, not closed: the port has no call that makes a driver forget a network). Review II, R2-P3-net-01, R2-P3-net-02. Pinned by `cluster/core:TestFailedRejoinAtStartIsRetriedWithABackoff`, `TestFailSafeExpiryRejoinsTheCommittedNetworkAfterAFailedJoin`, `TestFailSafeExpiryLeavesNoUncommittedNetworkJoined`, `TestAFailedJoinKeepsTheReportedLinkConnected`, `TestAFailSafeExpiryLeavesARunningRejoinTheDriver`, `TestACommandCancelsARunningRejoinAndTakesItsTurn`, `TestAScanEndingLeavesARejoinStartedMeanwhileTheDriver` and `TestADisabledInterfaceStopsTheRejoin`.

### BD-chip-WiFiScanResponseBounded — a ScanNetworksResponse carries the 15 strongest results

Under the Ahead row of `BD-chip-WiFiNetworkCommissioningServer`. connectedhomeip bounds the results of a scan response at `kMaxNetworksInScanResponse` = 15 — "each item will cost ~60 bytes in TLV, thus 15 is a safe upper bound of scan results" (`src/app/clusters/network-commissioning/constants.h:26-28` at `6170af84`). Its Wi-Fi response encodes the results in the order it is handed them and stops at the count (`src/app/clusters/network-commissioning/WifiScanResponse.cpp:63-69`); its Thread response keeps the strongest, sorted by RSSI (`ThreadScanResponse.cpp:42-88`). This module takes the number and, for Wi-Fi, the Thread response's choice: `maxNetworksInScanResponse` = 15 (`cluster/core/network_commissioning_wifi.go`), the strongest, those without a known RSSI last. Which 15 is the departure from connectedhomeip's Wi-Fi response, and it is chosen: the order of a driver's results says nothing about the access point a commissioner looks for, and its signal does. Who reaches it: a scan that finds more than 15 access points. Reason: the response has to fit its message; before, every result was encoded, and a scan that found too many was answered ResourceExhausted. Review II, R2-P3-net-04. Pinned by `cluster/core:TestScanNetworksResponseIsBounded` and `fabrictest:TestScanNetworksAnswersInACrowdedBand`; the limit is in `docs/guides/limits.md`.

### BD-chip-TCP-InboundConnectionsBounded — an inbound TCP listener holds a bounded number of connections in all, and a failed accept is retried

matter.js bounds the connections one peer address may hold — `MAX_CONNECTIONS_PER_PEER_IP` = 3, a further one is closed (`packages/protocol/src/transport/tcp/TcpTransport.ts:27-28`, `:81-85` at `b25ed960`) — and closes a new connection that receives no data (`:89-96`); nothing at `:78-96` counts the connections in all. Its accept is the platform listener's (`:73-76`), whose handling of a failed accept was not read (unverified). connectedhomeip sizes its pool with `CHIP_CONFIG_MAX_ACTIVE_TCP_CONNECTIONS`, "Maximum Number of TCP connections a device can simultaneously have" (`src/transport/raw/TCPConfig.h:39-46`, `src/app/server/Server.h:100` at `6170af84`), reclaims, when it is out of space, the connections no message claimed (`src/transport/raw/TCP.cpp:133-163`), and on a failed accept logs the error while the endpoint keeps listening (`src/inet/TCPEndPointImplSockets.cpp:796-805`, `src/transport/raw/TCP.cpp:680-683`). Here (`transport/tcp/listener.go`) a listener holds at most `Config.MaxInboundConnections` connections in all, beside matter.js's cap per address. The bound is a field of each role's TCP configuration (`bridge.TCPConfig`, the type of `node.Config.Network.TCP`, and `controller.TCPConfig`), a negative value refused; its default is connectedhomeip's 4 on the device (`tcp.MaxInboundConnections`) and 256 on the controller (`defaultMaxInboundTCPConnections`, `controller/tcp.go`), a number chosen without a reference, set equal to the controller's bound on inbound unsecured sessions (owner decision 56). At the bound a new connection takes the place of the held one idle longest — no message received or sent for the longest time, counted from its accept when it carried none — among those that carried no traffic within `idleGrace` = 5 min (`matter.tcp.reclaim`), and is closed when every held one did (`matter.tcp.reject`). That a connection which delivered a message is no longer exempt is this module's rule, where connectedhomeip reclaims only a connection no message has claimed (amended 2026-11-14; review II, R2-P3-dr-net-02); the grace is a number of this module carried over, `secure/operational.SessionIdleTimeout`, after which the session reaper closes a session without traffic, so that a connection past it carries no session the module still keeps alive, and traffic counts both directions because a session's liveness does. A failed accept, for any reason but the listener's close, is logged (`matter.tcp.accept_error`) and retried after `acceptRetryFirst` = 5 ms, doubling up to `acceptRetryMax` = 1 s — the pace of Go's `net/http`, which retries only an error that reports itself temporary (`src/net/http/server.go:3583-3593` at go1.27.4); before, the first failed accept ended TCP service. A connection that has carried a message is still not closed for being idle while the listener has room; that connectedhomeip has no such close either was the fix's reading and was not repeated (unverified). Who reaches it: a peer that connects while every held connection carried traffic within the last 5 minutes, which is refused; and a peer whose connection, idle for longer, gave its place to a new one, which loses the sessions on it and connects again for its next interaction. Review II, R2-P3-ctl-lan-03, R2-P3-ctl-lan-04, R2-P3-lan-dev-05. Pinned by `transport/tcp:TestListenerHoldsAtMostMaxInboundConnections`, `TestListenerHoldsAtMostItsConfiguredInboundConnections`, `TestListenerReclaimsAConnectionWithoutAMessageWhenFull`, `TestListenerGivesTheIdleLongestPlaceToANewConnection`, `TestIdleGraceIsTheSessionIdleTimeout` and `TestServeRetriesAFailedAccept`, and by `controller:TestControllerConnectsAgainAfterItsIdleTCPConnectionWasReplaced`; the limits are in `docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js bounds its inbound connections in all.

Review II, phase 6a. A connection that never carried a message is spared from reclaim for `reclaimAgeFloor` = 2 s after its accept, so silent connections cannot take its place before its first message — connectedhomeip's reclaim has no age exemption (`src/transport/raw/TCP.cpp:133-163` at `6170af84`; R2-P6-bound-0203, owner decision 134). And at the bound only a secure session's messages keep a connection's place: a connection the host notes (`tcp.Conn.NoteSessionTraffic`; the bridge and the controller note every message of a session bound to the connection) is measured by those notes alone, and one that carried no session keeps its place for `sessionlessGrace` = 1 min after its accept (2 s when silent), whatever frames it sends (N3-finnet-4); 1 min is this module's, the PASE pairing time. The cost: a party that renews silent connections from two addresses inside the floor (four every 2 s), or that closes and reopens within the minute with one frame each (3 per address, 4 in all), holds every place no session holds, and a new connection is then refused; the per-address cap and the grace are the whole bound.

### BD-Matter-Controller-DclRequestsBounded — a revocation lookup bounds its CRL downloads, a download keeps https across redirects, and every GitHub request has a deadline

matter.js starts the download of every distribution point of a revocation lookup at once — `Promise.allSettled` over `crlPoints`, each handed the lookup's `revocationTimeout` (`packages/protocol/src/dcl/DclCertificateService.ts:1587-1596` at `b25ed960`) — with no count of the downloads open and no bound on the lookup as a whole at these lines; how one point's download is bounded was not read (unverified). It fetches an OTA image with a timeout and no `redirect` option (`packages/protocol/src/dcl/DclOtaUpdateService.ts:690-693`), and gives a GitHub request a deadline only when a timeout is configured (`packages/general/src/util/Github.ts:131-133`). Here, in `controller/dcl`: a revocation lookup holds at most `maxConcurrentCRLDownloads` = 4 downloads open, further points waiting for a free place, and ends after `revocationLookupTimeout` = 10 s — incomplete then, not cached, the CRLs that arrived still counted; an OTA image or CRL download refuses a redirect from `https` to another scheme, whichever `http.Client` the host supplies, within the ten redirects of `net/http` (`src/net/http/client.go:845-850` at go1.27.4); and `GitHubConfig.Timeout` 0 means `DefaultTimeout`, the ledger client's 5 s, a negative value none. 4 and 10 s are chosen, with no reference; the fix's reasoning: an issuer lists one distribution point in practice, 4 keeps the connections few, and 10 s keeps a lookup inside a commissioning's fail-safe. Who reaches them: an issuer with more than four distribution points, whose lookup takes longer; a lookup that needs more than 10 s, which reports what arrived; a ledger record whose image or CRL redirects to `http://`, which fails; and a host that relied on `Timeout` 0 for no deadline, which sets a negative value. Reason: these requests go to hosts the ledger names, not to fabric peers, and each costs a connection and up to the size bound of its answer. Review II, R2-P3-net-05, R2-P3-net-06, R2-P3-net-07. Pinned by `controller/dcl:TestRevocationLookupBoundsItsConcurrentDownloads`, `TestOTADownloadRefusesARedirectFromHTTPSToHTTP`, `TestCRLDownloadRefusesARedirectFromHTTPSToHTTP` and `TestGitHubRequestsCarryADeadline`; the limit is in `docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js bounds these requests.

Review II, phase 6b (R2-P6-bound-1905): matter.js filters the points (`packages/protocol/src/dcl/DclCertificateService.ts:1575-1579` at `b25ed960`) and downloads every one (`:1587-1596`), with no cap. Here a lookup takes at most `maxCRLPointsPerIssuer` = 64 points per issuer; the rest are dropped and logged once (`dcl.revocation.too_many_points`), and the lookup, incomplete, is not cached, so each such lookup costs 64 downloads. 64 is this module's judgement. Pinned by `controller/dcl:TestRevocationPointsPerIssuerBounded`.

### BD-Matter-MdnsUnicastAnswersBounded — the mDNS responder answers one source by unicast at most once per service a second

matter.js answers by unicast whenever every question of the query asks for it and the quarter-TTL rule allows — no answer's record was multicast longer ago than a quarter of its TTL (`packages/protocol/src/mdns/InterfaceResponder.ts:352-354` at `b25ed960`); nothing at these lines counts the unicast answers a source gets. Here (`mdns/answer.go`) a source is answered by unicast with one service's records at most once per `unicastInterval` = 1 s, and the responder remembers at most `maxUnicastSources` = 64 sources at a time; a QU query beyond either is answered by multicast, which the one-second rule between multicasts of a record paces. The interval is the one second of RFC 6762 §6, as the code cites it — the RFC was not re-read (unverified) — applied to the destination of a unicast answer, which is this module's reading; the count follows `maxTruncatedQueries`, the file's bound on its other table per source, and is chosen. Who reaches it: a querier that sends several QU queries for one service within a second, which gets the later answers by multicast. Reason: the source of an mDNS query is not authenticated, and a unicast answer is sent to it. Review II, R2-P3-lan-dev-06. Pinned by `mdns:TestUnicastAnswersToOneSourceAreBounded`; the limit is in `docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js paces its unicast answers.

### BD-Matter-Controller-CommissioningRaceBounded — the commissioning race holds at most 16 attempts in its places and starts each at most 16 s after its device was found

matter.js staggers the race's attempts by their registration index: `CROSS_DEVICE_STAGGER_DELAY` is one second (`packages/node/src/behavior/system/controller/discovery/ParallelPaseDiscovery.ts:30` at `b25ed960`), an attempt's stagger is its index times that (`:102-103`), and every registered attempt starts after its stagger unless the race is decided (`:110-116`). Nothing at these lines counts the attempts running or caps the wait, and an attempt that has ended still counts for the index of those after it. connectedhomeip was not read (unverified). Here (`client/discovery/session_kinds.go`) the race keeps the one-second stagger (`CrossDeviceStagger`) and departs from matter.js in three ways. An attempt that has ended holds no slot: the next one starts one stagger after the latest start while an attempt still runs, and at once when none does (review II, R2-P3-ble-01, R2-P3-ctl-lan-06). At most `maxRaceAttempts` = 16 attempts hold a place at once, and a start waits at most `raceStaggerCeiling` = 16 s after its device was found (owner decision 55). And a candidate whose ceiling has come while 16 run ends the oldest attempt whose device has not answered PASE — no PBKDFParamResponse, which an attempt reports through `discovery.AttemptAnswered` — and takes its place at once (`matter.controller.discovery.attempt_replaced`); the ended attempt runs on until it returns, at most `maxRaceUnwinding` = 16 of them beside the places, and past those an ended attempt keeps its place until it returns (owner decision 559); an answered attempt is never ended for a later candidate, and while every place holds one the candidate waits. Both numbers are chosen, not read from a reference: 16 is carried over from the module's bounds on the handshake messages that await an acknowledgement at one moment (`unsecuredEntryLimit`, `bridge/outbound_reliable.go`; `inboundUnsecuredAckWaitLimit`, `client/exchange/manager.go`) — bounds on inbound tables applied to outbound attempts, the fix agent's transposition — and 16 s is 16 times the stagger, the time it takes to fill every place, so a race of up to 16 candidates runs as matter.js's does. Who reaches it: a race in which more than 16 candidates are found before one has answered, whose oldest unanswered attempt ends for the seventeenth; a device found behind any number of candidates, which is attempted within 16 s of being found while a place holds an unanswered attempt and fewer than 16 ended attempts are still returning; a sender that keeps 16 ended attempts unreturned and every place holding one ended for an earlier candidate has it dropped. Reason: the candidates of a race are what DNS-SD and BLE advertisements name, neither of them authenticated, so the wait of a device's attempt must not grow with the number of candidates found before it. Pinned by `client/discovery:TestCommissioningRace_DeviceAfterUnansweredCandidatesIsAttempted`, `TestRace_OldestUnansweredAttemptGivesItsPlace` and `TestRace_AnsweredAttemptsKeepTheirPlaces`, and by `controller/commissioner:TestCommissionTellsTheRaceItsDeviceAnswered`; the limit is in `docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js bounds the race's attempts and their wait.

Review II, N3-rwrace-2: an attempt over BLE is answered once the peripheral accepted the connection (`ble.Dial`). Pinned by `controller/ble:TestDialMarksTheRaceAttemptAnsweredOnConnect`.

Review II, close-out C3 (R2-C2-bound-2153) and run 3 (R3-bound-3501, owner decisions 552 and 559): at most `maxRaceWaiting` = 16 (= `maxRaceAttempts`) candidates wait unreleased beside those an ended attempt is keeping a place for. When another is found, the one found longest ago takes a place at once, in a free place or by replacing the oldest unanswered attempt as a candidate past its ceiling does. It is dropped unattempted (`matter.controller.discovery.candidate_dropped`; `client/discovery/session_kinds.go` `overflowLocked`) only when no place can be given. That is the case when every place holds an answered attempt, where it would have waited without bound before the C3 bound as well. It is also the case when every place holds an answered attempt or one ended for an earlier candidate, which happens only while `maxRaceUnwinding` = 16 ended attempts have not returned. An ended attempt gives its place up at its cancel, not at its return, while fewer than 16 ended attempts are unwinding (`replaceLocked`, `unwindLocked`). The running attempts then exceed 16 by at most 16, for as long as the ended ones take to return. So the race holds at most 32 running attempts and at most 32 waiting candidates (16 while no ended attempt keeps a place). A device found behind any number of candidates starts within 16 s while a place holds an unanswered attempt and fewer than 16 ended attempts are unwinding, also in the burst the Fable diff read of G3 measured (16 unanswered places, 16 candidates, the device, 16 candidates, attempts returning 5 ms after their cancel; before decision 559 it was dropped at the 33rd arrival). These are this module's own bounds beside `maxRaceAttempts` (decision 55). matter.js bounds neither the attempts nor the waiting candidates: `#pending` is a `Set` and `this.#pending.add(attempt)` has no size check (`ParallelPaseDiscovery.ts:47`, `:150` at `b25ed960`, Fable diff read of G3). Whether what feeds `onDiscovered` is bounded upstream was not read (unverified). Pinned by `client/discovery:TestRace_WaitingCandidatesAreBounded`, `TestRace_DeviceFoundBehindAStreamOfCandidatesStartsWithinItsCeiling`, `TestRace_DeviceInABurstStartsWithinItsCeiling` and `TestRace_OverflowWhileReplacedAttemptsHaveNotReturnedIsBounded`.

### BD-Matter-BTP-SendQueueBounded — a BTP session's send queue holds at most 255 messages

matter.js queues every outgoing message: `sendMatterMessage` pushes it onto `queuedOutgoingMatterMessages` (`packages/protocol/src/ble/BtpSessionHandler.ts:390` at `b25ed960`), an array declared without a limit (`:42`). connectedhomeip chains each message onto its send queue, `mSendQueue->AddToEnd`, with no count (`src/ble/BLEEndPoint.cpp:591-602` at `6170af84`). Here (`transport/btp/session.go`) a session's queue of messages waiting for room in the peer's window holds at most `maxQueuedMessages` = `MaximumWindowSize` = 255; a `Send` past it is refused with a `FlowError`, the queued messages stay and the session lives. The number and what happens at it are both chosen, with no reference: the number is the largest window a session may negotiate — as many messages as that window has segments — and refusing the newest message was chosen over closing the session. How many messages wait is the peer's to decide, since the ack-received timeout (`AckTimeout`, 15 s) bounds an unacknowledged window in time only. Who reaches it: a sender to a central that acknowledges too little for 255 messages to leave. A commissioning does not, its messages being paced by acknowledgements and responses; that is the fix agent's reasoning, not a measurement. Review II, phase 3 rework. Pinned by `transport/btp:TestSession_SendQueueIsBounded`; the limit is in `docs/guides/limits.md`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js bounds the queue.

### BD-Matter-CASE-HandshakeStateBounded — the device holds state for at most 256 CASE handshakes, the oldest losing its place

matter.js holds a CASE handshake's state in the exchange it runs on: `onNewExchange` builds a messenger for the exchange and handles its Sigma1 (`packages/protocol/src/session/case/CaseServer.ts:61-64` at `db021da0`), and when the handshake ends the unsecured session it ran on is destroyed (`:95-98`); its unsecured sessions are a map by node id with no count over it (`packages/protocol/src/session/SessionManager.ts:257`). Nothing at these lines bounds the handshakes in flight, and the search went no further (unverified beyond them); connectedhomeip was not read (unverified). The device keeps two tables of its own for a handshake — the router's record of each Sigma1 it answered (`bridge/securechannel.go`, `markSigma1Replied`) and the adapters of a `PerExchangeCaseProvider` (`bridge/case_provider.go`) — keyed, since owner decision 51, by the initiator's unauthenticated node id and the exchange id, so that the key no longer bounds them. Both hold at most `maxCaseHandshakes` = `maxUnsecuredWindows` = 256: past it the oldest record loses its place, and once a new Sigma1 began a handshake on a provider's adapter, the adapter whose handshake began least recently; an adapter whose Sigma1 is being judged takes no place, and one whose Sigma1 began nothing leaves on its own, and that handshake ends as a reaped one does — its replies are no longer retransmitted, its staked session id is released, the provider's `SetOnEvict` callback runs — and its Sigma3 is answered as one of a handshake no Sigma1 began. The number is a constant of this module carried over, not read from a reference: each handshake holds one unsecured duplicate-detection window for as long as it holds its record, so the bound is the windows' own. Which one goes — the record made first, the adapter whose handshake began longest ago — is the fix agent's choice, after `unsecuredEntryLimit`'s. Only a Sigma1 that began a handshake takes a place: one the node refused leaves no record and evicts nothing, and since a record is made before its Sigma1 is judged, the records may pass the bound by the Sigma1s being judged at that moment (R2-P3-rr-dev-04). A completed handshake's record lives until the provider lets its adapter go, and counts. Who reaches it: the 257th CASE handshake in flight on one device, at whose Sigma1 the oldest handshake ends. Review II, R2-P3-dr-dev-03, R2-P3-rr-dev-04. Pinned by `bridge:TestSigma1RecordsAreBounded`, `TestCaseAdaptersAreBounded`, `TestSigma1WithoutHandshakeStateLeavesNoRecord` and `TestSigma1ThatBeginsNothingTakesNoRecordsPlace`; the limit is in `docs/guides/limits.md`. No register row: the tables are this module's own, and matter.js has no counterpart to bound. Retires when the tables do.

A Sigma1's bytes are held once across keys: the same bytes under another initiator node id or exchange id are acknowledged and not judged, so a captured Sigma1 sent again under other keys begins no handshake and takes no place (review II, R2-P6-sec-0301; pinned by `bridge:TestReplayedSigma1UnderOtherKeysEndsNoHandshake`, `TestCaseProviderEvictsOnlyForAHandshakeThatBegan`). A `PerExchangeCaseProvider` gives an adapter a place only once its Sigma1 began a handshake, `Forget` runs the eviction callback, and a `Resolve` no longer extends an adapter's lifetime; a resumption pickup that fails ends its adapter. What stays the entry's cost: a fabric member can mint fresh Sigma1s.

### BD-Matter-BLE-CentralWithoutPASEGivenUp — a BLE central without a secure session or a PASE handshake in flight is disconnected at the handshake bound

matter.js gives the BTP handshake 15 s — `BTP_CONN_RSP_TIMEOUT` (`packages/protocol/src/ble/BleConsts.ts:56` at `db021da0`) — and a PASE pairing 60 s (`PASE_PAIRING_TIMEOUT`, `packages/protocol/src/session/pase/PaseServer.ts:33`). What either reference does with a central that completes the BTP handshake and then starts no PASE was not read (unverified); connectedhomeip closes its BLE connections with the window (`BD-chip-BLE-WindowEndDisconnectsCentral`). Here (`bridge/ble.go`, `watchBLEPASE`, `connPASEState`) a central's connection is looked at `btp.ConnRspTimeout` = 15 s after its BTP handshake and at every 15 s step after: one that carries neither a secure session nor a PASE handshake in flight is disconnected (`matter.ble.central_dropped`), with or without an open commissioning window. A PASE handshake older than `pasePairingTimeout` = 60 s is not in flight — its claim on the single PASE place has expired too — so a central that abandoned its PASE gives the place up at the next step (R2-P3-rr-dev-02). The single PASE claim runs 60 s from the PBKDFParamRequest that took it and is not renewed, and a claim that runs out counts as a failed pairing, so twenty abandoned PASE handshakes close the commissioning window and start the lockout, as twenty failed ones do. A further PBKDFParamRequest of the same handshake is counted as a failed pairing and ends it — as matter.js takes an unexpected message on the accepted exchange (`PaseServer.ts:80-86` ignores only a new exchange; `packages/protocol/src/securechannel/SecureChannelMessenger.ts:95-98`, `PaseServer.ts:94-95`) — and is answered with a StatusReport InvalidParameter unless a reply of the handshake still awaits its acknowledgement, as matter.js's `cancelPairing` (`PaseServer.ts:103-104`, `:210`); a failure report under another source node id releases no connection's hold, so a central cannot keep a PASE handshake in flight past the 60 s (review II, R2-P6-sec-0304; pinned by `bridge:TestRepeatedPBKDFParamRequestEndsThePairing`, `TestPaseClaimRunsFromItsFirstRequest`, `TestFailureReportOfAnotherInitiatorKeepsTheHold`). The watch ends with the connection's first secure session; a central whose session closes later is not watched again. The two numbers are the references' constants (connectedhomeip's `BTP_CONN_RSP_TIMEOUT_MS`, 15000, `src/ble/BleConfig.h:215`, and `kPASESessionEstablishmentTimeout`, 60 s, `src/app/server/CommissioningWindowManager.cpp:200` at `6170af84`, beside matter.js's two above); the rule they are applied to is this module's, and so is the repetition every 15 s, the fix agent's reading of it. Who sees it: a central that connects and starts no PASE, or abandons one, which is disconnected and may connect again; a commissioner whose PASE is under way keeps its place. Reason: the peripheral serves one central at a time, and between two windows, or after a failed PASE attempt, nothing else ended the connection of one that never armed a fail-safe. Review II, R2-P3-dr-net-03, R2-P3-rr-dev-02. Pinned by `bridge:TestBLECentralWithoutPASEIsDroppedAfterTheHandshakeBound`, `TestBLECentralKeepsItsPlaceWhilePASERuns` and `TestBLECentralWithAnAbandonedPASEGivesUpItsPlace`; the limit is in `docs/guides/limits.md`. No register row, as for the window's end. Retires when matter.js bounds a central without PASE.

### BD-chip-GroupWrite-ListAppendApplied — a group write that appends to a list is applied, as connectedhomeip applies it; matter.js writes no group ADD

A group WriteRequest whose path carries a null ListIndex (ADD) is applied on every member endpoint as an append (`HandleGroupWriteRequest`, `im/group.go:192-207`), as connectedhomeip applies a group write's list operation on each endpoint the group maps to (`ProcessGroupAttributeDataIBs`, `src/app/WriteHandler.cpp:434`, the write at `:559` at `6170af84`), every endpoint appending the request's own element — connectedhomeip hands each mapped endpoint a fresh reader over the request's data (`:555-559`), and the dispatcher starts every resolved location from the request's value (`endpoint/dispatcher.go:523-532`; review II, R2-P4-dr-im-01); its Busy rule for an ADD that does not follow its attribute stands in the unicast loop only (`:364-371`). matter.js writes no group ADD: it takes an ADD only after a write to the same attribute (`packages/node/src/node/server/InteractionServer.ts:511-531` at `db021da0`), remembers that attribute for a concrete path only (`:536-537`; a path without an endpoint is not concrete, `:82-84`), and so answers a group ADD Busy, an answer a suppressed response never sends (`:550-553`). By design (owner decision 63; review II, R2-P4-imwrite-09): a controller that chunks a list into a REPLACE and ADDs, as matter.js's own client does by default (`chunkLists = true`, `packages/protocol/src/action/request/Write.ts:65`, `:155-166`), would otherwise leave the list empty on this node. Who sees it: a controller that group-writes a list in chunks finds the list filled here and, by the lines above, empty on a matter.js node (read, not run).

### BD-Matter-Transitions-CyclicAtBound — a cyclic property without a target starts at its bound and wraps

matter.js `Transitions.start` takes a cyclic transition into its cyclic branch only when it has a target (`packages/node/src/behavior/Transitions.ts:152-164` at `b25ed960`). One without — a hue moved by MoveHue or by a colour loop (`moveHueLogic`, `packages/node/src/behaviors/color-control/ColorControlServer.ts:485`; `startColorLoopLogic`, `:1201-1204`; the hue properties are `cyclic`, `:1679`, `:1684`) — falls into the bounded branch, whose check does not start it at the minimum moving down or at the maximum moving up (`:165-169`). `cluster/transition` applies that check to bounded properties only, so a hue at its bound moves on and wraps (`cluster/transition/transition.go:47-54`). By design (owner decision 66; review II, R2-P4-applight-03): on a wheel a bound is no end, and matter.js's check reads as unintended there. Who sees it: a controller that sends MoveHue Up at the top of the wheel, or starts a colour loop there — the hue turns here and, by the lines above, stands in matter.js (read, not run).

### BD-Matter-Scenes-FabricSceneInfoForEveryFabric — FabricSceneInfo holds an entry for every fabric of the node from the start

matter.js builds FabricSceneInfo from the fabrics known when the server initialises (`#initializeFabricSceneInfo`, `packages/node/src/behaviors/scenes-management/ScenesManagementServer.ts:977-999` at `db021da0`) and adds an entry only when a fabric's scene count is updated (`:1002-1023`); the fabric event it reacts to at `:190` is `deleting`. A fabric commissioned after the start therefore has no entry until its first scene or a restart — inferred from these lines, not run; matter.js's own snapshot of a node holds `fabricSceneInfo: []` (`packages/node/test/node/ClientNodeTest.ts:5111`). `cluster/core.ScenesManagement` serves an entry for every fabric of the node, also one that never stored a scene (`cluster/core/scenes_management.go:514-524`). By design (owner decision 66; review II, R2-P4-applight-05): what a fabric reads does not depend on when it was commissioned relative to the last restart. connectedhomeip was not read (unverified).

### BD-Matter-LevelControl-HandOffSceneInvalidation — on the hand-off path every plain level command the host's port accepts ends the current scene

matter.js ends the current scene only past its own ExecuteIfOff gate: MoveToLevel, Move, Step and Stop return before `#invalidateScenes` when the options do not allow execution (`packages/node/src/behaviors/level-control/LevelControlServer.ts:269-276`, `:354-359`, `:421-426`, `:482-487` at `b25ed960`). `levelcontrol.Server` does the same under the transition engine and over the module's `NativeSource`, whose gate it can ask (`cluster/levelcontrol/scenes.go:32-41`, `:54-77`). On the hand-off path a host's `LevelSource` applies the gate where the server cannot see it, so every plain command the port accepts counts as executed and ends the scene (`handOffExecutes`, `:67-80`). By design (review II, R2-P4-applight-01): the port reports no "gated" result, and the contract stays as it is. Who sees it: a controller reading FabricSceneInfo's SceneValid after a plain level command the host's own gate turned into a no-op — false here, still true in matter.js. Pinned by `cluster/levelcontrol:TestHandOffCommandsInvalidateTheScene` and `TestCommandsInvalidateTheSceneAfterTheGate`.

### BD-Matter-Invoke-HoldsHostReports — while a command runs against a cluster instance, the host's change reports on it are held and leave with the command's one DataVersion

While a command runs against a cluster instance, the change reports of its servers on that instance are held, a change the host reports through a `ChangeNotifier` included; when the command ends the DataVersion advances once and the held attributes are marked together with those the command changed, and two commands that overlap on one instance share one commit (`invokeCommitTable`, `bridge/receive_dispatch.go:980-1055`). In matter.js a write takes the datasource's lock for its transaction: `#startWrite` adds the resource and calls `beginSync` (`packages/node/src/behavior/state/managed/Datasource.ts:1345-1350` at `db021da0`), which locks with `acquireLocksSync` (`packages/general/src/transaction/Tx.ts:260-279`) and throws `SynchronousTransactionConflictError` on a resource another transaction holds (`packages/general/src/transaction/ResourceSet.ts:82-106`); the host's API, `Endpoint.set` and `setStateOf`, begins its transaction and awaits `tx.addResources` (`packages/node/src/endpoint/Endpoint.ts:256-273`, `:325-339`), which waits in `acquireLocks` until the command's transaction is done (`Tx.ts:194-203`; `ResourceSet.ts:51-75`), and each transaction then advances the version on its own commit (`Datasource.ts:1456-1457`). Who sees it: a subscriber gets the host's change and the command's under one version here and under two in matter.js; a read in between returns the host's value here already, where in matter.js it is not written before the command commits (read from the lines, not run). By design: one version for a command's commit, without a lock that would make a host's notifier wait on an interaction. Review II, R2-P4-cert-12, R2-P2-dr-req-03. Pinned by `bridge:TestCommandAdvancesTheDataVersionOnce`.

### BD-Matter-CommissionableDeviceType-RootNodeWithoutApplicationEndpoint — a node that serves no application endpoint advertises RootNode and stays commissionable

matter.js infers the commissionable device type from its endpoints (`packages/node/src/behavior/system/product-description/ProductDescriptionServer.ts:43-63`, `:93-126` at `b25ed960`) and, while none yields one, does not advertise as commissionable (`packages/node/src/behavior/system/commissioning/CommissioningServer.ts:280-283`) and refuses to enter commissionable mode, "you must add an endpoint or set the device type" (`:309-314`). The module infers the same way (`inferDeviceType`, `node/commissionable_device_type.go:54-66`) and advertises RootNode (0x0016) while nothing is found (`resolve`, `:40-53`). By design (review II, phase 4, with owner decision 72): a bridge started before its host's devices arrive stays commissionable, and the facade's own window has no counterpart to an application that opens the window later. One difference in timing beside it: matter.js fixes the type at the first change of its endpoint tree that yields one (`:55-62`), the module at the first announcement of a window that finds one, so a host that adds one device, removes it and adds another before the first window advertises the first one's type in matter.js and the second one's here. Who sees it: a commissioner that browses `_T22` or reads `DT=22` on a node without application endpoints, where a matter.js node shows no commissionable record. Pinned by `node:TestParityMatterJS_CommissionableDeviceType`.

### BD-Matter-OTAProvider-ACLGrantedFabrics — the OTA provider's ACL entry goes into the fabrics the host grants, and into none unasked

matter.js writes the provider's Operate/CASE entry into the ACL of `fabricAuthority.fabrics[0]`, the first fabric whose root certificate is its own authority's, and into none while there is none (`packages/node/src/behaviors/ota-software-update-provider/OtaSoftwareUpdateProviderServer.ts:116-154`; `packages/protocol/src/fabric/FabricAuthority.ts:112-114`, `:126-128` at `db021da0`). A `node.Node` has no authority of its own, so the set of such fabrics is empty and it writes into no fabric unasked; `OTAProviderConfig.GrantFabric` names, per fabric, the ones a host opens the provider to, asked at Start and after each CommissioningComplete, nil granting none; a grant only adds — one that is withdrawn removes nothing, the node not being able to tell an entry it wrote from one the fabric's administrator wrote (`node/ota_provider.go:43-63`, `:214-243`; review II, R2-P4-dr-core-01). By design (owner decision 74, which retired `BD-Matter-OTAProvider-ACLEveryFabric`): a node writes into a fabric's ACL only what that fabric's administrator or the host asked for. Who sees it: a requestor on a fabric the host did not grant is refused by the access check until that fabric's administrator writes the entry. Pinned by `node:TestOTAProviderACLNotWrittenUnasked`, `TestOTAProviderACLOnGrantedFabrics` and `TestOTAProviderACLWithdrawnGrantKeepsTheEntry`.

### BD-chip-ElectricalEnergy-CumulativeEventOnChange — the projected ElectricalEnergyMeasurement emits CumulativeEnergyMeasured when the cumulative energy changes, not with every measurement

matter.js emits CumulativeEnergyMeasured with every `setMeasurement` call that carries a cumulative value, an unchanged one included (`packages/node/src/behaviors/electrical-energy-measurement/ElectricalEnergyMeasurementServer.ts:44-62` at `b25ed960`). connectedhomeip emits it for a value whose set reports a change (`CumulativeEnergySnapshot`, `src/app/clusters/electrical-energy-measurement-server/ElectricalEnergyMeasurementCluster.cpp:442-469` at `6170af84`). The measurement projection has no `setMeasurement` call — the host notifies a change, and the projected server is rebuilt on every dispatch — so the bridge observes the notification and emits the event when CumulativeEnergyImported changes to a value (`electricalEnergyEvents`, `bridge/subscribe.go:2775-2786`). By design (review II, R2-P4-nv-05a): "on change" is the one point the projection has, and it is connectedhomeip's. Who sees it: a subscriber to the event gets one per change here, one per measurement call in matter.js. Pinned by `bridge:TestCumulativeEnergyMeasuredEvent`.

### BD-Matter-AttributeOrder-ModelOrder — a cluster's attributes are reported in the model's member order; a server's own reordering and the order of endpoints and clusters are not mirrored

Mirrored (owner decision 62; review II, R2-P4-imread-12): every report lists a cluster's attributes in the order of matter.js's cluster model, `Scope.membersOf` — the model's members, then the globals the cluster does not define in `GLOBAL_IDS` order 0xFFFD, 0xFFFC, 0xFFFB, 0xFFFA, 0xFFF9, 0xFFF8 (`packages/model/src/logic/Scope.ts:18`, `:167`, `:339-358` at `b25ed960`). matter.js builds a cluster's attribute list by iterating it (`packages/node/src/node/integration/ProtocolService.ts:449-451`) and a wildcard walks the list as built (`packages/protocol/src/action/server/AttributeReadResponse.ts:378-380`). The snapshot carries the order (`attributeOrder` per cluster and `globalAttributeOrder`, `parity/schema.json`) and `im.CompareAttributeIDs` applies it to a Read, a priming report and a change report alike (`im/read_expansion.go:301-320`); an attribute the order does not list comes first, ascending — the module's rule, since the order in which a server's schema adds members is not in the snapshot. Not mirrored, by design (owner decision 83): neither is a property of the model — the first is how one server or device type extends its schema, the second the order in which a node's endpoints and clusters were added. (1) a server's own order. Review II's order probe ran a matter.js node at `b25ed960` (Dimmable Light, On/Off Plug-in Unit, Temperature Sensor, Window Covering) through a full wildcard read: 22 of the 30 clusters served came in the model's order, 8 did not — BasicInformation (UniqueID first; its server extends the schema, `packages/node/src/behaviors/basic-information/BasicInformationServer.ts:155-158`), LevelControl on the Dimmable Light (CurrentLevel, MinLevel, MaxLevel first; the device type's `.alter()`, `packages/node/src/devices/dimmable-light.ts:59-67`), and Groups and ScenesManagement on three endpoints each (FeatureMap before ClusterRevision; the cause was not traced, unverified). The run is the probe's and was not repeated for this entry. The module serves the model's order for these clusters too. (2) the order of endpoints and of an endpoint's clusters. matter.js sorts nothing in a read: a wildcard walks the node's endpoints and an endpoint's clusters as they were added (`AttributeReadResponse.ts:183-185`, `:337-339`); the probe measured endpoint 0 as 0x001F, 0x0028, 0x0030, 0x0033, 0x003C, 0x003E, 0x003F, 0x0065 and 0x001D last. The module reports ascending endpoint and cluster ids, which its comment explains by Apple Home needing the Descriptor before the clusters it names (`bridge/subscribe_dispatch.go:55-66`). Who sees either: a controller that depends on the order of a wildcard report's items. Pinned, for the mirrored part, by `im:TestCompareAttributeIDsOnOffIsMatterJSsOrder`, `TestCompareAttributeIDsFollowsTheSnapshotOrder` and `TestCompareAttributeIDsUnlistedMembersFirst`.

### BD-Matter-ACLRemovedEventEntry — AccessControlEntryChanged(Removed) carries the entry the write removed

For each entry a shorter ACL write removes, matter.js runs `j` over the writing fabric's old entries but reads `latestValue: oldValue[j]`, an index into the unfiltered list of every fabric (`oldFabricAcls` at `packages/node/src/behaviors/access-control/AccessControlServer.ts:305`, the loop at `:328-336`, at `b25ed960`), so with more than one fabric its Removed event can carry another fabric's entry under the writing fabric's FabricIndex (read from the lines, not run). The module emits the writing fabric's own removed entry (`emit(AccessControlChangeTypeRemoved, oldEntries[j])`, `cluster/core/access_control.go:926`). By design (review II, R2-P4-coresec-11): the index is a defect in matter.js, not a behaviour to mirror, and the event names what was removed. Who sees it: an administrator subscribed to AccessControlEntryChanged on a node with several fabrics.

### BD-Matter-Invoke-OversizedResponseResourceExhausted — a lone invoke response too large for a message is answered RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED for its path

An invoke response that does not fit a message on its own — above `reportChunkHardCap`, the datagram size less 200, over UDP (`bridge/reply.go:435`) — is replaced, after the command ran, by a CommandStatusIB RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED for its path (`chunkInvokeResponse`, `oversizedInvokeEntry`, `bridge/receive_dispatch.go:1199-1206`, `:1254-1261`). matter.js has no such answer: it sends the message whatever its size, with a warning over UDP and a `MessageTooLargeError` over TCP (`packages/protocol/src/protocol/MessageChannel.ts:104-116` at `db021da0`); that its invoke path adds no bound of its own before that was the fix agent's reading of `InteractionServer.ts:1123-1151` and was not repeated (unverified). By design (review II, R2-P4-imwrite-13): the UDP listener here refuses a datagram above its cap, so without the replacement the controller would get no answer at all.

### BD-Matter-RequestCheck-RelaxationTable — every relaxation of the model's request and write check is one entry of clustergen's table, written into the definition

matter.js validates a request against the model before the invoker runs (`packages/protocol/src/action/server/CommandInvokeResponse.ts:484-487` at `db021da0`), and a server that wants to judge a field itself extends its schema with the constraint "none" or sets a `Supervision` on a command. The module holds every request and every written value to the generated definition — the request decoder (`spec.Command.DecodeRequest`; the bridge's hand-decoded requests pass it first, `bridge/fields_reader.go:88-101`) and `spec.CheckWritten` in the dispatcher's write entry, before any server runs (owner decision 64) — and states every departure in one table, `script/clustergen/relaxed.go:51-157`, one section per server, each entry with its reference line; the generator writes it into the definition (`spec.Field.Relaxed`, `spec.Attribute.Relaxed`, `spec.Command.Check`) beside the model's constraint, which stays verbatim.
