The sections that mirror matter.js: ICDManagement's VerificationKey (`packages/node/src/behaviors/icd-management/IcdManagementServer.ts:65-74`), OperationalCredentials' AttestationNonce and CsrNonce (`OperationalCredentialsServer.ts:62-66`), OpenCommissioningWindow's PAKE fields and Discriminator (`AdministratorCommissioningServer.ts:33-44`), Groups' AddGroup and AddGroupIfIdentifying (`GroupsServer.ts:31-42`), ScenesManagement's scene ids, TransitionTime and SceneName (`ScenesManagementServer.ts:140-159`), DoorLock — since the pin lift to `b25ed960` (#5012, unit P1-B) no longer unchecked as a whole (matter.js's cluster-wide skip is gone; `RequestCheck.Unchecked` is deprecated): INVALID_COMMAND for the fifteen commands of `DoorLockServer.ts:1498-1516` and the get*Schedule index fields judged by the handler (`:1520-1526`); OperationalCredentials' CertificateChainRequest answers INVALID_COMMAND (`OperationalCredentialsServer.ts:635-638`), GeneralCommissioning's SetRegulatoryConfig.NewRegulatoryConfig (`GeneralCommissioningServer.ts:288-289`) and Identify's TriggerEffect fields (`IdentifyServer.ts:162-166`) are the handler's — and Thermostat's Presets and Schedules, whose written value goes to the atomic write's pending state (`packages/node/src/behaviors/thermostat/AtomicWriteHandler.ts:252-264`) for the server to judge (the presets at `ThermostatServer.ts:1367-1375`). The sections that follow connectedhomeip under an owner decision: EnergyEvse's ChargingTargets (`BD-chip-EVSE-TargetsServerHeld`), PushAvStreamTransport's stream lists and MotionSensitivity (`BD-chip-PushAvStreamTransport-RulesInServer`) and LaundryWasherControls' NumberOfRinses (`BD-chip-Appliance-RulesInServer`), decision 69. The sections that follow connectedhomeip gain CameraAvStreamManagement's SetStreamPriorities entries (`BD-chip-CameraAvStreamManagement-RulesInServer`, coordinator decision C-12 of pin-lift wave P1, the first relaxation of a list's entries). Since `b25ed960` matter.js's TLV layer still holds an enum to uint32 only (`packages/types/src/tlv/TlvNumber.ts:303`, `TlvOfModel.ts:221-224`; this module's decoder holds the enum's wire width, findings F-b25ed960-33) and the request gate after it refuses a value its enum does not define with CONSTRAINT_ERROR, a command's own Refusal answering the first error (`ProtocolService.ts:671-705`) — for a server held to its definition (spec.Server, InvokeHeld, Hooks; the other servers are findings F-b25ed960-29). One thing the check does not do, as matter.js: a deprecated enum value stays writable — matter.js compiles a bare "D" as optional, which is the fix's reading and was not repeated (unverified). By design: the mechanism is one table instead of a schema extension in each server, because the definitions are generated (ADR 0013) and a relaxation has to survive the regeneration; the behaviour is matter.js's except in the four sections named. Pinned by `script/clustergen:TestRelaxationTableResolves`, `cluster/spec:TestRequestCheckParityMatterJS`, `bridge:TestHandDecodedRequestsAreHeldByTheirDefinition` and `endpoint:TestWrittenValueIsHeldByTheDefinition`.

### BD-Matter-WindowCovering-UnknownPositionTravelStopped — a simulated travel from an unknown position reads Stopped, where matter.js's test node keeps Opening or Closing

With `Config.MoveStep`, the server's simulated travel and the counterpart of matter.js's CHIP test node, a movement command on an axis whose position is unknown does not travel and the axis reads Stopped (`cluster/cover/windowcovering_server.go:930-937`), `#computeOperationalState`'s answer for a null position (`packages/node/src/behaviors/window-covering/WindowCoveringServer.ts:273-275` at `b25ed960`). matter.js's test node does not travel either — "Current position is not set" (`support/chip-testing/src/cluster/TestWindowCoveringServer.ts:55-62`) — but leaves the Opening or Closing the server set when the movement began (`WindowCoveringServer.ts:412-420`). ### BD-Matter-ArmDuringRollbackWaits — an ArmFailSafe that arrives while an expired fail-safe is rolled back waits for the rollback and arms a fresh fail-safe

Three answers. connectedhomeip marks its context busy when the fail-safe expires, before it schedules the disarm (`ScheduleFailSafeCleanup`, `src/app/FailSafeContext.cpp:84`, `:103` at `6170af84`), `ArmFailSafe` refuses while it is busy (`:106-108`), and the command answers BusyWithOtherAdmin (`src/app/clusters/general-commissioning-server/GeneralCommissioningCluster.cpp:419-420`, `:446-449`). matter.js sends an arm to `extend` while its context exists (`packages/node/src/behaviors/general-commissioning/GeneralCommissioningServer.ts:89-94` at `db021da0`; the commissioner drops the context only once it is destroyed, `packages/protocol/src/protocol/DeviceCommissioner.ts:162-171`), and `extend` re-arms through `this.#failsafe?.reArm` (`packages/protocol/src/common/FailsafeContext.ts:90-92`), which calls nothing once `close` has cleared `#failsafe` ahead of its rollback (`:198-201`); the breadcrumb is then stored because the commissioner still reads as armed (`GeneralCommissioningServer.ts:117-120`), and the answer is SUCCESS with no fail-safe armed. That is read from these lines — `extend`'s wait on a construction that is being destroyed resolving without an error (`packages/general/src/util/Construction.ts:332-344`, `:443-448`) — and was not run. `reArm`'s "FailSafe already expired." (`packages/protocol/src/common/FailsafeTimer.ts:48-51`), which the command's catch turns into BusyWithOtherAdmin (`GeneralCommissioningServer.ts:121-128`), is not reached on that path. This module waits for the rollback, one in flight or the one the arm runs itself, and then judges the fail-safe fresh: it arms a new one, or answers FAILURE when the rollback ended the arming session (`settleArmLocked`, `settleExpiryLocked`, `cluster/core/general_commissioning_rollback.go:171-184`, `:186-194`; `BD-Matter-ArmOverDueWindowEndedSession`). By design (owner decision 77; review II, phase 4): the arm asks for a fail-safe and one rollback later the node can give it, where matter.js's answer is a success that arms nothing. Who sees it: an administrator that arms while an expired window is being rolled back gets its fail-safe here, BusyWithOtherAdmin from connectedhomeip and, by the lines above, an unarmed SUCCESS from matter.js. Pinned by `cluster/core:TestGencomm_ArmInTheExpiryGapWaitsForTheRollback` and `TestGencomm_ArmOverADueWindowRollsItBack`.

### BD-Matter-ACL-NoAdministerEntryAtStart — a fabric whose ACL holds no entry gets no Administer entry at start

When its node comes online, matter.js gives every fabric whose ACL holds no entry an Administer entry for CASE with the subject `fabric.rootNodeId` on the whole node, "Backward compatibility to Matter.js before 0.9.1" (`#online`, `packages/node/src/behaviors/access-control/AccessControlServer.ts:83-103` at `b25ed960`); the reaction is bound to the node's `online` lifecycle (`:79-80`), so it runs at every start. This module writes a fabric's Administer entry once, for the CaseAdminSubject of its AddNOC (`cluster/core/operational_credentials.go:2271-2281`), and nothing at start adds one — `NewAccessControl` loads the stored extensions and no more (`cluster/core/access_control.go:280-287`) — so an ACL its administrator emptied stays empty across a restart. By design (owner decision 79; review II, R2-P4-coresec-08): the module grants no privilege unasked; matter.js's entry migrates its own older data, and granted at every start it would undo an administrator that emptied the ACL on purpose. Who sees it: an administrator that removed every entry of its fabric's ACL and restarts the node finds one Administer entry on a matter.js node and none here. No test pins the empty ACL across a restart (none was found; unverified); connectedhomeip was not read (unverified).

### BD-Matter-WebRtcRequestor-ACLGrantedFabrics — the WebRTC requestor's ACL entry goes into the fabrics the host grants, and into none unasked

matter.js writes the requestor's Operate/CASE entry into the ACL of `fabricAuthority.fabrics[0]`, the first fabric whose root certificate is its own authority's, and into none while there is none (`packages/node/src/behaviors/web-rtc-transport-requestor/WebRtcTransportRequestorServer.ts:56-94`, `:58`; `packages/protocol/src/fabric/FabricAuthority.ts:112-114`, `:126-128` at `db021da0`). By design (owner decision 84, as decision 74 for `BD-Matter-OTAProvider-ACLGrantedFabrics`): a node writes into a fabric's ACL only what that fabric's administrator or the host asked for. Who sees it: a camera on a fabric the host did not grant is refused by the access check on its signals until that fabric's administrator writes the entry. Pinned by `node:TestWebRTCRequestorACLNotWrittenUnasked`, `TestWebRTCRequestorACLOnGrantedFabrics`, `TestWebRTCRequestorACLWithdrawnGrantKeepsTheEntry` and `cluster/camera:TestParityMatterJS_RequestorACLInstall`, which grants its one fabric.

### BD-chip-WiFiInterfaceEnabled-DriverSwitch — a Wi-Fi InterfaceEnabled write switches the interface through an optional driver capability; without it false is INVALID_ACTION, and true succeeds

Under the Ahead row of `BD-chip-WiFiNetworkCommissioningServer`. connectedhomeip hands a write of InterfaceEnabled to the driver's `SetEnabled` and answers INVALID_ACTION when that returns `CHIP_ERROR_UNSUPPORTED_CHIP_FEATURE`, quoting "If not supported, a write to this attribute with a value of false SHALL fail with a status of INVALID_ACTION" (`src/app/clusters/network-commissioning/NetworkCommissioningCluster.cpp:1120-1132`; `NetworkCommissioningCluster.h:134`, `:144` at `6170af84`); the base driver's `SetEnabled` returns that error and its `GetEnabled` true (`src/include/platform/NetworkCommissioning.h:225-234`), and no file under `src/platform/Linux` names either (searched). The module follows it through the optional `contract.WiFiInterfaceSwitcher` (`contract/wifi.go:49-60`; owner decision 80; review II, R2-P4-cert-04): a write that changes the value asks the driver to switch, and the attribute takes the value once it did; without the capability, or when the driver answers `errors.ErrUnsupported`, the write is INVALID_ACTION (`switchInterface`, `cluster/core/network_commissioning_wifi.go:746-769`). Two differences from connectedhomeip follow from one rule, that a write of the value already held changes nothing (`:752-754`; matter.js's rule for every attribute, `packages/node/src/behavior/state/managed/Datasource.ts:1456-1457`, `:1476-1481` at `db021da0`): a write of true to a driver without the switch succeeds — the attribute reads true there — where connectedhomeip's base driver refuses `SetEnabled(true)` as well and the write answers INVALID_ACTION; and an unchanged write calls no driver and advances no DataVersion, where connectedhomeip calls `SetEnabled` on every write (`:1124`). By design (owner decision 80): true is accepted as it is. A false an earlier version stored without a switch is not restored, InterfaceEnabled reads true (`:716-728`). Who sees it: a controller that writes true to a node whose driver cannot switch its interface. Pinned by `cluster/core:TestWiFiInterfaceEnabledWithoutASwitch`, `TestWiFiInterfaceEnabledSwitchesTheInterface` and `TestWiFiInterfaceEnabledDataVersionAdvancesOnlyOnAChange`.

### BD-Matter-FailedReadAnswersItsPath — a read that fails in a server answers FAILURE for its path, where matter.js fails the interaction

An error thrown while matter.js answers a Read is caught by the request handler, which answers the exchange with one StatusResponse — FAILURE for an error that is no StatusResponseError (`InteractionServerMessenger.handleRequest`, `packages/protocol/src/interaction/InteractionMessenger.ts:425-459` at `db021da0`); neither `packages/protocol/src/action/server/AttributeReadResponse.ts` nor `handleReadRequest` (`packages/node/src/node/server/InteractionServer.ts:335-391`) holds a catch of its own (searched; read from the lines, not run). Here the dispatcher answers per path: a request's read of a fabric-scoped attribute that its server lists and could not read answers FAILURE on that path — no other read stands in for it — and the other paths of the request are answered (`readOne`, `fabricScopedReadFailed`, `endpoint/dispatcher.go:882-945`); under a wildcard endpoint the path is left out, like every other path without a value (`:332`). By design (review II, R2-P4-rr-sec-01): a failure of the store behind one list is that list's, and the rest of the report is still true. Who sees it: a controller whose read meets a store failure gets a report with one FAILURE status here and a StatusResponse FAILURE for the whole read from matter.js. Pinned by `endpoint:TestFabricScopedReadFailureAnswersFailure` and `TestFabricScopedReaderNotOkOnARequest`.

### BD-Matter-GKM-StoredKeySet0Removed — a stored GroupKeyMap entry that maps a group to key set 0 is removed when the server is constructed

The model holds GroupKeyMapStruct's GroupKeySetId to "1 to 65535" (`packages/model/src/standard/elements/group-key-management.element.ts:109` at `db021da0`), and matter.js validates a behavior's state against its schema once its initialiser has run (`packages/node/src/behavior/internal/ServerBehaviorBacking.ts:45-72`, the validation at `:60-63`), an error there ending the backing's construction in a `BehaviorInitializationError` (`packages/node/src/behavior/internal/BehaviorBacking.ts:95-114`); what that does to the node's start was not traced (unverified). `NewGroupKeyManagement` removes every stored entry that maps a group to key set 0 and logs each at Warn (`dropMappingsToKeySet0`, `cluster/core/group_key_management.go:180`, `:184-204`); a store error is logged and the entry stays for the next start. By design (review II, R2-P4-dr-core-02): the one invalid shape is one an earlier version of this module stored, and the module repairs it rather than serve it or refuse to start. Who sees it: a fabric whose GroupKeyMap held such an entry reads the list without it after the upgrade. Pinned by `cluster/core:TestGKM_StoredMappingToKeySet0_DroppedAtConstruction`.

### BD-Matter-NetworkInterfaces-RootNetworkType — every NetworkInterfaces entry carries the root's network type, where matter.js on Node.js reports Ethernet

matter.js's GeneralDiagnostics gives a NetworkInterfaces entry the type its platform reports, and the type it derives from the root's NetworkCommissioning features — Wi-Fi, Thread, else Ethernet — only when the platform reports none (`type: type ?? networkType`, `packages/node/src/behaviors/general-diagnostics/GeneralDiagnosticsServer.ts:477-494`, `:527` at `db021da0`). Under Node.js the platform always reports one: `getNetInterfaces` starts every interface at `InterfaceType.Ethernet` and replaces it only from a configured mapping, "Each network interface which has no mapped type is returned as Ethernet for now" (`packages/nodejs/src/net/NodeJsNetwork.ts:184`, `:195-202`), the mapping being the `network.interface` variable, and the runtime passes the type on (`packages/node/src/behavior/system/network/ServerNetworkRuntime.ts:102-126`). So a matter.js node on Node.js whose root has the Wi-Fi feature serves Ethernet for every interface the application did not map (read from the lines, not run). This module has no platform mapping of interfaces to types and takes the server's fallback for every entry: the root's network type, WiFi on a node with a Wi-Fi driver and Ethernet otherwise (`enumerateNetworkInterfaces`, `cluster/core/general_diagnostics.go:1139-1154`; `SetNetworkInterfaceType`, `:193`; `setNetworkInterfaceRules`, `node/node.go:1490-1493`). By design (review II, phase 4, the citation pass): the rule is the one matter.js's server states for a platform that knows no type, and on a Wi-Fi node it names the interface for what it is. Who sees it: a controller reading NetworkInterfaces on a Wi-Fi root — WiFi here, Ethernet from a matter.js node on Node.js without a mapping. Pinned by `cluster/core:TestGeneralDiagnosticsNetworkInterfacesTypeAndOperational` and `node:TestNetworkInterfacesFollowTheRootNetworkAndTheAdvertiser`.

### BD-Matter-SendIntervalNotBelowSubscriberFloor — a subscription's send interval is never below the subscriber's MinIntervalFloor

matter.js takes half the max interval as the send interval and, when that is under a minute, the larger of the subscriber's MinIntervalFloor and 0.8 of the max interval; the last step compares with the publisher's own minimum — `subscriptionMinInterval`, `MIN_INTERVAL` 2 s unless the application configures more — and not with the subscriber's floor (`#determineSendingIntervals`, `packages/node/src/node/server/ServerSubscription.ts:270-292`, `:73`, `:111`, `:188-190` at `db021da0`). With a max interval of two minutes or more the subscriber's floor therefore does not enter: a floor of 100 s under a max interval of 120 s gives a send interval of 60 s there (from the formula, not run). The module's last step holds the send interval to the subscriber's MinIntervalFloor as well as to the 2 s (`sendIntervalLocked`, `im/subscription/subscription.go:274-284`), 100 s in that case. By design, the module's own: the floor is the least time between two reports the subscriber asked for, and the module holds its keep-alive to it as it holds every other report. Found by the citation pass of review II, phase 4, which corrected the comment that gave matter.js's formula this step. Who sees it: a subscriber whose MinIntervalFloor is above half its max interval gets its keep-alives no sooner than the floor. Pinned by `im/subscription:TestSendInterval_FloorAboveSessionIdleTimeoutIsKept`.

### BD-Matter-CASE-Sigma1OverCompletedAcknowledgedOnly — a Sigma1 that begins no handshake while a handshake's record stands, in progress or completed, is acknowledged and not answered

A CASE handshake's state on the device is one record per initiator node id and exchange (owner decision 51), made for the Sigma1 that began the handshake. It stands through the singleton handler until the handshake ends by its own events — a completed one when its success report is acknowledged or given up, one in progress at the responder's wait for Sigma3 or at the give-up of its Sigma2 (`sigma1RecordOver`, `bridge/securechannel.go:2074-2093`) — and through a provider until the provider lets the handshake's adapter go, its TTL. While a reply of the handshake waits for its acknowledgement, a message under its initiator and exchange that does not acknowledge that reply is refused on receive — not acknowledged, not answered — before it reaches the router, as matter.js throws a flow error for it before the CASE server sees it (`packages/protocol/src/protocol/MessageExchange.ts:521-534` at `db021da0`) and before the exchange takes up its acknowledgement (`:553-561`); review II, phase 7, decision 277. A message that passes that rule — it acknowledges the reply, or no reply waits — reaches the router: a Sigma1 that begins no handshake — one that does not decode, one the responder refuses — leaves the record as it is and is acknowledged and not answered, and the handler's failure report is not sent (`markSigma1Replied`, `bridge/securechannel.go:1701-1721`; `handleSigma1`, `:1918-1961`; `dropHandshakeNotBegun`, `:425-431`); a Sigma2_Resume the responder receives is acknowledged and not answered under every key and reaches no handler (`dispatchSigma2Resume`, `:754-756`). The handshake's state stays with its record: the responder judges a Sigma1 on locals and commits only one it accepts (`processSigma1Locked`, `tryResume`, `secure/sigma/protocol.go:912-1096`, `:633-829`), so the singleton handler's responder keeps the Sigma2 and the keys of a handshake in progress and the session keys of a finished one, and through a provider the adapter of a handshake in progress or established stays (`CaseAdapter.ProcessSigma1`, `bridge/handlers.go:882-1003`). A Sigma1 with the bytes of the one the record was made for is dropped unanswered and is not judged while the record stands, a completed handshake's included (`markSigma1Replied`; `BD-Matter-CASE-Sigma1RepeatedWhileInProgress`). matter.js acknowledges a duplicate (`MessageExchange.ts:501-511`), and a Sigma2_Resume that opens an exchange is not taken (`packages/protocol/src/securechannel/SecureChannelProtocol.ts:146-153`). The two differ for a Sigma1 or Sigma2_Resume on the handshake's live exchange that passes the receive rules — it acknowledges the Sigma2, or none waits, or the handshake runs over TCP: in matter.js it is queued (`MessageExchange.ts:562`), is what the CASE server's typed read gets (`packages/protocol/src/session/case/CaseServer.ts:275-279`, `case/CaseMessenger.ts:35-36`, `securechannel/SecureChannelMessenger.ts:95-98`, "Received unexpected message type"), and the server's catch answers InvalidParam and closes the handshake's session (`CaseServer.ts:65-99`, the report at `:93`, skipped for an exchange that is closing or still has an unacknowledged message, `:84`); here it is acknowledged, not answered, and the record stands (owner decisions 51, 70) — the deliberate divergence this entry records. They differ too once that exchange is gone. matter.js's CASE server sends the success report (`CaseServer.ts:332`) and then detaches and closes the handshake's unsecured session (`:95-98`), which leaves the manager's table (`packages/protocol/src/session/UnsecuredSession.ts:94-102`); a Sigma1 of that initiator then gets a new session and a new exchange (`packages/protocol/src/protocol/ExchangeManager.ts:312-328`, `:401`, `:478`), the CASE server takes it as the start of a fresh handshake, with a random and a key pair of its own (`CaseServer.ts:61-64`, `:102-146`, `:236`, `:241`), and one it cannot take is answered with a failure report — NoSharedTrustRoots for an unknown fabric, InvalidParam otherwise (`:65-94`). Here the same holds once the record has ended: a Sigma1 again, the bytes of the completing one included, begins afresh, and a finished responder answers it with a fresh Sigma2, not the finished handshake's (`processSigma1Locked`, `secure/sigma/protocol.go:912-1096`; review II, R2-P4-fr-sec-01). Until then the record stands in that span — through the singleton handler until the success report's acknowledgement, through a provider for the rest of the adapter's TTL, which is past the point where matter.js would begin afresh — and such a Sigma1, when it passes the receive rules, is acknowledged only, or dropped when it repeats the recorded bytes; that over TCP no success report waits for an acknowledgement, so that the span begins at the completion, is the fix's note and was not read further (unverified). By design (review II, R2-P4-rr-sec-04, R2-P4-fr-sec-01 and R2-P4-fr-sec-03, with owner decisions 51 and 70): one record per initiator and exchange keeps a handshake in progress for its Sigma3; a completed handshake's record answers no Sigma3 — one that passes the receive rules, the completing bytes over the completing route included, is acknowledged, not answered, and reaches no handler (`dispatchSigma3`, `bridge/securechannel.go:656-737`; review II, phase 7, decision 284), as in matter.js, where it is a duplicate on the live exchange or an opening message SecureChannel does not take (`MessageExchange.ts:501-511`, `SecureChannelProtocol.ts:152-153`); while the success report waits, a retransmitted Sigma3 is acknowledged as a duplicate and not processed, or — when the counter window no longer knows it — refused on receive, since it acknowledges the Sigma2 and not the report, and the report's own retransmission serves the peer (decision 277); a message that begins nothing takes no handshake's place and is acknowledged, not answered. Who sees it: the sender of a Sigma1 that begins nothing under the initiator node id and exchange id of a handshake in progress or completed gets an acknowledgement here when no reply of the handshake waits or the message acknowledges it — otherwise nothing, as in matter.js — and, in matter.js, a failure report from the CASE server on the live exchange or, once the exchange has ended, from a fresh handshake. Pinned by `bridge:TestSigma1ThatBeginsNothingKeepsACompletedHandshake`, `TestSigma3OfACompletedHandshakeIsAcknowledgedOnly`, `TestMessagesUnderAHandshakeInProgressChangeNothing`, `TestAcknowledgingMessagesUnderAHandshakeInProgressChangeNothing`, `TestSigma1OverARecordIsJudgedOnce`, `TestSigma1AgainAfterCompletionBeginsAfresh` and `TestDispatchSC_Sigma2ResumeReachesNoHandler`, and by `secure/sigma:TestRefusedSigma1LeavesTheResponderAsItWas`.

### BD-Matter-CASE-Sigma1RepeatedWhileInProgress — a Sigma1 repeated while its handshake is in progress is not judged again: the router drops it, and the responder answers it with the Sigma2 it sent

matter.js's CASE server keeps no Sigma2 to send again and no record of the Sigma1s it answered: its entry points are `onNewExchange` and `#handleSigma1` (`packages/protocol/src/session/case/CaseServer.ts:61-64`, `:102-146` at `db021da0`), and a repeated Sigma1 meets its exchange layer, which acknowledges a duplicate or kicks the retransmission of the pending message (`packages/protocol/src/protocol/MessageExchange.ts:501-511`) and sends the pending reply again to a message whose id that reply acknowledges (`:512-520`). This module has two steps of its own in that place. The router keeps the hash of the Sigma1 a handshake's record was made for and drops a Sigma1 of the same bytes under that initiator and exchange unanswered, its concurrent copies included (`markSigma1Replied`, `bridge/securechannel.go:1357-1372`; the drop, `:522-528`); the Sigma2 goes out again from the unsecured session's retransmission table, as any reliable reply. And `sigma.Responder` answers the Sigma1 of the handshake it has in progress, arriving again, with the Sigma2 it sent, byte for byte (`processSigma1Locked`, `secure/sigma/protocol.go:811-825`) — while that handshake is in progress only: once it finished or failed, the same Sigma1 is taken as any other (review II, R2-P4-fr-sec-01; `BD-Matter-CASE-Sigma1OverCompletedAcknowledgedOnly`). By design, the module's own: an initiator that sends one Sigma1 over several routes at once, or again before it saw the Sigma2, takes the first Sigma2 it receives, and a second Sigma2 with a random and a key of its own would fail that initiator's Sigma3 — the comments at both steps record the case that led to them; one handshake per Sigma1 is what both steps keep. No register row: neither step has a counterpart in matter.js to catch up with, as for `BD-Matter-CASE-HandshakeStateBounded`. Who sees it: the initiator of a repeated Sigma1 gets the first Sigma2 again, by retransmission or from the responder's cache, and never a second one for the same handshake. Pinned by `bridge:TestDispatchSC_Sigma1MulticastReplayDropped` and `TestCaseAdapter_Sigma1ReplayDoesNotReopenTheEstablishedGate`, and by `secure/sigma:TestProcessSigma1ConcurrentReplayDeterministic`.

### BD-Matter-CASE-EvictedSigma2HoldsSingletonRecord — through the singleton handler, a handshake whose Sigma2 lost its place in the retransmission table unacknowledged keeps its record until 60 s after the Sigma2

matter.js ends a CASE handshake by its own events: the CASE server reads Sigma3 once `sendSigma2` returned, which is at the Sigma2's acknowledgement, with the exchange's timeout (`packages/protocol/src/session/case/CaseServer.ts:266-279`; `packages/protocol/src/protocol/MessageExchange.ts:822-830`, `:872-886` at `db021da0`), a Sigma2 the exchange gives up ends the send (`:971-976`), and either way the server's `finally` closes the handshake's unsecured session (`CaseServer.ts:95-98`). The records of the handshakes the singleton handler runs end the same way (review II, R2-P4-fr-sec-02, R2-P4-fr-sec-05): at the give-up of the handshake's reply (`unsecuredReplyGivenUp`, `bridge/securechannel.go:1715-1729`), and for a Sigma2 that was acknowledged at the responder's wait for Sigma3, which is derived as matter.js derives it (`caseSigma3Wait`, `:1775-1791`: `MRP.maxPeerResponseTimeOf`, `packages/protocol/src/protocol/MRP.ts:79-120`, with `EXPECTED_CRYPTO_PROCESSING_TIME`, `packages/protocol/src/securechannel/SecureChannelMessenger.ts:55`, `:83-89`). One case has no counterpart. This module's retransmission table for the unsecured session is bounded, and a reply that loses its place there loses its retransmissions and nothing else (`unsecuredEntryLimit`, `bridge/outbound_reliable.go:310`; owner decision 23): an evicted Sigma2 was sent, is neither acknowledged nor given up, and its handshake can still complete. Its record holds until `unsecuredEntryLifetime` = 60 s after the Sigma2 was sent, the longest the table would have kept the reply (`sigma1RecordOver`, `bridge/securechannel.go:1656-1657`; `bridge/outbound_reliable.go:327`), unless the Sigma2's acknowledgement arrives, from which the wait for Sigma3 then runs. By design, the module's own: eviction costs a reply its retransmissions and nothing else, so it does not end the handshake, and the record takes the table's own lifetime as its end — a bound reused, not a number read from a reference. No register row: matter.js has no retransmission table to evict from, as for `BD-Matter-CASE-HandshakeStateBounded`. Who sees it: nobody on the wire; the device holds one record and one duplicate-detection window for up to 60 s for such a handshake. Through a provider a record ends with its adapter, and the entry does not apply. Pinned by `bridge:TestSingletonUnfinishedHandshakeEndsAtTheSigma3Wait`, whose case of a Sigma2 that is never acknowledged ends the record once the lifetime ran out, and `TestSingletonRecordEndsAtTheGiveUpOfItsReply`; an evicted Sigma2 has no case of its own in that file. The limit is in `docs/guides/limits.md`.

### BD-Matter-BooleanState-EventFollowsReadings — a projected BooleanState's StateChange follows the readings its source takes, not the attribute on the wire

matter.js emits StateChange when StateValue changes: `BooleanStateServer` reacts to `stateValue$Changed` under the ChangeEvent feature and emits the event with the new value (`packages/node/src/behaviors/boolean-state/BooleanStateServer.ts:20-28` at `b25ed960`), so the event and the attribute move together. For a BooleanState projected from a host's measurement source the bridge emits StateChange from the readings the source takes (`booleanStateEvents`, `bridge/subscribe.go:3061-3128`; `BooleanStateServer.ObservedStateValue`, `cluster/measurement/measurement.go:708-711`): a reading that differs from the last one taken emits the event, the first one included, and a source without a reading — which reads false on the wire, StateValue having no null (`L01-D09`) — emits none and is not remembered. The event and the attribute part in two cases. A reading of false taken by a source that had none — its first reading, or the next after a reading of true was lost — emits StateChange with false while StateValue stays false on the wire. And a reading of true that is lost turns StateValue to false on the wire, and back to true when the same reading returns, each time with a report and without an event. By design (review II, R2-P4-dr-app-07; recorded with R2-P4-fr-im-05): an event states what was observed, so a value the source did not read is no StateChange and the first reading is one; the attribute cannot say that there is no reading, the event can stay silent. OccupancyChanged of a projected OccupancySensing follows the same rule (`occupancyEvents`, `bridge/subscribe.go:3130`). The device kit's own server, `measurement.HeldBooleanState`, whose value the host sets, is the port of matter.js's reaction and is not under this rule. Who sees it: a controller that follows the state by StateChange alone misses a lost reading, and is told false for a sensor whose StateValue already read false. Pinned by `bridge:TestBooleanStateChangeEventFollowsObservedReadings`.

### BD-Matter-OnOff-RecallBypassesHandle — a scene recall reaches OnOff's own on and off logic, never a host's `Handle` handler

matter.js recalls a scene through the apply function each cluster registers (`packages/node/src/behaviors/scenes-management/ScenesManagementServer.ts:452`, `:902` at `db021da0`), and OnOff's (`#applySceneValues`, `packages/node/src/behaviors/on-off/OnOffServer.ts:268-289`) calls the command methods `this.on()` / `this.off()` — at once for a transition time of 0 (`:277-282`), otherwise from a timer (`:283-288`, `:297-308`) — the methods a host subclass overrides, so a host's override is reached by a recall. Here the recall reaches the server's own logic (`applySceneValues`, `cluster/onoff/server.go:549-563`, → `s.on` / `s.off`), and a handler a host installs with `Handle` for On or Off sits in `MatterInvoke` only and is not called. By design (owner decision 112): `Handle` replaces the whole command, and a recall is not a command. LevelControl needs no entry: matter.js's recall goes to the logic below its command method there too (`LevelControlServer.ts:757`, `moveToLevelLogic`). ColorControl's apply function was not read (unverified). Who sees it: a host that replaces On or Off through `Handle` and expects a scene recall to run its handler. LevelControl's case is pinned by `cluster/levelcontrol:TestSceneRecallBypassesTheHostHandler`; OnOff's has no test of its own.

### BD-Matter-FabricScopedEntryWithoutIndexRefused — an entry of a fabric-scoped list without a valid FabricIndex answers the read FAILURE for its path, as connectedhomeip

matter.js treats an entry of a fabric-scoped list whose `fabricIndex` is absent or 0 as visible to every fabric under a fabric-filtered read and serves it (`FabricFilteredListProxyHandler.#isVisible`, `packages/node/src/behavior/state/managed/values/ListManager.ts:480-481` at `db021da0`). connectedhomeip's list encoder refuses such an entry with `CHIP_ERROR_INVALID_FABRIC_INDEX` when its index is `kUndefinedFabricIndex`, 0 (`src/app/AttributeValueEncoder.h:100`, `src/lib/core/DataModelTypes.h:69` at `6170af84`), and the report engine rolls the attribute back and answers its path with that error's status (`src/app/reporting/Engine.cpp:487-498`), which is FAILURE: the error is neither an IM cluster status nor a global one (`src/app/data-model-provider/ActionReturnStatus.cpp:125-128`; `src/protocols/interaction_model/StatusCode.cpp:41-63`, `:62`; `src/lib/core/CHIPError.h:1335`). That branch has no test of an expanded path; that the same loop serves a read, a priming report and a change report is read from the loop's structure (`Engine.cpp:403-428`, not read in full: unverified). The module follows connectedhomeip: `im.MaskFabricScoped` refuses an entry without a FabricIndex or with one outside 1 to 254, and the path is answered FAILURE on every read, wildcard included, and in a subscription's priming report, re-established too, and its change reports, where the bridge otherwise leaves a failing path out. By design (owner decision 111): the scope rests on every entry naming its fabric, and the model gives every fabric-scoped entry a FabricIndex field. Who sees it: a controller reading a list whose server returned such an entry, which gets FAILURE for the path here and the entry from matter.js. Pinned by `im:TestMaskFabricScopedRefusesWhatItCannotScope`.

### BD-Matter-FabricScope-OneMaskBelowEveryServer — fabric-scoped reads are scoped by one generated table, applied to the encoded value below every server

matter.js scopes a fabric-scoped list through its managed state. The list proxy filters a fabric-filtered read to the accessing fabric's entries, and a fabric-sensitive list on every read outside a command (`createProxy`, `packages/node/src/behavior/state/managed/values/ListManager.ts:609-616` at `db021da0`). On an unfiltered read the struct's getters answer nothing for a fabric-sensitive member of another fabric's entry (`packages/node/src/behavior/state/managed/values/StructManager.ts:110-113`, `:303-306`, `:373-378`; `packages/protocol/src/action/server/AccessControl.ts:342-356`), and the encoder leaves it out (`packages/types/src/tlv/TlvObject.ts:128-134`; `packages/protocol/src/interaction/InteractionMessenger.ts:579-582`, `:866`). The module has no managed state. The dispatcher attaches the scope of a table generated from the schema snapshot (`schema.AttributeFabricScope`) to every request's read, and one function that knows no cluster applies it to the encoded value (`im.MaskFabricScoped`): the accessing fabric's entries whole, another fabric's entry without its fabric-sensitive fields, and none of another fabric's entries on a fabric-filtered read or in a fabric-sensitive list. The servers return every fabric's entries whole. A server of a cluster outside the snapshot declares its lists' scope (`contract.FabricScopeDeclarer`); for a snapshot cluster the table alone counts. By design (owner decisions 85, 110 and 113): the same rule, taken from the schema, held in one place below every server rather than in each server. Who sees it: nobody; the wire is matter.js's in every case but an entry without a FabricIndex (`BD-Matter-FabricScopedEntryWithoutIndexRefused`). Pinned by `schema:TestFabricScopeTableMatchesSnapshot`, `script/fabricscopecheck:TestEveryFabricSensitivePathHasARowAndAWalkCase` and `node:TestFabricSensitiveFieldsWithheldFromOtherFabrics`.

### BD-Matter-SessionParameters-BitmapRange — a SUPPORTED_TRANSPORTS value above 16 bits refuses the session parameters, as connectedhomeip

A SessionParameters structure whose SUPPORTED_TRANSPORTS (tag 8) value does not fit 16 bits is refused, as connectedhomeip reads it (`src/protocols/secure_channel/PairingSession.cpp:247-248` at `6170af84`, `Get(uint16_t)`). matter.js decodes the field as `TlvBitmap(TlvUInt16, …)` (`packages/protocol/src/session/pase/PaseMessages.ts:51` at `b25ed960`): the wrapper's decode keeps the flags it knows and its validation checks the number re-encoded from them, never the wire value (`packages/types/src/tlv/TlvWrapper.ts:24-34`, `packages/types/src/schema/BitmapSchema.ts:86-115`), so it accepts a 4-byte 0x10000 there (read, not run). Here `secure/sessionparams.DecodeFields` holds tag 8 to 16 bits, as every other known field to its width. By design, the module's own: the field is a uint16, and the stricter reading of the CSA reference costs nothing to a peer that sends a well-formed one. Who sees it: a peer that encodes a value above 16 bits at tag 8, refused here and accepted by matter.js. Pinned by `secure/sessionparams:TestDecodeIsStrict` (row "uint32 0x10000 at the uint16 bitmap [8]").

### BD-Matter-Subscription-ThirdFailureClosesEveryKind — the third failed update in a row ends the subscription whatever the failure

At the third failed update in a row the module ends the subscription whatever the failure (`noteSubscriptionSendError`, `bridge/subscribe.go`). matter.js counts every failure and owes the data again while the count is at most 2 (`packages/node/src/node/server/ServerSubscription.ts:564`, `:569-584` at `db021da0`), and at the third closes the subscription, leaving the session alone, only when the failure is a TransientPeerCommunicationError, NoResponseTimeoutError, NetworkError or SessionClosedError (`:590-603`; `causedBy`, `packages/general/src/util/Error.ts:58-82`); any other failure is rethrown and logged (`:605`, `:527`), the subscription stays, the update's data is dropped, and the counter stays above the limit until a report is answered (`:555-557`). The communication kinds — no answer, retransmissions run out, the session closed, a failed write — close here as there. The rest — an encode or chunking failure, a message above the TCP limit, a missing listener, an encryption failure — close here too. By design, the module's own: matter.js's choice leaves a subscriber with stale data and no signal; closing makes the controller resubscribe and prime again. Who sees it: a subscriber whose report fails three times in a row for a local reason, whose subscription ends here and stays, missing data, in matter.js. Pinned by `bridge:TestUndeliveredReportIsOneFailedUpdateParity` (the communication kind) and `TestReport_PeerUnreachable_ClosesSubscriptionWithoutMRP`.

### BD-Matter-PeerPath-TwoStacksOnePath — the device side's peer path composes two stacks, the bridge's and the client stack's

matter.js holds a peer's sessions in one set over one exchange layer: the peer's session set holds every fabric session whoever opened it (`packages/protocol/src/peer/PeerSet.ts:104`, `:108-110`, `:116-125` at `db021da0`), and `Peer.connect` first reuses the newest live session of the required transport (`packages/protocol/src/peer/Peer.ts:369-376`, `:440-448`, `:449-460`), newest meaning the highest `activeTimestamp` among the sessions neither closing nor peer-lost (`:582-602`). This module keeps two stacks, the bridge's (its server socket, `secure/operational`) and `client/` (its own socket, `exchange.Manager`), and a session lives in exactly one. `node` composes them into one unexported peer path (`node/peer_path.go`): the requirement comes from the command (Large Message → TCP), the live session of either stack that meets it and on which the peer sent last is reused, and a new session is established on the client stack, built on demand when `Config.Client` is nil (ADR 0032, Shape 1). By design (owner decision 115): the Large Message gate needs the path now, and one session layer for both roles is ADR 0032's direction, decided after review II under its own ADR. What the cut leaves is recorded in [`matter_behaviour_findings.md`](./matter_behaviour_findings.md): a session the client stack opened is served with the bridge's gates but not the rest of the bridge's server. Who sees it: a peer, only through what the cut leaves; the path itself reuses a live session of either stack and opens TCP for a Large Message command. Pinned by `node:TestPeerPathEstablishesTCPBesideAUDPSession`, `bridge:TestLivePeerSessionNewestByPeerActivity` and `client/handshake:TestStoreResumptionOneRecordForBothRoles`.

### BD-Matter-Controller-DclDownloadDestination — a URL a ledger names is fetched from public addresses only, an OTA record's over https only

matter.js hands a ledger record's OTA URL to the platform's `fetch` with the method and a timeout and no redirect option (`packages/protocol/src/dcl/DclOtaUpdateService.ts:690-693` at `db021da0`), so redirects are the platform fetch's default, and a CRL distribution point's URL the same way (`packages/protocol/src/dcl/DclCertificateService.ts:1639-1641`), with no check of the scheme in that file; the schema text it carries allows either scheme for a distribution point, "All URLs SHALL use either the http or https scheme" (`packages/types/src/dcl/device-attestation-revocation.ts:98-101`). connectedhomeip's revocation-set script fetches a distribution point with no scheme check either (`credentials/generate_revocation_set.py:356`, `:459` at `6170af84`). Here, in `controller/dcl`, without a host `Client.HTTPClient`: a URL a ledger record names (an OTA image, or a CRL distribution point over http or https) and a URL the GitHub development-certificate mirror's API answers name connect to public addresses only. Loopback, private, link-local, unspecified and multicast destinations (IPv4, IPv6, IPv4-mapped) are refused at the dial, for the URL and every redirect hop. Behind the environment's proxy, a URL or redirect hop whose host is `localhost` or such an IP address is refused before it is handed over; the host is judged as net/http sends it, lower-cased, without a trailing dot, an IPv4 address in any inet_aton-style spelling counts, a host outside ASCII is not handed to a proxy, and a host name behind a proxy is the proxy's to resolve. Other special-use ranges (100.64.0.0/10, 64:ff9b::/96, 2002::/16) are not refused. A ledger record's OTA URL is fetched over `https:` only. A URL the host supplies itself (`OTAVersions.DownloadHostURL`, which `softwareupdate.Images.UpdateInfoFromURL` uses) keeps http and any address. `Client.AllowPrivateDestinations` admits the refused destinations, read from the client of the download (the `TestClient` for a test-net record); a host `HTTPClient` is the host's policy and is not guarded. By design (owner decisions 116 and 116a): these URLs come from ledger data, not from the host; a distribution point keeps http, as the schema allows and both references fetch it. Who sees it: a lab whose ledger names hosts on its local network, which sets `AllowPrivateDestinations`; a ledger record whose OTA URL is `http:`, whose download fails. Pinned by `controller/dcl:TestPublicDestination`, `TestOTADownloadConnectsToPublicDestinationsOnly`, `TestOTADownloadByURLSchemesAndDestinations` and `TestGuardJudgesTheHostAsSent`, and by `controller/softwareupdate:TestImagesDownloadByOrigin`.

### BD-Matter-OwedFabricEvents — a fabric's rolled-back add or update is recorded in the store until the fabric hooks have heard it

matter.js records nothing durably about a fabric event still to be emitted. `FabricManager`'s construction loads `"fabrics"` and `"nextFabricIndex"` and adds each fabric, reading no pending or commit marker (`packages/protocol/src/fabric/FabricManager.ts:54-80` at `db021da0`); the fail-safe state is in memory, its only storage access `persistFabrics()` (`packages/protocol/src/common/FailsafeContext.ts:142`); a fail-safe rollback deletes an added fabric or restores an updated one (`FailsafeContext.ts:271-320`), and the events are emitted in the call chain of the change (`FabricManager.ts:215-217`, `:272`). connectedhomeip keeps one durable record, a commit marker written before a fabric's commit (`src/credentials/FabricTable.cpp:1952` at `6170af84`) and cleared when the commit returns (`:2079`); at init an aborted commit's fabric is deleted (`:1129-1148`), and `Server::Init` delivers the owed notification later, as a removal (an update is treated as an add), before it clears the marker (`src/app/server/Server.cpp:662-695`). Here `RollbackFabric` records the owed event, the fabric's removal for a pending add and its update for a pending update with the fabric's identity, in its own write, and for a pending update deletes the fabric's resumption records in the same write; `node.Start` delivers every owed event to the fabric hooks and then acknowledges it (`deliverOwedFabricEvents`, `node/node.go`; `store.Fabrics.OwedFabricEvents`, `AckOwedFabricEvent`), so a hook may hear an event twice and misses none. Ahead of matter.js, which has no start-up revert and no durable marker, and wider than connectedhomeip, whose marker covers an aborted commit only and only as a removal (owner decision 109). Who sees it: a host whose fabric hooks keep state of their own; after a stop between a rollback and its hooks, the hooks hear the event at the next start. Pinned by `node:TestOwedFabricRemovalOutlivesAProcessThatNeverStarted` and `TestOwedFabricRemovalReplaysAfterACrashBehindTheHook`, and by the storetest case `fabrics/rollback-owes-event`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js records an owed fabric event durably.

### BD-Matter-OTA-AttestedIdentityKept — the controller keeps a node's attested vendor and product and logs a QueryImage that names another pair

matter.js checks a QueryImage only against the peer's self-reported BasicInformation (`#validatePeerDetails`, `packages/node/src/behavior/system/software-update/SoftwareUpdateManager.ts:368-373` at `db021da0`), and its attestation validator returns only `{ dacPublicKey, findings }` (`packages/protocol/src/certificate/DeviceAttestationValidator.ts:644`, taken at `packages/protocol/src/peer/ControllerCommissioningFlow.ts:1299-1300`), so no attested pair is kept — none was found in the files searched. connectedhomeip's provider marks both ids unused (`src/app/clusters/ota-provider/OTAProviderCluster.cpp:189-190` at `6170af84`), so there is no behaviour to follow. This module keeps the attested vendor/product pair on the peer record (`controller/client.Record.AttestedVendorID`, `AttestedProductID`), set only when attestation verified the DAC chain against the trust store and no error finding stands — nil without a trust store, for a failed attestation and for an error finding the policy accepted (owner decision 119) — and nil for unknown, and `controller/softwareupdate` logs `ota.manager.attested_identity_mismatch` when a query names another pair; the answer to the query is unchanged, no query is refused (owner decision 105: a refusal rule only after a further read of the references). Ahead of matter.js. Who sees it: an operator reading the controller's log, which names a node whose QueryImage differs from the pair its attestation showed. Pinned by `controller/client:TestRecordAttestedProduct`, `TestRecordKeepsTheAttestedProduct`, `controller/commissioner:TestAttestedPairWithheld` and `controller/softwareupdate:TestNoteAttestedIdentity`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js keeps the attested identity.

Since review II decision 214 (R2-P6-sec-1803) the pair is recorded only when, beyond the rules above, the attestation chain ends in a root the trust store holds as production (`attestation.Result.TestPAA` false) and the Certification Declaration is not signed by the Matter test CD signer (`Result.TestCDSigner` false). Under a store that accepts test certificates both raise no finding, and their private keys are public, so a pair attested by them is anyone's to claim. `TestPAA` is the store's `Production` flag, so the pair is as good as that flag (`BD-Matter-Controller-DclProductionBytes`). The mismatch at QueryImage stays one Warn line; no rule is added there. Since owner decision 193 a DAC without a ProductID, a PAI ProductID other than the DAC's and, with a clock, an expired DAC are error findings, so the pair is withheld for them too. Tests: `controller/attestation:TestResultCarriesTheTrustFacts`, `controller/commissioner:TestAttestedPairNeedsProductionTrust`, `controller/client:TestRecordKeepsTheAttestedProduct`.

### BD-Matter-SealedAtRest — the store seals its secret columns under a host-supplied key that lives outside the database

matter.js stores the operational keypair, the IPK and the resumption secret as plain JSON through drivers with no protection (`Fabric.config`, `packages/protocol/src/fabric/Fabric.ts:172`, `:175-176`, written by `persistFabrics`, `packages/protocol/src/fabric/FabricManager.ts:194-197`; `sharedSecret`, `packages/protocol/src/session/SessionManager.ts:102`, `:907` at `db021da0`). Its one encryption at rest is the DoorLock's credential data, AES-128-CCM by default (`packages/node/src/behaviors/door-lock/DoorLockServer.ts:103-105`, `:248-250`), under a key that is a nonvolatile field of the same State and is persisted next to the ciphertext (`:1570-1574`). connectedhomeip stores the operational key through plain storage by default (`src/app/server/Server.h:295-300`, `src/crypto/PersistentStorageOperationalKeystore.cpp:83` at `6170af84`) and offers the `Crypto::OperationalKeystore` interface as the hook for a protected keystore (`src/crypto/OperationalKeystore.h:28-31`), for the operational key only. This module seals the store's secret columns and settings under a host-supplied `store.Sealer` whose key lives outside the database (`store/seal.go`; `store.NewAESGCMSealer`, AES-256-GCM, a random nonce per value, a 32-byte key); each value is bound to its table, column and row, so a value moved to another row or column does not open, and the upgrade seals every clear row in one transaction. Sealing is opt-in. It keeps a copy of the file from giving the secrets without the key; it does not authenticate the database, and an older sealed value still opens. Ahead of matter.js (owner decision 108). Who sees it: a host that passes a sealer; a store without the sealer reads a sealed value as an error. Pinned by `store:TestNewSealedSealsAClearDatabase` and `TestSealedStoreWrongKeyOrNoSealer`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js seals fabric secrets at rest.

Review II, phase 6a (owner decisions 130–132): the first `NewSealed` marks the database with a sealed canary in a reserved `matter_settings` row; every `NewSealed` checks the key on it, and a marked database refuses clear secret rows and a sealer-less store's secret writes (a `store.New` open checks nothing until its first secret write); Erase drops it. The canary is a mark and a wrong-key check, not tamper protection. A new secret column or setting therefore needs an upgrade step that seals it in a marked database (owner decision 157; `TestSecretsAddedAfterV11ShipAnUpgradeStep`). `store.Reseal` rotates the key in one transaction, canary last, then scrubs; a Reseal whose scrub does not finish is `ErrScrubIncomplete` and the scrub stays owed. A `NewSealed` whose scrub cannot finish leaves the store open and the scrub owed (`Store.ScrubOwed`). Scrub truncates a kept rollback journal (`journal_size_limit = 0` for the run). The Rotating Device Identifier's unique id is a sealed setting.

Review II, phase 6b (owner decisions 194, 195): the controller's node registry (`controller/client/sqlstore`) carries its own seal canary in the reserved `matter_client_metadata` row `sqlstore.seal_canary` (schema v3), with the store's rules — opened first by every `NewSealed`, a clear secret value refused in a marked registry, `sqlstore.New` refusing secret writes into it. The controller's factory reset drops it once the registry is empty; v3's Down refuses a registry the canary marks, as the store's v10 Down refuses a database its canary marks. An unfinished owed scrub opens the registry (`Store.ScrubOwed`, owner decision 132). `sqlstore.Reseal` rotates the registry alone; `controller.Reseal` rotates a controller's database — both stores — in one transaction, each store's canary after its own values (store: values, canary, owed; registry: values, canary, owed), and scrubs once; with one commit that order carries no state.

### BD-chip-DoorLock-RecordSource — GetUser and GetCredentialStatus answer a record's creator and last-modified fabric only when Matter made the change, as connectedhomeip

matter.js implements both commands and answers the stored indices of a record (`packages/node/src/behaviors/door-lock/DoorLockServer.ts:375-376`, `:598-599` at `db021da0`) and null for an empty slot (`:352-365`, `:583-591`); it models no record made outside Matter: the creator and last-modified fabric of a user and a credential are non-nullable fields with no creation source beside them (`packages/node/src/behaviors/door-lock/LockAuth.ts:67-71`, `:97-101`), and every write path takes the fabric of the invoking context (`DoorLockServer.ts:935-941`). connectedhomeip sets each index only when the creation, respectively the last modification, came through Matter IM, and leaves it null otherwise (`src/app/clusters/door-lock-server/CodegenIntegration.cpp:570-578`, `:967-974` at `6170af84`). `cluster/lock` follows connectedhomeip: each record keeps whether its creation and its last modification came through Matter (`fabricThroughMatter`, `cluster/lock/users.go`, `cluster/lock/credentials.go`), and a record a host seeds in `DoorLockConfig.Initial` answers null; rows stored before schema v10 take "through Matter", so a record seeded before then answers the index it was seeded with. Who sees it: a controller reading a host-seeded user or credential. Pinned by `cluster/lock:TestParity_DoorLock_RecordSource`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js models a record's source.

### BD-Matter-Subscription-ReportWaitBound — the wait for an ongoing report's StatusResponse runs from the send and adds a term for the peer's retransmissions

matter.js waits for the peer's StatusResponse to a report with `waitForSuccess`, giving no timeout of its own while the subscription is open (`packages/protocol/src/interaction/InteractionMessenger.ts:839-844`, `:221-227` at `db021da0`), so the exchange's maximum peer response time bounds the wait (`calculateMaximumPeerResponseTime`, `packages/protocol/src/protocol/MessageExchange.ts:872-886`), and its expiry is a `PeerMessageMissingError` (`:892-894`). The peer's retransmission term is 0 there, `includeMaximumSendingTime` being passed undefined (`MessageExchange.ts:882`; `packages/protocol/src/protocol/MessageChannel.ts:231-249`, `:240`): over UDP the bound is this node's own retransmission schedule plus 2 s of expected processing plus 5 s (`packages/protocol/src/protocol/MRP.ts:94-109`, `:55`, `:61`; `maxResponseTimeOf`, `:198-224`), over TCP and BLE max(30 s, processing) plus 5 s (`:90-92`, `:111-113`). The wait starts once `exchange.send` returned, at the report's acknowledgement (`MessageExchange.ts:822-830`); a missing acknowledgement fails the send (`:796-798`). The module takes the same formula and the same failure kind with two differences: one timer runs from the send (`awaitReportAnswer`, `bridge/subscribe.go`), and over UDP the bound adds a term for the peer's retransmission schedule, on one base interval and without a sender pad, to cover the time before the acknowledgement (`chunkStatusResponseTimeout`); over a reliable connection it is the 35 s above. By design, the module's own (a coordinator decision of review II, phase 5b): one timer from the send rather than a second wait started at the acknowledgement. Who sees it: a peer that acknowledges a report and never answers it, which becomes a failed update here later than in matter.js, by the peer term less the time its acknowledgement took. Whether the module's own retransmissions can outlast the peer term, so that the bound comes out shorter than matter.js's, was not read or measured (unverified). The matter.js half was read again in review II, phase 6a (R2-P6-par-0707): `MessageExchange.ts:878-885` passes `undefined` for `includeMaximumSendingTime` (`:882`), `MessageChannel.ts:239-240` then hands no `peerSessionParameters`, and `MRP.ts:102` makes that term 0 — matter.js's wait has no peer term. Pinned by `bridge:TestChunkStatusResponseTimeoutOverAConnection`.

### BD-Matter-OTAImage-HiddenUntilVerified — a streamed OTA image is not listed or opened while it is checked

matter.js stores a downloaded image under its final file name and verifies it afterwards: the download hands the response body to `store` (`packages/protocol/src/dcl/DclOtaUpdateService.ts:703` at `db021da0`), which writes the blob under the final name (`:558-559`, `:569-576`), then verifies it (`#verifyUpdate`, `:388-408`) and writes its metadata, deleting both on a failure (`:581-592`); the file keeps no set of names still being checked, and `find` lists the blob keys and reads their headers (`:1098-1122`). That a concurrent `find` sees an unverified image there is inferred from these lines; whether a blob is visible while it streams was not read (unverified). The module mirrors the order — write, then verify, then the record, both removed on a failure — and hides the name for the time of the checks: `downloadInto` hides it (`hide`, `controller/softwareupdate/images.go`), `Find` skips a hidden name and `Open` refuses it (`isHidden`). By design, the module's own: an image is offered or served only once its checks passed. Who sees it: a caller of `Find` or `Open`, or a node's QueryImage, during a download — it does not see the image until the checks end. Pinned by `controller/softwareupdate:TestImagesStreamedImageHiddenUntilVerified`.

### BD-Matter-OTAImage-LedgerChecksumRequired — an update from the ledger is made available only when its record states the whole-file checksum

matter.js checks the checksum only when the record carries one, `if (updateInfo.otaChecksum)`, and otherwise validates the image by its header, payload size and file size and stores or reuses it (`packages/protocol/src/dcl/DclOtaUpdateService.ts:394-408`, `:433-439`, `:569-574` at `db021da0`; `packages/protocol/src/ota/OtaImageReader.ts:88-107`); the ledger's empty checksum becomes undefined before that (`packages/protocol/src/dcl/DclClient.ts:394-395`), and its applicability filter asks for no checksum (`DclOtaUpdateService.ts:786-819`). The module refuses the missing checksum: `Images.DownloadUpdate` refuses a production or test-net record without `otaChecksum` with `ErrOTA` and a `dcl.ota.no_checksum` line before it downloads or reuses anything, and a stored prod or test image whose provenance record (`<file>.origin`) names neither a ledger checksum it was checked against nor the host is not offered by `Images.CheckForUpdate`, not opened by `Images.Open` and no candidate of `Manager.UpdateExistsFor`; the file is kept, and a later reuse under a record with the checksum binds it (`controller/softwareupdate/images.go`, `controller/softwareupdate/manager.go`). `ImagesConfig.AllowUnverifiedLedgerImages` admits these and logs each admission (`dcl.ota.no_checksum_admitted`); an image the host supplies itself needs no checksum. The rest mirrors matter.js: an absent checksum type is SHA-256, and an unsupported type and a mismatch are errors (`DclOtaUpdateService.ts:397-400`, `OtaImageReader.ts:88-93`; `dcl/ota.go`). By design (owner decision 117): matter.js's own record type documents that both checksum fields "SHALL be provided if the OtaUrl field is populated" (`packages/types/src/dcl/device-software-version.ts:103-109`, `:111-113`), and the CSA's post-certification check reports a valid record with an `otaUrl` and no checksum keys and compares the downloaded image with them (connectedhomeip `src/python_testing/post_certification_tests/production_device_checks.py:287-289`, `:306-323` at `6170af84`); the option covers test ledgers and laboratories. Whether the specification text makes the checksum mandatory was not read (unverified). Who sees it: a host whose ledger record carries no checksum, which gets no update without the option; images stored by a release before the provenance record, which are served again once a ledger update with the checksum reuses them. Pinned by `controller/softwareupdate:TestImagesRequireTheLedgersChecksum`, `TestManagerOffersOnlyServableStoredImages` and `TestImagesProvenanceNamesItsBytes`.

### BD-chip-SessionEvictionFabricFirst — at a full session id space the least recently active session of the fabric that holds the most sessions is closed

matter.js closes the least recently used session of the node when every session id is taken: `findOldestInactiveSession` calls `#leastRecentlyUsedSession(() => true)` (`packages/protocol/src/session/SessionManager.ts:564-572`, `:567`; `:553-562` at `db021da0`), which filters by no fabric; it bounds sessions per peer only (`:201-205`) — `MAX_SESSIONS_PER_PEER`, `:205`, is that file's only cap constant, and a bound in another matter.js file was not read. connectedhomeip evicts from the fabric that holds the most sessions first and uses last activity only as the final tie-break (`src/transport/SecureSessionTable.cpp:228-337`, DefaultEvictionPolicy, Key1 `:239-244`, Key6 `:333-335` at `6170af84`), in a pool sized for three CASE sessions per fabric (`src/lib/core/CHIPConfig.h:808-821`); it counts by `GetFabricIndex()` equality, sessions without a fabric included (`SecureSessionTable.cpp:149-151`). When live sessions hold every session id, this module closes the least recently active session of the fabric that holds the most live sessions — PASE sessions and sessions not yet adopted by a fabric count as one group — so one fabric's administrator who fills the id space evicts its own sessions, not another fabric's idle ones (`secure/operational/manager.go` `leastRecentlyActiveLocked`). It applies chip's first and last key only; Key2 `:246-257` (the hint's fabric), Key3 `:259-265` (the peer holding the most), Key4 `:286-303` (the hinted peer) and Key5 `:305-330` (session state) are not applied — re-read them at the next pin lift; Key3 is the one a later refinement could add. The trigger is the module's id space (`SessionIDSpace = 0xFFFE`), not chip's pool. Review II, R2-P6-bound-0107, owner decision 134. Pinned by `secure/operational:TestAllocateIDAtAFullTableEvictsInsideTheFabricHoldingTheMost`. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js chooses the session it closes by fabric.

### BD-chip-RotatingDeviceIdentifier — the commissionable record carries a Rotating Device Identifier when the host enables it

matter.js puts no RI among the commissionable TXT values (`packages/protocol/src/advertisement/mdns/CommissionableMdnsAdvertisement.ts:84-97` at `b25ed960`) and reads RI only as a scanner (`packages/protocol/src/common/Scanner.ts:46-47`, `:71`). With `node.Commissioning.RotatingDeviceID` the commissionable record carries RI as connectedhomeip derives it (`src/setup_payload/AdditionalDataPayloadGenerator.cpp:81-111`, `:113-127` at `6170af84`), off by default as chip's `chip_enable_rotating_device_id = false` (`src/setup_payload/BUILD.gn:19-22`). The lifetime counter is advanced and persisted before each advertised window (own, enhanced, basic) — this module's rule; connectedhomeip advances it at every start of its commissioning advertisement — a window's open and each new listen after a failed PASE attempt (`src/app/server/CommissioningWindowManager.cpp:160-173`, `:313`, `:502-507`) — where `CHIP_ENABLE_ADDITIONAL_DATA_ADVERTISING` is set (`:504`; default false, `src/platform/BUILD.gn:43`), and persists it on every advance (`LifetimePersistedCounter.h:92-99`). The unique id is random and persisted where chip's generic platform keeps a compile-time constant in RAM (`GenericConfigurationManagerImpl.h:128-130`), and sealed under `store.NewSealed`; the RI is not carried on BLE. Before, the record carried an RI derived from vendor, product, serial number and label with counter 0 — constant and computable; `mdns.DeriveUniqueIDFromIdentity` is deprecated with it. Review II, R2-P6-sec-0207, owner decision 137. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js advertises an RI.

### BD-Matter-TcpSendBounded — a TCP send fails when its frame is not handed to the socket within 30 s

matter.js awaits the socket's write callback for a send with no timeout (`packages/nodejs/src/net/NodeJsTcpConnection.ts:105-115`, `packages/protocol/src/transport/tcp/TcpChannel.ts:125` at `b25ed960`), so a peer that takes nothing holds the sender. Here `tcp.Conn.Send` fails when its frame is not handed to the socket within 30 s — an absolute deadline per send, renewed by the next send — wrapping `os.ErrDeadlineExceeded`, and closes the connection (`transport/tcp/conn.go`). 30 s is chosen, with no reference; 64 000 bytes in 30 s is no constraint on a live link. Review II, R2-P6-bound-0202. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js bounds a send.

### BD-Matter-ResumptionRecordsPerFabric — the store keeps at most 16 of the CASE responder's and 1024 of the CASE client's resumption records per fabric

The store keeps at most 16 of the CASE responder's resumption records per fabric and, when one more peer's record is written, evicts the fabric's responder record the store wrote longest ago — by its own write sequence (`write_seq`, schema v11), not the clock; a rewrite counts as a write (`store/resumption.go` UpsertResumption, `store/memstore`; host backends are held to it by storetest `resumption/cap-per-fabric` and `resumption/cap-counts-responders-only`). It follows neither reference: matter.js keeps one resumption record per peer without a cap (`packages/protocol/src/session/SessionManager.ts:261-262`, `:912-913` at `db021da0`); connectedhomeip caps the node at `CHIP_CONFIG_CASE_SESSION_RESUME_CACHE_SIZE` = 3 × `CHIP_CONFIG_MAX_FABRICS` records in one index (`DefaultSessionResumptionStorage.h:38-42`) and, when it is full, drops the entry at its head — the peer first saved longest ago of any fabric; a re-save keeps the entry's place (`DefaultSessionResumptionStorage.cpp:55-90`, `:95-99` at `6170af84`; `src/lib/core/CHIPConfig.h:1336-1343`). Per fabric, because a fabric's administrator mints the node ids its peers authenticate with and must not grow or evict another fabric's records. Review II, R2-P6-bound-0106, owner decision 134. The cap bounds the records a peer makes the node write by connecting to it, the responder's. The records the CASE client of `client/handshake` writes as initiator (`client/handshake.StoreResumption`: a controller's, the node's client stack's) are neither counted nor evicted by it. A controller's are of peers its host chose. The node's client stack also connects to the provider an AnnounceOTAProvider names and to a camera's WebRTC requestor (`node/peer_path.go`); such a record is written only after a CASE handshake the target completed with a NOC of the fabric for that node id. The node's handshakes that re-establish former subscriptions (`node/security.go` caseInitiatorProvider) store their record without the role, so it counts as the responder's. The client's records have a per-fabric bound of their own, 1024, the least recently written evicted first; each role evicts only its own records (owner decision 273; storetest `resumption/cap-per-role`). The store keeps one record per peer for both roles, and the record carries the role of its last write (`store.ResumptionRecord.Initiator`, the column `initiator` of schema v12); a rewrite by the other role takes that role. A record stored before v12 did not record its role and counts as the responder's, so it stays under the cap. Review II, R2-P7-sec-01, owner decision 270. Register row above; the row closes when matter.js bounds its resumption records.

### BD-Matter-CASEServer-ResumptionRecordSingleUse — the device's resumption record is consumed when a resume is accepted

The device's resumption record is consumed when a resume is accepted. The responder claims the record's id; concurrent Sigma1 presenting it take the full handshake. The record is replaced when the session is installed, before Sigma2_Resume is sent, and the host hears `OnSessionOpened` then. matter.js sends Sigma2_Resume, adds the session once the send is acknowledged and saves the record after the initiator's success report (`packages/protocol/src/session/case/CaseServer.ts:196-201`, `:211`, `:216`, `:219`; `packages/protocol/src/protocol/MessageExchange.ts:822-830` at `db021da0`). Copies arriving during that wait resume again. connectedhomeip saves the record and activates the session at the success report (`src/protocols/secure_channel/CASESession.cpp:2315-2339`, `src/protocols/secure_channel/PairingSession.cpp:62-66` at `6170af84`). A session whose Sigma2_Resume is not acknowledged is closed: when its retransmissions are spent, when its 60 s on the unsecured session run out, when its send fails, or when its handshake is ended. That is matter.js's outcome, which closes on a failed send including a missing acknowledgement (`CaseServer.ts:202-206`). The close is a liveness rule, not a defence: an acknowledgement authenticates nothing. An entry evicted from the full unsecured retransmit table leaves its session to the idle reaper. An initiator's failure StatusReport acknowledges the Sigma2_Resume and keeps the installed session, as in matter.js (`:211`, `:216`; its handler's `finally` closes only the unsecured session, `:95-98`; owner decision 232); connectedhomeip discards it (`CASESession.cpp:2583-2593`, `:2609-2612`). A resume whose session is not installed releases the responder's claim of its resumption id (`sigma.Sigma1ProcessResult.Claim`, `sigma.ResumeClaim.Release`), so the id resumes again; a claim stays while its install is under way, and for the life of the process when the record could not be replaced (a persist failure, `node/security.go` `resumeClaims`). Review II, R2-P6-sec-3320, owner decisions 198, 231, 232, 243. Pinned by `bridge:TestR2P6Sec3320Closes`, `TestR2P6Sec3320KeepsAcknowledged`, `TestR2P6Sec3320Ends`, `TestR2P6Sec3320Release`, `fabrictest:TestR2P6Sec3320Replay`, `TestR2P6Sec3320Concurrent`.

### BD-Matter-UdpOrderedBacklogLongestSubqueue — a full ordered backlog of a session gives a place to the source address holding fewer datagrams

No reference line: neither reference was found to hold a session's datagrams in such a backlog (review II, the verify of R2-P6-bound-0211: not performable); this is the module's own rule over its own queue (`transport/udp/ordered.go`). A session's ordered backlog holds 256 datagrams. When it is full, a datagram of a source address holding fewer queued datagrams than the largest holder takes the place of that holder's newest; otherwise it is dropped. Ports are merged and IPv4-mapped addresses unmapped. A source alone may fill the backlog; a flood from any number of ports of one address cannot keep the genuine peer out, and against a few flooding addresses the peer keeps at least a 1/(addresses+1) share. Not held off: a flooder that forges the peer's address, and one that changes its source address per datagram (256 addresses leave the peer one place, more none); the shared in-flight budget (`maxConcurrentDispatch`) is not per source. Queued datagrams of one source never change their relative order — a session sees a loss, which MRP repairs, never an inversion. Review II, R2-P6-bound-0211.

### BD-Matter-AccessControl-AuxiliaryAdminPerFabric — AuxiliaryAccessUpdated names, per changed fabric, the node of that fabric's own change

matter.js names one administrator for every fabric a synchronisation pass changed — from the provider's context, else its own (`packages/node/src/behaviors/access-control/AccessControlServer.ts:524-536` at `b25ed960`). The module names, per changed fabric, the node of that fabric's own change: a change a Groupcast command's batch deferred keeps its own request's node, the closing command's node goes only to its own fabric, and a fabric changed by another fabric's request names none, so a fabric-sensitive event never carries another fabric's node id (`cluster/core/access_control_auxiliary.go` syncAuxiliary); a change without a request — a reload's, a forget's — neither records nor displaces the node a request recorded. For this per-fabric rule no observable difference was found where matter.js emits (inferred, not run). Which node id is named — the request's CASE subject rather than the fabric's root node id (`AccessControlServer.ts:275-283`) — is `BD-Matter-AuxiliaryAccessAdminNode`. The kept "Mirrors matter.js #syncAuxAcl" on syncAuxiliary covers the recomputation only. Review II, R2-P6-conc-1007.

### BD-chip-FabricLabelBytes — UpdateFabricLabel counts the label's bytes, as connectedhomeip

matter.js counts a label's UTF-8 bytes since #4995: the string constraint counts `Bytes.utf8Length` (`packages/node/src/behavior/state/validation/constraint.ts:203-206` at `b25ed960`), `TlvString` measures `byteLengthOf(value)` (`packages/types/src/tlv/TlvString.ts:69-77`), the fabric holds its label to `Fabric.MAX_LABEL_BYTES = 32` (`packages/protocol/src/fabric/Fabric.ts:194`, `:664`, `:727`), and `FabricManager` shortens a stored label over it at load (`packages/protocol/src/fabric/FabricManager.ts:39-48`, `:86`, `:93-102`); the model says "max 32" (`operational-credentials.element.ts:124`). Until db021da0 it counted UTF-16 code units, which is what this entry was written against. connectedhomeip counts bytes: `label.size() > 32` on the decoded `CharSpan` answers InvalidCommand (`src/app/clusters/operational-credentials-server/OperationalCredentialsCluster.cpp:711`, `:716`, with a TODO naming ConstraintError at `:713-714`), and the fabric table holds a label of at most 32 bytes (`src/credentials/FabricTable.h:48` `kFabricLabelMaxLengthInBytes = 32`, the 33-byte buffer `:237`; the size test `FabricTable.cpp:2142` at `6170af84`). This module counts bytes (`cluster/core/operational_credentials.go`, UpdateFabricLabel), as both references now do, and answers an over-long label with ConstraintError where chip answers InvalidCommand. In matter.js the request field is `Label "max 32"` and the constraint counts bytes, so an over-long label is a constraint error of the request before `updateFabricLabel` runs and `fabric.setLabel`'s ImplementationError (`OperationalCredentialsServer.ts:405`, `Fabric.ts:194-198`) is not reached from the wire; the request validation call and the ConstraintError-to-status mapping were not read end to end (unverified, inferred). The entry stays until that path is read: if matter.js answers ConstraintError, the remaining difference is chip's status alone and the entry closes. Reason (owner decision 155): the label is stored and served as connectedhomeip's data model holds it, at most 32 bytes. Review II, N4-coresec-1; matter.js's side re-read at the pin lift to b25ed960 (unit P2b-A).

Review II, phase 6b (R2-P6-par-1854, owner decision 155): the controller's own fabric label is held to the same bound. matter.js's `Fabric.setLabel` bounds the label at 32 UTF-8 bytes since #4995 (`packages/protocol/src/fabric/Fabric.ts:194`, `MAX_LABEL_BYTES` `:727` at `b25ed960`; at `db021da0` 32 UTF-16 code units, `:193-201`, set before it persists; the creation check `:654-657` there). `controller/commissioner` bounds it at `MaxLabelLength` = 32 bytes at creation, at load and in `SetLabel`, and a changed label is persisted before it takes effect. Pinned by `controller/commissioner:TestFabricLabelIsBoundInBytes`.

Neither reference refuses a read from inside a cluster: matter.js decides by `session.authorityAt` alone (`packages/protocol/src/action/server/AttributeReadResponse.ts:468` at `db021da0`; the value is a state lookup, `:301`, and the file has no try/catch), connectedhomeip by the ACL (`src/app/reporting/Engine.cpp:65-89` at `6170af84`). ### BD-Matter-Spec-HostPatchJudgedWhole — a host `SetAttributes` is judged against the state its whole patch makes

matter.js validates each assigned property alone against the siblings assigned before it (`packages/node/src/behavior/state/managed/values/StructManager.ts:278-291` at `db021da0`), so it accepts an incoherent patch in a suitable order that this module refuses, and refuses a coherent one in an unsuitable order. matter.js moves the hardware inside the command (`packages/node/src/behaviors/door-lock/DoorLockServer.ts:1033-1041` at `db021da0`) and saves at the transaction commit after it (`packages/protocol/src/action/server/CommandInvokeResponse.ts:493`); a failed commit answers FAILURE (`:509-520`) with the state rolled back (`packages/node/src/behavior/state/managed/Datasource.ts:1331-1341`; that the lock's state is that datasource is inferred) while the LockOperation event already emitted stays. go-fabric answers FAILURE too but keeps the physical outcome: the records keep what the operation did (a DisposableUser stays disabled), the auto-relock follows the lock, the save error is logged (`matter.doorlock.records_not_saved`), and the next commit saves the records (`cluster/lock/doorlock_server.go` `commitMoved`). Chosen because the door moved: a rolled-back DisposableUser would open it again, and matter.js's armed relock cannot fire on a rolled-back Locked state (`DoorLockServer.ts:971`), leaving the door unlocked.
